\noindent{\sphinxincludegraphics[height=200\sphinxpxdimen]{{vrna}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The core of the \sphinxstylestrong{ViennaRNA Package} (Lorenz \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id29}{2011}{]}, Hofacker \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id19}{1994}{]})
is formed by a collection of routines for the prediction and comparison
of RNA secondary structures. These routines can be accessed through
stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone programs, such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAfold}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAdistance} etc., which should
be sufficient for most users. For those who wish to develop their own
programs we provide \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}, a C\sphinxhyphen{}library that can be linked to your own
code or even used in your scripts and pipelines through our {\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{SWIG Wrappers}}}}
for {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python}}}} and Perl 5.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The latest version of the package including source code and html
versions of the documentation can be found at
\sphinxurl{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA} and \sphinxurl{https://github.com/ViennaRNA/ViennaRNA}.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Installation}
\label{\detokenize{install:installation}}\label{\detokenize{install::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ViennaRNA Package comes with a variety of executable programs
and scripts as well as a C\sphinxhyphen{}library that provides access to our
implemented algorithms. Moreover, the C\sphinxhyphen{}library is wrapped to
scripting languages such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Perl 5}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Python}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For best portability the ViennaRNA package uses the GNU
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{autoconf}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{automake}} tools to prepare the compilation
from source code. Read the {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Configuration}}}} section
\sphinxstyleemphasis{before} you install our software if you intend to deviate
from the default setup.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Installing from Source}
\label{\detokenize{install:installing-from-source}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The instructions below are for installing the ViennaRNA package
from source. However, pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled binaries for various Linux
distributions, as well as for Windows users are available at the
\sphinxhref{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/\#download}{download section}
of the official ViennaRNA homepage.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{install:binary-packages}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Binary packages}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{install:using-conda}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Using conda}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{install:python-interface-only}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Python interface only}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Quick\sphinxhyphen{}start}
\label{\detokenize{install:quick-start}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually you’ll just download the \sphinxhref{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/\#source\_code\_packages}{latest source tarball},
unpack, configure and make. To do this type:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{tar} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{zxvf} \PYG{n}{ViennaRNA}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.6}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.4}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{tar}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{gz}
\PYG{n}{cd} \PYG{n}{ViennaRNA}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.6}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.4}
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{configure}
\PYG{n}{make}
\PYG{n}{sudo} \PYG{n}{make} \PYG{n}{install}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Installing from git repository}
\label{\detokenize{install:installing-from-git-repository}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also get the latest source code from \sphinxhref{https://github.com/ViennaRNA/ViennaRNA}{our git repository}
hosted at \sphinxurl{https://github.com}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/ViennaRNA/ViennaRNA.git
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, to proceed with the configuration and installation you need to perform
some additional steps \sphinxstylestrong{before} actually running the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./configure}} script:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unpack the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libsvm}} archive to allow for SVM Z\sphinxhyphen{}score regression with the
program \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNALfold}}:

\end{enumerate}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
tar\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xzf\PYG{+w}{ }src/libsvm\PYGZhy{}3.31.tar.gz\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }src
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unpack the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dlib}} archive to allow for concentration dependency computations with the
program \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAmultifold}}:

\end{enumerate}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
tar\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xjf\PYG{+w}{ }src/dlib\PYGZhy{}19.24.tar.bz2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }src
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Install the additional maintainer tools \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gengetopt}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{help2man}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flex}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xxd}},
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{swig}} if necessary. For instance, in RedHat based distributions, the following
packages need to be installed:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gengetopt}} (to generate command line parameter parsers)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{help2man}} (to generate the man pages)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{yacc}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flex}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flex\sphinxhyphen{}devel}} (to generate sources for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAforester}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vim\sphinxhyphen{}common}} (for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xxd}} program)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{swig}} (to generate the scripting language interfaces)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblapacke}} (for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAxplorer}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblapack}}  (for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAxplorer}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fortran}} compiler, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gcc\sphinxhyphen{}gfortran}} (for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAxplorer}})

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, run the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{autoconf}}/\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{automake}} toolchain:

\end{enumerate}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
autoreconf\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}i
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After that, you can compile and install the ViennaRNA Package as if obtained
from the distribution tarball.


\subsection{Building the reference manual}
\label{\detokenize{install:building-the-reference-manual}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Our implementations are documented with extra comments that are automatically
parsed by \sphinxhref{https://www.doxygen.nl/}{doxygen}. The extracted API documentation
is then processed further by \sphinxhref{https://breathe.readthedocs.io/}{breathe} and finally
integrated into a comprehensive reference manual written in
\sphinxhref{https://docutils.sourceforge.io/rst.html}{ReStructuredText}. This manual is then
usually compiled into HTML and PDF format by \sphinxhref{https://www.sphinx-doc.org/}{Sphinx}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We provide pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled versions of the reference manual in our distribution
tarballs and HTML versions at \sphinxurl{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/ViennaRNA/refman} and
\sphinxurl{https://viennarna.readthedocs.io}. However, under certain circumstances users might
want to compile the reference manual themselves, e.g. when \DUrole{xref,std,std-ref}{installing from git repository}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To succeed with the compilation the following tools are required:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doxygen}} (to extract the API documentation)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sphinx\sphinxhyphen{}build}} (to compile the manual)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pdflatex}} (to compile a PDF version of the manual)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition, we use the following sphinx extensions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sphinx\sphinxhyphen{}multiproject}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{myst\sphinxhyphen{}parser}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sphinx\sphinxhyphen{}copybutton}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sphinxcontrib\sphinxhyphen{}bibtex}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sphinx\sphinxhyphen{}rtd\sphinxhyphen{}theme}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If all the above programs and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python}} packages are available, compilation
of the reference manual should succeed without any further problems.


\subsection{Installation without root privileges}
\label{\detokenize{install:installation-without-root-privileges}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you do not have root privileges on your computer, you might want to install the ViennaRNA
Package to a location where you actually have write access to. To do so, you can set the
installation prefix of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./configure}} script like so:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{configure} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{prefix}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{home}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{username}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{local}
\PYG{n}{make} \PYG{n}{install}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will install the entire ViennaRNA Package into your home’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textasciitilde{}/.local/}} directory that
is commonly used for user\sphinxhyphen{}installed software. Just make sure that your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}} environment
variable contains the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$HOME/.local/bin}} directory such that our executables are looked\sphinxhyphen{}up
for at the proper location.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{tip}{Tip:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}prefix}} can be any other directory if you want to keep your installed
software separate from each other. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make install}} command will then create the corresponding
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bin/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{share/}} directories within the directory you specified.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{MacOS X users}
\label{\detokenize{install:macos-x-users}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Although users will find \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/bin/gcc}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/bin/g++}} executables in their directory
tree, these programs are not at all what they pretend to be. Instead of including the GNU
programs, Apple decided to install \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clang}}/\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{llvm}} in disguise. Unfortunately, the default
version of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clang}}/\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{llvm}} does not support \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OpenMP}} (yet), but only complains at a late
stage of the build process when this support is required. Therefore, it seems necessary to
deactivate OpenMP support, e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}disable\PYGZhy{}openmp
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:openmp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{OpenMP}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:universal-binaries}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Universal binaries}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{faq:missing-extern-h}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Missing EXTERN.h}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Using conda}
\label{\detokenize{install:using-conda}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ViennaRNA Package is also available for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{conda}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mamba}} package
manager. The only requirement is to set up the \sphinxhref{https://bioconda.github.io/}{bioconda}
channels

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
conda\PYG{+w}{ }config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}add\PYG{+w}{ }channels\PYG{+w}{ }defaults
conda\PYG{+w}{ }config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}add\PYG{+w}{ }channels\PYG{+w}{ }bioconda
conda\PYG{+w}{ }config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}add\PYG{+w}{ }channels\PYG{+w}{ }conda\PYGZhy{}forge
conda\PYG{+w}{ }config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}set\PYG{+w}{ }channel\PYGZus{}priority\PYG{+w}{ }strict
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and then you can easily install the
\sphinxhref{http://bioconda.github.io/recipes/viennarna/README.html}{viennarna bioconda package}
through

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
conda\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }viennarna
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Binary packages}
\label{\detokenize{install:binary-packages}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For convenience, we provide pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled binary packages and
installers for several Linux\sphinxhyphen{}based platforms, Microsoft Windows, and
Mac OS X. They can be obtained from
\sphinxhref{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/\#binary\_packages}{our official website}.


\section{Python interface only}
\label{\detokenize{install:python-interface-only}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Python 3 interface for the ViennaRNA Package library is
\sphinxhref{https://pypi.org/project/ViennaRNA/}{available at PyPI} and can
be installed independently using Python’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{python} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{m} \PYG{n}{pip} \PYG{n}{install} \PYG{n}{viennarna}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Building the Python package}
\label{\detokenize{install:building-the-python-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Our source tree allows for building/installing the Python 3 interface
separately. For that, we provide the necessary packaging files
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pyproject.toml}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup.cfg}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup.py}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MANIFEST.in}}.
They are created by our \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{autoconf}} toolchain after a successful
run of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./configure}}. Particular default compile\sphinxhyphen{}time features may be
(de\sphinxhyphen{})activated by setting the corresponding boolean flags in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup.cfg}}. Running

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }build
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
will then create a source distribution (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sdist}}) and a binary
package (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{wheel}}) in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dist/}} directory. These files can be
easily installed via Python’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are about to create the Python interface from a fresh
clone of our git repository, you require additional steps after
running \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./configure}} as described above. In particular, some
autogenerated static files that are compiled into RNAlib must
be generated. To do so, run

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }src/ViennaRNA/static
make
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }../../..
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additionally, if building the reference manual is not explicitly
turned off, the Python interface requires docstrings to be generated.
They are taken from the doxygen xml output which can be created by

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }doc
make\PYG{+w}{ }refman\PYGZhy{}html
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }..
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, the swig wrapper must be build using

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }interfaces/Python
make\PYG{+w}{ }RNA/RNA.py
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }../..
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After these steps, the Python \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sdist}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{wheel}} packages can
be build as usual.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Unofficial Julia Interface}
\label{\detokenize{install:unofficial-julia-interface}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An unofficial interface of the ViennaRNA Package for the
\sphinxhref{https://julialang.org/}{Julia Programming Language} exists at
\sphinxhref{https://juliahub.com/ui/Packages/ViennaRNA/lOl0n/}{JuliaHub}.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Configuration}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:configuration}}\label{\detokenize{configuration::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ViennaRNA Package includes additional executable programs such as
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAforester}},

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Kinfold}},

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Kinwalker}},

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAlocmin}}, and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAxplorer}}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Furthermore, we include several features in our C\sphinxhyphen{}library that may be
activated by default, or have to be explicitly turned on at configure\sphinxhyphen{}time.
Below we list a selection of the available configure options that affect
the features included in all executable programs, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} C\sphinxhyphen{}library,
and the corresponding scripting language interface(s).


\section{Streaming SIMD Extension}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:streaming-simd-extension}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since version 2.3.5 our sources contain code that implements a faster
multibranch loop decomposition in global MFE predictions, as used e.g.
in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}. This implementation makes use of modern processors
\sphinxstyleemphasis{streaming SIMD extension} (SSE) that provide the capability to execute
particular instructions on multiple data simultaneously (\sphinxstyleemphasis{SIMD \sphinxhyphen{} single
instruction multiple data}, thanks to W. B. Langdon for providing the
modified code). Consequently, the time required to assess the minimum of
all multibranch loop decompositions is reduced up to about one half
compared to the runtime of the original implementation. This feature is
enabled by default since version 2.4.11 and a dispatcher ensures that
the correct implementation will be selected at runtime. If for any
reason you want to disable this feature at compile\sphinxhyphen{}time use the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}disable\PYGZhy{}simd
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Scripting Language Interfaces}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:scripting-language-interfaces}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ViennaRNA Package comes with scripting language interfaces for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Perl 5}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Python}} (provided by \sphinxhref{https://www.swig.org/}{SWIG}), that allow one to
use the implemented algorithms directly without the need of calling an
executable program. The necessary requirements are determined at
configure\sphinxhyphen{}time and particular languages may be deactivated automatically
if the requirements are not met.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Building the Python 2 interface is deactivated by default since it reached
its end\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}life on January 1st, 2020. If for any reason you still want to
build that interface, you may use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}with\sphinxhyphen{}python2}} configure option
to turn it back on.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You may also switch\sphinxhyphen{}off particular languages by passing the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}without\sphinxhyphen{}perl}} and/or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}without\sphinxhyphen{}python}} configure options, e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}without\PYGZhy{}perl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}without\PYGZhy{}python
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
will turn\sphinxhyphen{}off the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Perl 5}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Python 3}} interfaces.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{tip}{Tip:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Disabling the scripting language support all\sphinxhyphen{}together can be accomplished using the
following switch:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}without\PYGZhy{}swig
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Cluster Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:cluster-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The programs \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{AnalyseSeqs}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{AnalyseDists}} offer some cluster analysis
tools (split decomposition, statistical geometry, neighbor joining, Ward’s method)
for sequences and distance data. To also build these programs add \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}with\sphinxhyphen{}cluster}}
to your configure options.


\section{Kinfold}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:kinfold}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kinfold}} program can be used to simulate the folding dynamics of an RNA
molecule, and is compiled by default. Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}without\sphinxhyphen{}kinfold}} option to
skip compilation and installation of Kinfold.


\section{RNAforester}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:rnaforester}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAforester}} program is used for comparing secondary structures using tree
alignment. Similar to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kinfold\textasciigrave{}, use the \textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}without\sphinxhyphen{}forester}} option to skip
compilation and installation of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAforester}}.


\section{Kinwalker}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:kinwalker}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kinwalker}} algorithm performs co\sphinxhyphen{}transcriptional folding of RNAs, starting at
a user specified structure (default: open chain) and ending at the minimum free
energy structure. Compilation and installation of this program is deactivated by
default. Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}with\sphinxhyphen{}kinwalker}} option to enable building and installation
of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kinwalker}}.


\section{RNAlocmin}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:rnalocmin}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAlocmin}} program is part of the \sphinxstylestrong{Basin Hopping Graph Framework} and reads
secondary structures and searches for local minima by performing a gradient walk
from each of those structures. It then outputs an energetically sorted list of
local minima with their energies and number of hits to particular minimum, which
corresponds to a size of a gradient basin. Additional output consists of barrier
trees and Arhenius rates to compute various kinetic aspects. Compilation and
installation of this program is activated by default. Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}without\sphinxhyphen{}rnalocmin}}
option to disable building and installation of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAlocmin}}.


\section{RNAxplorer}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:rnaxplorer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAxplorer}} is a multitool, that offers different methods to explore RNA
energy landscapes. In default mode it takes an RNA sequence as input and produces
a sample of RNA secondary structures. The repellant sampling heuristic used in
default mode iteratively penalizes base pairs of local minima of structures that
have been seen too often. This results in a diverse sample set with the most
important low free energy structures.
Compilation and installation of this program is activated by default. Note, that
this tool depends on the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAPACK}} library. Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}without\sphinxhyphen{}rnaxplorer}}
option to disable building and installation of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAxplorer}}.


\section{Link Time Optimization}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:link-time-optimization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To increase the performance of our implementations, the ViennaRNA Package tries
to make use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Link Time Optimization} (LTO) feature of modern C\sphinxhyphen{}compilers.
If you are experiencing any troubles at make\sphinxhyphen{}time or run\sphinxhyphen{}time, or the configure
script for some reason detects that your compiler supports this feature although
it doesn’t, you can deactivate it using the flag:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}disable\PYGZhy{}lto
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note, that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gcc}} before version 5 is known to produce unreliable LTO code,
especially in combination with {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:streaming-simd-extension}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SIMD}}}}.
We therefore recommend using a more recent compiler (GCC 5 or above) or to turn off
one of the two features, LTO or SIMD optimized code.


\section{OpenMP}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:openmp}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To enable concurrent computation of our implementations and in some cases
parallelization of the algorithms we make use of the \sphinxhref{https://www.openmp.org/}{OpenMP}
API. This interface is well understood by most modern compilers. However, in
some cases it might be necessary to deactivate OpenMP support and therefore transform
\sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} into a C\sphinxhyphen{}library that is not entirely \sphinxstyleemphasis{thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe}. To do so, add the
following configure option:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}disable\PYGZhy{}openmp
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{POSIX threads}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:posix-threads}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To enable concurrent computation of multiple input data in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}, and for our
implementation of the concurrent unordered insert, ordered output flush data structure
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/buffers:c.vrna_ostream_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_ostream\_t}}}}} we make use of POSIX threads (pthread). This should be
supported on all modern platforms and usually does not pose any problems. Unfortunately,
we use a threadpool implementation that is not compatible with Microsoft Windows yet.
Thus, POSIX thread support can not be activated for Windows builds until we have
fixed this problem. If you want to compile \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} without POSIX threads
support for any other reasons, add the following configure option:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}disable\PYGZhy{}pthreads
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{SVM Z\sphinxhyphen{}score filter}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:svm-z-score-filter}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNALfold}} that comes with the ViennaRNA Package allows for Z\sphinxhyphen{}score
filtering of its predicted results using a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Support Vector Machine} (SVM) provided
by the \sphinxhref{https://www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/~cjlin/libsvm/}{LIBSVM} library. However, this
library is statically linked to our own \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}. If this introduces any problems for
your own third\sphinxhyphen{}party programs that link against \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}, you can safely switch off
the Z\sphinxhyphen{}scoring implementation using:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}without\PYGZhy{}svm
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{GNU Scientific Library}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:gnu-scientific-library}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The program \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNApvmin}} computes a pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}energy perturbation vector that aims
to minimize the discrepancy of predicted, and observed pairing probabilities. For
that purpose it implements several methods to solve the optimization problem. Many
of them are provided by the \sphinxhref{https://www.gnu.org/software/gsl/}{GNU Scientific Library (GSL)},
which is why the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNApvmin}} program, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} C\sphinxhyphen{}library are required to
be linked against \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libgsl}}. If this introduces any problems in your own third\sphinxhyphen{}party
programs that link against \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}, you can turn off a larger portion of available
minimizers in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNApvmin}} and linking against \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libgsl}} all\sphinxhyphen{}together, using:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}without\PYGZhy{}gsl
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Multiple\sphinxhyphen{}precision Floating\sphinxhyphen{}Point Computations}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:multiple-precision-floating-point-computations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Our {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant Boltzmann Sampling}}}} implementation uses
multi\sphinxhyphen{}precision floating\sphinxhyphen{}point computations provided by the
\sphinxhref{https://www.mpfr.org/}{GNU MPFR library} by default. This requires linking against
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libmpfr}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libgmp}}. You can switch off this feature using:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}disable\PYGZhy{}mpfr
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Universal binaries}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:universal-binaries}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you intend to build the ViennaRNA for Mac OS X such that it runs \sphinxstyleemphasis{on both}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{x86\_64}}
and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{arm64}} (Apple Silicon Processors) architectures, you need to build a
so\sphinxhyphen{}called \sphinxstyleemphasis{universal binary}. Note, however, that to accomplish this task, you might
need to deactivate any third\sphinxhyphen{}party library dependency as in most cases, only one
architecture will be available at link time. This includes the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Perl 5}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Python}}
interfaces but might also concern also {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:multiple-precision-floating-point-computations}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{MPFR}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:gnu-scientific-library}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{GSL support}}}}, possibly even more.
In order to compile and link the programs, library, and scripting language interfaces
of the ViennaRNA Package for multiple architectures, we’ve added a new configure switch
that sets up the required changes automatically:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}enable\PYGZhy{}universal\PYGZhy{}binary
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With link time optimization turned on, MacOS X’s default compiler (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{llvm}}/\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clang}})
generates an intermediary binary format that can not easily be combined into a
multi\sphinxhyphen{}architecture library. Therefore, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}enable\sphinxhyphen{}universal\sphinxhyphen{}binary}} switch
turns off {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:link-time-optimization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Link Time Optimization}}}}!
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Disable C11/C++11 features}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:disable-c11-c-11-features}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, we use C11/C++11 features in our implementations. This mainly accounts
for unnamed unions/structs within \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}. The configure script automatically
detects whether or not your compiler understands these features. In case you are
using an older compiler, these features will be deactivated by setting a specific
pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor directive. If for some reason you want to deactivate C11/C++11
features despite the capabilities of your compiler, use the following configure
option:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{configure} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{disable}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{c11}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Deprecated symbols}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:deprecated-symbols}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since version 2.2 we are in the process of transforming the API of our \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}.
Hence, several symbols are marked as \sphinxstyleemphasis{deprecated} whenever they have been
replaced by the new API. By default, deprecation warnings at compile time are
deactivated. If you want to get your terminal spammed by tons of deprecation
warnings, enable them using:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{configure} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{enable}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{warn}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{deprecated}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Single precision}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:single-precision}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculation of partition functions (via \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold \sphinxhyphen{}p}}) uses double precision
floats by default, to avoid overflow errors on longer sequences. If your machine
has little memory and you don’t plan to fold sequences over 1,000 bases in
length you can compile the package to do the computations in single precision by
running:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{configure} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{enable}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{floatpf}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using this option is discouraged and not necessary on most modern computers.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Help}
\label{\detokenize{configuration:help}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a complete list of all \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./configure}} options and important environment variables,
type:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{configure} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{help}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For more general information on the build process see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{INSTALL} file.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Getting Started}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:getting-started}}\label{\detokenize{getting_started::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here you find some more or less elaborate tutorials and manuals on how
to use our software.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tutorials provided below are mostly taken from \sphinxhref{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/tutorial/}{A short Tutorial
on RNA Bioinformatics The ViennaRNA Package and related Programs}. Since they have not
been updated for quite some time, some of the described features may
not work as expected and novel features of our programs may not be
mentioned.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We will be working on extending this part of the documentation in
the future.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Global RNA Secondary Structure Prediction}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:global-rna-secondary-structure-prediction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Several tools for structure prediction of single RNA sequences are
available within the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}}, each with its own special
subset of implemented algorithms.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:the-program-rnafold}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Our first task will be to do a structure prediction using
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}. This should get you familiar with the input and output
format as well as the graphical output produced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} reads single RNA sequences, computes their minimum free energy
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}}) structures, and prints the result together with the corresponding
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation. This is the default mode if no
further command line parameters are provided. Please note, that the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}
program can either be used in \sphinxstyleemphasis{interactive mode}, where the program expects
the input from \sphinxstyleemphasis{stdin}, or in \sphinxstyleemphasis{batch processing mode} where
you provide the input sequences as text files.
\subsubsection*{Partition function}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To activate computation of the partition function for each sequence, the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}p}} option must be set. From the partition function
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Q = \sum_{s \in \Omega} exp(-E(s) / RT)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
over the ensemble of all possible structures \(\Omega\), with temperature \(T\) and gas
constant \(R\), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} then computes the ensemble free energy \(G = -RT \cdot ln(Q)\),
and frequency of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} structure \(s_{mfe}\) within the ensemble
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p = exp(-E(s_{mfe}) / RT) / Q\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Ensemble diversity}

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}p}} option also activates the computation
of base pairing probabilities \(p_{ij}\). From this data, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} then
determines the ensemble diversity
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle d \rangle = \sum_{ij} p_{ij} \cdot (1 - p_{ij}),\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the expected distance between any two secondary structure, as well as the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{centroid}} structure, i.e. the structure \(s_c\) with the least Boltzmann weighted
distance
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}d_\Omega(s_c) = \sum_{\substack{s \in \Omega}} p(s) d(s_c, s)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
to all other structures \(s \in \Omega\).
\subsubsection*{Maximum Expected Accuracy}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another useful structure representative one can determine from base pairing probabilities
\(p_{ij}\) is the structure that exhibits the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maximum expected accuracy (MEA)}. By
assuming the base pair probability is a good measure of correctnes of a pair \((i,j)\), the
expected accuracy of a structure \(s\) is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{EA}(s) = \sum_{\substack{(i,j) \in s}} 2\gamma p_{ij} + \sum_{\substack{i \\ \nexists (i,j) \in s}} q_i\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(q_i = 1 - \sum_j p_{ij}\) and weighting factor \(\gamma\) that allows us to
weight paired against unpaired positions. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} uses a dynamic programming
scheme similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Maximum Matching algorithm} of Ruth Nussinov to find the
structure \(s\) that minimizes the above equation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} program provides a large amount of additional
computation modes that will be partly covered below. To get a full list of all
computation modes available, please consult the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} man page or
the outputs of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold \sphinxhyphen{}h}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}detailed\sphinxhyphen{}help}}.


\subsubsection{MFE structure of a single sequence}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:mfe-structure-of-a-single-sequence}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use a text editor (emacs, vi, nano, gedit) to prepare an input file by pasting the text
below and save it under the name \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test.seq}} in your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Data}} folder:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}} \PYG{n}{test}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the best (MFE) structure for this sequence using \sphinxstyleemphasis{batch processing mode}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold test.seq
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA
...........((((...)))). ( \PYGZhy{}5.00)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
or use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{interactive mode} and redirect the content of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test.seq}}
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{stdin}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZlt{} text.seq
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA
...........((((...)))). ( \PYGZhy{}5.00)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
alternatively, you could use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{interactive mode} and manually enter the sequence
as soon as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} prompts for input

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold
Input string (upper or lower case); @ to quit
....,....1....,....2....,....3....,....4....,....5....,....6....,....7....,....8
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA
length = 23

CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA
...........((((...)))).
 minimum free energy =  \PYGZhy{}5.00 kcal/mol
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All the above variants to compute the MFE and the corresponding structure result in identical
output, except for slight variations in the formatting when true \sphinxstyleemphasis{interactive mode} is used.
The last line(s) of the text output contains the predicted MFE structure in \sphinxstyleemphasis{dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation}
and its free energy in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kcal/mol}}. A dot in the dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation represents an unpaired
position, while a base pair (i, j) is represented by a pair of matching parentheses at position
i and j.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the input was \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FASTA}} formatted, i.e. the sequence was preceded by a header line
with sequence identifier, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} creates a structure layout file named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_ss.ps}},
where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test}} is the sequence identifier as provided through the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FASTA}} header.
In case the header was omitted the output file name simply is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rna.ps}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s take a look at the output file with your favorite \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PostScript}} viewer, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gv}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In contrast to bitmap based image files (such as GIF or JPEG) PostScript files contain
resolution independent \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector graphics}, suitable for publication. They can be viewed
on\sphinxhyphen{}screen using a postscript viewer such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gv}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{evince}}. Also note the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\&}}
at the end of the following command line that simply detaches the program call and
immediately starts the program in the background.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{}\PYG{+w}{ }gv\PYG{+w}{ }test\PYGZus{}ss.ps\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZam{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare the dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation to the PostScript drawing shown in the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_ss.eps}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}t}} option to change the layout algorithm \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} uses
to produce the plot. The most simply layout is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{radial} layout that can be chosen
with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}t 0}}. Here, each nucleotide in a loop is equally spaced on its enclosing circle.
The more sophisticated \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Naview}} layout algorithm is used by default but may be explicitly
chosen through \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}t 1}}. A hidden feature can be found with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}t 2}}, where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}
creates a most simple circular plot.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The calculation above does not tell us whether we can actually trust the predicted structure.
In fact, there may be many more possible structures that might be equally probable. To find
out about that, let’s have a look at the equilibrium ensemble instead.


\subsubsection{Equilibrium ensemble properties}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:equilibrium-ensemble-properties}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}MEA
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
to compute the partition function, pair probabilities, centroid structure,
and the maximum expected accuracy (MEA) structure.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Have a look at the generated PostScript files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_ss.ps}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_dp.ps}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}MEA test.seq
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA
...........((((...)))). ( \PYGZhy{}5.00)
....\PYGZob{},\PYGZob{}\PYGZob{}...||||...)\PYGZcb{}\PYGZcb{}\PYGZcb{}. [ \PYGZhy{}5.72]
....................... \PYGZob{}  0.00 d=4.66\PYGZcb{}
......((...))((...))... \PYGZob{}  2.90 MEA=14.79\PYGZcb{}
 frequency of mfe structure in ensemble 0.311796; ensemble diversity 6.36
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here the last four lines are new compared to the text output without the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}p \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}MEA}}
options. The partition function is already a rough measure for the well\sphinxhyphen{}definedness of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}}
structure. The third line shows a condensed representation of the pair probabilities of each
nucleotide, similar to the dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation, followed by the ensemble free energy
(\(G = -kT \cdot ln(Z)\)) in units of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kcal/mol}}. Here, the dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket like notation consists
of additional characters that denote the pairing propensity for each nucleotide.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}} denotes bases that are essentially unpaired, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{,}} weakly paired,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{|}} strongly paired without preference, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{\}}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{()}} weakly (\(>\) 33\%) upstream (downstream)
paired or strongly (\(>\) 66\%) up\sphinxhyphen{}/downstream paired bases, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The next two lines represent (i) the centroid structure
with its free energy and distance to the ensemble, and (ii) the MEA structure, it’s free
energy and the actual accuracy. The very last line shows the frequency of the MFE structure in
the ensemble of secondary structures and the diversity of the ensemble as discussed above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the MFE structure is adopted only with 31\% probability, also the
diversity is very high for such a short sequence.


\subsubsection{Rotate the structure plot}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:rotate-the-structure-plot}}
\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.250\linewidth]{{test_ss}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To rotate the secondary structure plot that is generated by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}} provides the perl script utility \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rotate\_ss.pl}}.
Just read the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{perldoc}} for this tool to know how to handle the rotation and use
the information to get your secondary structure in a vertical position.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} perldoc rotate\PYGZus{}ss.pl
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{The base pair probability dot plot}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:the-base-pair-probability-dot-plot}}
\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.500\linewidth]{{test_dp}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dot plot} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_dp.ps}}) shows the pair probabilities within
the equilibrium ensemble as \(n\times n\) matrix, and is an excellent way to
visualize structural alternatives. A square at row \(i\) and column \(j\)
indicates a base pair. The area of a square in the upper right half of the
matrix is proportional to the probability of the base pair \((i,j)\) within the
equilibrium ensemble. The lower left half shows all pairs belonging to
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} structure. While the MFE consists of a single helix, several
different helices are visualized in the pair probabilities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
While a base pair probability dot\sphinxhyphen{}plot is quite handy to interpret for short
sequences, it quickly becomes confusing the longer the RNA sequence is. Still,
this is (currently) the only output of base pair probabilities for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}
program. Nevertheless, since the dot plot is a true \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PostScript}} file,
one can retrieve the individual base pair probabilities by parsing its textual
content.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open the dot plot with your favorite text editor

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Locate the lines that that follow the scheme

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{i} \PYG{n}{j} \PYG{n}{v} \PYG{n}{ubox}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(i\) and \(j\) are integer values and \(v\) is a floating point decimal
with values between \(0\) and \(1\). These are the data for the boxes drawn in
the upper triangle. The integer values \(i\) and \(j\) denote the nucleotide positions
while the value \(v\) is the square\sphinxhyphen{}root of the probability of base pair \((i,j)\).
Thus, the actual base pair probability \(p(i,j) = v \cdot v\).

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Mountain and Reliability plot}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:mountain-and-reliability-plot}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Next, let’s use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{relplot.pl}} utility to annotate which parts of a
predicted MFE structure are well\sphinxhyphen{}defined and thus more reliable. Also let’s use a real
example for a change and produce yet another representation of the predicted
structure, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mountain plot}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fold the 5S rRNA sequence and visualize the structure. (The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{5S.seq}} is shipped with the tutorial)

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{}\PYG{+w}{ }RNAfold\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}p\PYG{+w}{ }5S.seq
\PYGZdl{}\PYG{+w}{ }mountain.pl\PYG{+w}{ }5S\PYGZus{}dp.ps\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{|}\PYG{+w}{ }xmgrace\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pipe
\PYGZdl{}\PYG{+w}{ }relplot.pl\PYG{+w}{ }5S\PYGZus{}ss.ps\PYG{+w}{ }5S\PYGZus{}dp.ps\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }5S\PYGZus{}rss.ps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{\X{50}{100}\X{50}{100}}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{5S_mt}.png}
&
\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{5S_rot}.png}
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabular}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A mountain plot is especially useful for long sequences where conventional
structure drawings become terribly cluttered.  It is a xy\sphinxhyphen{}diagram plotting
the number of base pairs enclosing a sequence position \sphinxstyleemphasis{versus} the
position. The  \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Perl}} script \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mountain.pl}} transforms a dot
plot into the mountain plot coordinates which can be visualized with any
xy\sphinxhyphen{}plotting program, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xmgrace}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The resulting plot shows three curves, two mountain plots derived from
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} structure (red) and the pairing probabilities (black) and
a positional entropy curve (green). Well\sphinxhyphen{}defined regions are identified by low
entropy. By superimposing several mountain plots structures can easily
be compared.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The perl script \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{relplot.pl}} adds reliability
information to a RNA secondary structure plot in the form of color
annotation. The script computes a well\sphinxhyphen{}definedness measure we call
{\color{red}\bfseries{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}positional entropy’’
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S(i) = -\sum p_{ij}\log(p_{ij})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and encodes it as color hue, ranging from red
(low entropy, well\sphinxhyphen{}defined) via green to blue and violet (high
entropy, ill\sphinxhyphen{}defined). In the example above two helices of the 5S RNA are
well\sphinxhyphen{}defined (red) and indeed predicted correctly, the left arm is not quite
correct and disordered.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the figure above we had to rotate and mirror the structure plot, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} rotate\PYGZus{}ss.pl \PYGZhy{}a 180 \PYGZhy{}m 5S\PYGZus{}rss.ps \PYGZgt{} 5S\PYGZus{}rot.ps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Batch job processing}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:batch-job-processing}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In most cases, one doesn’t only want to predict the structure and equilibrium
probabilities for a single RNA sequence but a set of sequences. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}
is perfectly suited for this task since it provides several different mechanisms
to support batch job processing. First, in \sphinxstyleemphasis{interactive} mode, it only
stops processing input from \sphinxstyleemphasis{stdin} if it is requested to do so. This means
that after processing one sequence, it will prompt for the input of the next
sequence. Entering the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{@}} character will forcefully abort processing.
In situations where the input is provided through input stream redirection,
it will end processing as soon stream is closed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In constrat to that, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{batch processing mode} where one simply specifies
input files as so\sphinxhyphen{}called unnamed command line parameters, the number of input
sequences is more or less unlimited. You can specify as many input files as
your terminal emulator allows, and each input file may consist of arbitrarily
many sequences. However, please note that mixing \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FASTA}} and non\sphinxhyphen{}fasta
input is not allowed and will most likely produce bogus output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Assume you have four input files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{file\_0.fa}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{file\_1.fa}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{file\_2.fa}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{file\_3.fa}}. Each file contains a set of RNA
sequences in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FASTA}} format. Predicting secondary structures for all
sequences in all files with a single call to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} and redirecting
the output to a file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{all\_sequences\_output.fold}} can be achieved
like this:
.. code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold file\PYGZus{}0.fa file\PYGZus{}1.fa file\PYGZus{}2.fa file\PYGZus{}3.fa \PYGZgt{} all\PYGZus{}sequences\PYGZus{}output.fold
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The above call to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} will open each of the files and process the
sequences sequentially. This, however, might take a long time and the sequential
processing will most likely bore out your multi\sphinxhyphen{}core workstation or laptop computer,
since only a single core is used for the computations while the others are idle.
If you happen to have more than a single CPU core and want to take advantage of
the available parallel processing power, you can use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}j}} option of
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} to split the input into concurrent jobs.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}j file\PYGZus{}*.fa \PYGZgt{} all\PYGZus{}sequences\PYGZus{}output.fold
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command will uses as many CPU cores as available and, therefore, process
you input much faster. If you want to limit the number of concurrent jobs to
a particular number, say \(2\), to leave the remaining cores available for other
tasks, you can append the number of jobs directly to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}j}} option:
.. code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}j2 file\PYGZus{}*.fa \PYGZgt{} all\PYGZus{}sequences\PYGZus{}output.fold
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note here, that there must not be any space between the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{j}} and the number
of jobs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now imagine what happens if you have a larger set of
sequences that are not stored in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FASTA}} format. If you would serve such
an input to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}, it would happily process each of the sequences
but always over\sphinxhyphen{}write the structure layout and dot\sphinxhyphen{}plot files, since the default
names for these files are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rna.ps}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dot.ps}} for any sequence.
This is usually an undesired behavior, where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}auto\sphinxhyphen{}id}}
option becomes handy. This option flag forces \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} to automatically
create a sequence identifier for each input, thus using different file names for
each single output. The identifier that is created follows the form
.. code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{sequence\PYGZus{}XXXX}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sequence}} is a prefix, followed by the delimiting character \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_}},
and an increasing 4\sphinxhyphen{}digit number \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{XXXX}} starting at 0000. This feature is
even useful if the input is in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FASTA}} format, but one wants to enforce
a novel naming scheme for the sequences. As soon as the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}auto\sphinxhyphen{}id}} option
is set, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} will ignore any id taken from existing \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FASTA}}
headers in the input files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See also the man page of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} to find out how to modify the prefix,
delimiting character, start number and number of digits.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create an input file with many RNA sequences, each on a separate line, e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} randseq \PYGZhy{}n 127 \PYGZgt{} many\PYGZus{}files.seq
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the MFE structure for each of the sequences and generate output
ids with numbers between \(100\) and \(226\) and prefix \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_seq}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}auto\PYGZhy{}id \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}id\PYGZhy{}start=100 \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}id\PYGZhy{}prefix=\PYGZdq{}test\PYGZus{}seq\PYGZdq{} many\PYGZus{}files.seq
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Add constraints to the structure prediction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:add-constraints-to-the-structure-prediction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For some scientific questions one requires additional constraints that must be
enforced when predicting secondary structures. For instance, one might have resolved
parts of the structure already and is simply interested in the optimal conformation
of the remaining part of the molecule. Another example would be that one already
knows that particular nucleotides can not participate in any base pair, since they
are physically hindered to do so. These types of constraints are termed \sphinxstyleemphasis{hard}
constraints and they can enforce or prohibit particular conformations, thus include
or omit structures with these feature from the set candidate ensemble.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another type of constraints are so\sphinxhyphen{}called \sphinxstyleemphasis{soft} constraints, that enable one
to adjust the free energy contributions of particular conformations. For instance,
one could add a bonus energy if a particular (stretch of) nucleotides is left unpaired
to emulate the binding free energy of a single strand binding protein. The same can
be applied to base pairs, for instance one could add a penalizing energy term if a
particular base pair is formed to make it less likely.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} programs comes with a comprehensive hard and soft constraints
support and provides several convenience command line parameters to ease constraint
application.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The most simple hard constraint that can be applied is the maximum base pair span, i.e.
the maximum number of nucleotides a particular base pair may span. This constraint can
be applied with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}maxBPspan}} option followed by an integer number.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the secondary structure for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{5S.seq}} input file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now limit the maximum base pair span to \(50\) and compare both results:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}maxBPspan 50 5S.seq
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now assume you already know parts of the structure and want to \sphinxstyleemphasis{fill\sphinxhyphen{}in}
an optimal remaining part. You can do that by using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C}} option
and adding an additional line in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation to the input (after the sequence)
that corresponds to the known structure:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prepare the input file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{hard\_const\_example.fa}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}constrained\PYGZus{}sequence}
\PYG{n}{GCCCUUGUCGAGAGGAACUCGAGACACCCACUACCCACUGAGGACUUUCG}
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note here, that we left out the remainder of the input structure constraint that will
eventually be used to enforce a helix of 4 base pairs at the beginning of the sequence.
You may also fill the remainder of the constraint with dots to silence any warnings issued
by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the MFE structure for the input:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold hard\PYGZus{}const\PYGZus{}example.fa
\PYGZgt{}my\PYGZus{}constrained\PYGZus{}sequence
GCCCUUGUCGAGAGGAACUCGAGACACCCACUACCCACUGAGGACUUUCG
........((((((...((((.................))))..)))))) ( \PYGZhy{}8.00)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now compute the MFE structure under the provided constraint:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}C hard\PYGZus{}const\PYGZus{}example.fa
\PYGZgt{}my\PYGZus{}constrained\PYGZus{}sequence
GCCCUUGUCGAGAGGAACUCGAGACACCCACUACCCACUGAGGACUUUCG
..((((.....))))....(((((..((((........)).))..))))) ( \PYGZhy{}7.90)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Due to historic reasons, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C}} option alone only forbids any base pairs
that are incompatible with the constraint, rather than enforcing the constraint. Thus,
if you compute equilibrium probabilities, structures that are missing the small helix in
the beginning are still part of the ensemble. If you want to compute the pairing probabilities
upon forcing the small helix at the beginning, you can add the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}enforceConstraint}} option:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZhy{}C \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}enforceConstraint hard\PYGZus{}const\PYGZus{}example.fa
\PYGZgt{}my\PYGZus{}constrained\PYGZus{}sequence
GCCCUUGUCGAGAGGAACUCGAGACACCCACUACCCACUGAGGACUUUCG
..((((.....))))....(((((..((((........)).))..))))) ( \PYGZhy{}7.90)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Have a look at the differences in ensemble free energy and base pair probabilities between
the results obtained with and without the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}enforceConstraint}} option.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A more thorough alternative to provide constraints is to use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}commands}} option
and a corresponding \sphinxstyleemphasis{commands file}. This allows one to specify constraints on nucleotide
or base pair level and even to restrict a constraint to particular loop types. A commands file
is a simple multi column text file with one constraint on each line. A line starts with a one\sphinxhyphen{} or
two\sphinxhyphen{}letter command, followed by multiple values that specify the addressed nucleotides, the loop
context restriction, and, for soft constraints, the strength of the constraint in \(kcal/mol\).
The syntax is as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{F} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0} \PYG{n}{k}   \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{TYPE}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{ORIENTATION}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Force nucleotides i...i+k\PYGZhy{}1 to be paired}
\PYG{n}{F} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{n}{j} \PYG{n}{k}   \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{TYPE}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Force helix of size k starting with (i,j) to be formed}
\PYG{n}{P} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0} \PYG{n}{k}   \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{TYPE}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Prohibit nucleotides i...i+k\PYGZhy{}1 to be paired}
\PYG{n}{P} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{n}{j} \PYG{n}{k}   \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{TYPE}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Prohibit pairs (i,j),...,(i+k\PYGZhy{}1,j\PYGZhy{}k+1)}
\PYG{n}{P} \PYG{n}{i}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{j} \PYG{n}{k}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{l} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{TYPE}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Prohibit pairing between two ranges}
\PYG{n}{C} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0} \PYG{n}{k}   \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{TYPE}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Nucleotides i,...,i+k\PYGZhy{}1 must appear in context TYPE}
\PYG{n}{C} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{n}{j} \PYG{n}{k}          \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Remove pairs conflicting with (i,j),...,(i+k\PYGZhy{}1,j\PYGZhy{}k+1)}
\PYG{n}{E} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0} \PYG{n}{k} \PYG{n}{e}        \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Add pseudo\PYGZhy{}energy e to nucleotides i...i+k\PYGZhy{}1}
\PYG{n}{E} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{n}{j} \PYG{n}{k} \PYG{n}{e}        \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Add pseudo\PYGZhy{}energy e to pairs (i,j),...,(i+k\PYGZhy{}1,j\PYGZhy{}k+1)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{TYPE}\PYG{p}{]}        \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}} \PYG{n}{E}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{H}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{I}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{M}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{A} \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{ORIENTATION}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}} \PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{D} \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prepare a commands file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test.constraints}} that forces the first 5 nucleotides to pair and the
following 3 nucleotides to stay unpaired as part of a multi\sphinxhyphen{}branch loop:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{F} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0} \PYG{l+m+mi}{5}
\PYG{n}{C} \PYG{l+m+mi}{6} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3} \PYG{n}{M}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{randseq}} program to generate multiple sequences and compute the MFE structure
for each under the constraints prepared earlier:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} randseq \PYGZhy{}n 20 | RNAfold \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}commands test.constraints
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Inspect the output to assure yourself that hte commands have been applied

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A few much more sophisticated constraints will be discussed below.


\subsubsection{SHAPE directed RNA folding}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:shape-directed-rna-folding}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to further improve the quality of secondary structure predictions, mapping experiments like
SHAPE (selective 2’\sphinxhyphen{}hydroxyl acylation analyzed by primer extension) can be used to exerimentally determine
the pairing status for each nucleotide.
In addition to thermodynamic based secondary structure predictions, RNAfold supports the incorporation of this additional
experimental data as soft constraints.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to use SHAPE data to guide the folding process, please make sure that your experimental data is present in a text file,
where each line stores three white space separated columns containing the position, the abbreviation and the normalized SHAPE reactivity for
a certain nucleotide.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{l+m+mi}{1} \PYG{n}{G} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.134}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{2} \PYG{n}{C} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.044}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{3} \PYG{n}{C} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.057}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{4} \PYG{n}{G} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.114}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{5} \PYG{n}{U} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.094}
   \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
   \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
   \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{71} \PYG{n}{C} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.035}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{72} \PYG{n}{G} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.909}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{73} \PYG{n}{C} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.224}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{74} \PYG{n}{C} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.529}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{75} \PYG{n}{A} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.475}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second column, which holds the nucleotide abbreviation, is optional.
If it is present, the data will be used to perform a cross check against the provided input sequence.
Missing SHAPE reactivities for certain positions can be indicated by omitting the reactivity column or the whole line.
Negative reactivities will be treated as missing.
Once the SHAPE file is ready, it can be used to constrain folding:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}shape=rna.shape \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}shapeMethod=D \PYGZlt{} rna.seq
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A small compilation of reference data taken from Hajdin \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id52}{2013}{]} is available online
\sphinxurl{https://weeks.chem.unc.edu/data-files/ShapeKnots\_DATA.zip}. However, the included
reference structures are only available in connect (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.ct}}) format and require conversion into
dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation to compare them against predicted structures with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}.
Furthermore, the normalized \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SHAPE}} data is available as Excel spreadsheet and
also requires some pre\sphinxhyphen{}processing to make it available for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}.


\subsubsection{Adding ligand interactions}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:adding-ligand-interactions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
RNA molecules are known to interact with other molecules, such as additional RNAs, proteins,
or other small ligand molecules. Some interactions with small ligands that take place in
loops of an RNA structure can be modeled in terms of soft constraints. However, to stay
compatible with the recursive decomposition scheme for secondary structures they are
limited to the unpaired nucleotides of hairpins and internal loops.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAlib}} library of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}} implements a most general
form of constraints capability. However, the available programs do not allow for a full
access to the implemented features. Nevertheless, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} provides a convenience
option that allows to easily include ligand binding to hairpin\sphinxhyphen{} or interior\sphinxhyphen{}loop like aptamer
motifs. For that purpose, a user needs only to provide motif and a binding free energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider the following example file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{theo.fa}} for a theophylline triggered
riboswitch with the sequence:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{theo}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{switch}
\PYG{n}{GGUGAUACCAGAUUUCGCGAAAAAUCCCUUGGCAGCACCUCGCACAUCUUGUUGUC}
\PYG{n}{UGAUUAUUGAUUUUUCGCGAAACCAUUUGAUCAUAUGACAAGAUUGAG}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The theopylline aptamer structure has been actively researched during the last two decades.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.750\linewidth]{{theo_aptamer}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Although the actual aptamer part (marked in blue) is not a simple interior loop, it
can still be modeled as such. It consists of two delimiting base pairs (G,C) at the
5’ site, and another (G,C) at its 3’ end. That is already enough to satisfy the requirements
for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}motif}} option of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}. Together with the aptamer sequence
motif, the entire aptamer can be written down in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket form as:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{GAUACCAG}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{CCCUUGGCAGC}
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note here, that we separated the 5’ and 3’ part from each other using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\&}}
character. This enables us to omit the variable hairpin end of the aptamer from the
specification in our model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The only ingredient that is still missing is the actual stabilizing energy contribution
induced by the ligand binding into the aptamer pocket. But several experimental and computational
studies have already determined dissociation constants for this system. Jenison \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id53}{1994}{]},
for instance, determined a dissociation constant of \(K_d = 0.32\mu M\) which, for standard
reference concentration \(c = 1 mol/L\), can be translated into a binding free energy
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta G = RT \cdot \ln \frac{K_d}{c} \approx -9.22~kcal/mol\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, we can compute the MFE structure for our example sequence

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}v \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}motif \PYGZdq{}GAUACCAG\PYGZam{}CCCUUGGCAGC,(...((((\PYGZam{})...)))...),\PYGZhy{}9.22\PYGZdq{} theo.fa
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare the predicted MFE structure with and without modeling the ligand interaction.
You may also enable partition function computation to compute base pair probabilities,
the centroid structure and MEA structure to investigate the effect of ligand binding
on ensemble diversity.


\subsubsection{G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplexes}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:g-quadruplexes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
G\sphinxhyphen{}Quadruplexes are a common conformation found in G\sphinxhyphen{}rich sequences where four runs of
consecutive G’s are separated by three short sequence stretches.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.500\linewidth]{{gquad_pattern}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
They form local self\sphinxhyphen{}enclosed stacks of G\sphinxhyphen{}quartets bound together through 8 Hogsteen\sphinxhyphen{}Watson
Crick bonds and further stabilized by a metal ion (usually potassium).

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.500\linewidth]{{gquad}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To acknowledge the competition of regular secondary structure and G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex formation,
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}} implements an extension to the default recursion scheme.
For that purpose, G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplexes are simply considered a different type of substructure
that may be incorporated like any other substructure. The free energy of a particular
G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex at temperature \(T\) is determined by a simple energy model
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(L, l_{tot}, T) = a(t) \cdot (L - 1) + b(T) \cdot ln(l_{tot} - 2)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that only considers the number of stacked layers \(L\) and the total size of the three
linker sequences \(l_{tot} = l_1 + l_2 + l_3\) connecting the G runs. Linker sequence
and assymetry effects as well as relative strand orientations (parallel, anti\sphinxhyphen{}parallel
or mixed) are entirely neglected in this model. The free energy parameters
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a(T) = H_a + TS_a\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}b(T) = H_b + TS_b\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
have been determined from experimental UV\sphinxhyphen{}melting data taken from Zhang \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id54}{2011}{]}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} allows one to activate the G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex implementation by simply
providing the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}g}} switch. G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplexes are then taken into account for
MFE and equilibrium probability computations.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} echo \PYGZdq{}GGCUGGUGAUUGGAAGGGAGGGAGGUGGCCAGCC\PYGZdq{} | RNAfold \PYGZhy{}g \PYGZhy{}p
GGCUGGUGAUUGGAAGGGAGGGAGGUGGCCAGCC
((((((..........++.++..++.++)))))) (\PYGZhy{}21.39)
((((((..........(..........))))))) [\PYGZhy{}21.83]
((((((..........++.++..++.++)))))) \PYGZob{}\PYGZhy{}21.39 d=0.04\PYGZcb{}
 frequency of mfe structure in ensemble 0.491118; ensemble diversity 0.08
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The resulting structure layout and dot plot \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PostScript}} files depict the
prediced G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplexes as hairpin\sphinxhyphen{}like loops with additional bonds between the
interacting G’s, and green triangles where the color intensity encodes the G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex
probability, respectively. Have a closer look at the actual G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex probabilities
by opening the dot plot \sphinxstyleemphasis{PostScript} file with a text browser again.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.750\linewidth]{{gquad_menon}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A better drawing of the predicted G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex might look as follows

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.500\linewidth]{{gquad_menon_nice}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Repeat the above analysis for other RNA sequences that might contain and form
