a G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex, e.g. the human telomerase RNA component hTERC:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{hTERC}
\PYG{n}{AGAGAGUGACUCUCACGAGAGCCGCGAGAGUCAGCUUGGCCAAUCCGUGCGGUCGG}
\PYG{n}{CGGCCGCUCCCUUUAUAAGCCGACUCGCCCGGCAGCGCACCGGGUUGCGGAGGGUG}
\PYG{n}{GGCCUGGGAGGGGUGGUGGCCAUUUUUUGUCUAACCCUAACUGAGAAGGGCGUAGG}
\PYG{n}{CGCCGUGCUUUUGCUCCCCGCGCGCUGUUUUUCUCGCUGACUUUCAGCGGGCGGAA}
\PYG{n}{AAGCCUCGGCCUGCCGCCUUCCACCGUUCAUUCUAGAGCAAACAAAAAAUGUCAGC}
\PYG{n}{UGCUGGCCCGUUCGCCCCUCCCGGGGACCUGCGGCGGGUCGCCUGCCCAGCCCCCG}
\PYG{n}{AACCCCGCCUGGAGGCCGCGGUCGGCCCGGGGCUUCUCCGGAGGCACCCACUGCCA}
\PYG{n}{CCGCGAAGAGUUGGGCUCUGUCAGCCGCGGGUCUCUCGGGGGCGAGGGCGAGGUUC}
\PYG{n}{AGGCCUUUCAGGCCGCAGGAAGAGGAACGGAGCGAGUCCCCGCGCGCGGCGCGAUU}
\PYG{n}{CCCUGAGCUGUGGGACGUGCACCCAGGACUCGGCUCACACAUGC}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{SSB protein interaction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:ssb-protein-interaction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to the ligand interactions discussed above, a single strand binding
(SSB) protein might bind to consecutively unpaired sequence motifs. To model
such interactions the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}} implements yet another
extension to the folding grammar to cover all cases a protein may bind to,
termed \sphinxstyleemphasis{unstructured domains}. This is in contrast to the ligand binding
example above that uses the soft constraints implementation, and is, therefore,
restricted to unpaired hairpin\sphinxhyphen{} and interior\sphinxhyphen{}loops.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To make use of this implementation in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} one has to resort
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{command files} again. Here, an unstructured domain (UD) can be easily
added using the following syntax:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{UD} \PYG{n}{m} \PYG{n}{e} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{LOOP}\PYG{p}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} is the sequence motif the protein binds to in IUPAC format,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{e}} is the binding free energy in \(kcal/mol\), and the optional \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LOOP}}
specifier allows for restricting the binding to particular loop types, e.g.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{M}} for multibranch loops, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E}} for the exterior loop. See the
syntax for command files above for an overview of all loop types available.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, consider the protein binding experiment taken from Forties and Bundschuh {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id55}{2010}{]}.
Here, the authors investigate a hypothetical unspecific RNA binding protein with a
footprint of \(6~nt\) and a binding energy of \(\Delta G = -10~kcal/mol\) at
\(1~M\). With \(T = 37^\circ C\) and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta G = RT \cdot \ln \frac{K_d}{c}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
this translates into a dissociation constant of
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}K_d = exp(\Delta G / RT) = 8.983267433 \cdot 10^{-8}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hence, the binding energies at \(50~nM\), \(100~nM\), \(400~nM\), and \(1~\mu M\) are \(0.36~kcal/mol\),
\(-0.07~kcal/mol\), \(-0.92~kcal/mol\), and \(-1.49~kcal/mol\), respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The RNA sequence file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{forties\_bundschuh.fa}} for this experiment is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{forties\PYGZus{}bundschuh}
\PYG{n}{CGCUAUAAACCCCAAAAAAAAAAAAGGGGAAAAUAGCG}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which yields the following MFE structure

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.500\linewidth]{{forties_ss}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To model the protein binding for this example with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} we require
a commands file for each of the concentrations in question. Thus, one simply creates
text files with a single line content:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{UD} \PYG{n}{NNNNNN} \PYG{n}{e}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{e}} is the binding free energy at this specific protein concentration
as computed above. Note here, that we use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NNNNNN}} as sequence motif that is
bound by the protein to acknowledge the unspecific interaction between protein and
RNA. Finally, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} is executed to compute equilibrium base pairing and
per\sphinxhyphen{}nucleotide protein binding probabilities
.. code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}commands forties\PYGZus{}50nM.txt forties\PYGZus{}bundschuh.fa
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and the produced probability dot plot can be inspected.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.500\linewidth]{{forties_50nM_dp}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As you can see, the dot plot is augmented with an additional linear array of blue squares
along each side that depicts the probability that the respective nucleotide is bound
by the protein. Now, repeat the computations for different protein concentrations and
compare the probabilities computed with the unstructured domain feature of the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}} with those in Fig. 3(a) of the publication.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note, that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} allows for an unlimited number of different proteins
specified in the commands file. This easily allows one to model RNA\sphinxhyphen{}protein binding
interaction within a relatively complex solution of different competing proteins.


\subsubsection{Change other model settings}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAfold:change-other-model-settings}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} also allows for many other changes of the implemented Nearest Neighbor
model. For instance, you can explicitly prohibit \((G,U)\) pairs, change the temperature
that is used for evaluation of the free energy of particular loops, select a different
dangling\sphinxhyphen{}end energy model or load a different set of free energy parameters, e.g. for
DNA or parameters derived from computational optimizations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the man pages of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} for a complete overview of all available options
and command line switches. Additional energy parameter collections are distributed together
with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}} as part of the contents of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{misc/}} directory,
and are typically installed in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{prefix/share/ViennaRNA}}, where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{prefix}} is the
path that was used as installation prefix, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$HOME/Tutorial/Progs/VRP}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr}} when installed globally using a package manager.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNApvmin}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNApvmin:the-program-rnapvmin}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNApvmin::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNApvmin:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The program \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNApvmin}} reads a RNA sequence from \sphinxstyleemphasis{stdin} and uses an iterative minimization
process to calculate a perturbation vector that minimizes the discripancies between predicted
pairing probabilites and observed pairing probabilities (deduced from given shape
reactivities) {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id7}{Washietl \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.}, 2012}{]}.
The experimental SHAPE data has to be present in the file format described above.
The application will write the calculated vector of perturbation energies to \sphinxstyleemphasis{stdout},
while the progress of the minimization process is written to \sphinxstyleemphasis{stderr}.
The resulting perturbation vector can be interpreted directly and gives usefull insights into the
discrepancies between thermodynamic prediction and experimentally determined pairing status.
In addition the perturbation energies can be used to constrain folding with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNApvmin rna.shape \PYGZlt{} rna.seq \PYGZgt{}vector.csv
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}shape=vector.csv \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}shapeMethod=W \PYGZlt{} rna.seq
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The perturbation vector file uses the same file format as the SHAPE data file.
Instead of SHAPE reactivities the raw perturbation energies will be storred in the last column.
Since the energy model is only adjusted when necessary, the calculated perturbation energies may be used
for the interpretation of the secondary structure prediction, since they indicate
which positions require major energy model adjustments in order to yield a prediction
result close to the experimental data. High perturbation energies for just
a few nucleotides may indicate the occurrence of features, which are not explicitly
handled by the energy model, such as posttranscriptional modifications and
intermolecular interactions.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAsubopt:the-program-rnasubopt}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAsubopt::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAsubopt:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} calculates all suboptimal secondary structures within a
given energy range above the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} structure {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id33}{Wuchty \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.}, 1999}{]}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Be careful, the number of structures returned grows exponentially with both
sequence length and energy range.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Suboptimal folding}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAsubopt:suboptimal-folding}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Generate all suboptimal structures within a certain energy range
from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} specified by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}e}} option:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAsubopt \PYGZhy{}e 1 \PYGZhy{}s \PYGZlt{} test.seq
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA   \PYGZhy{}500    100
...........((((...)))).  \PYGZhy{}5.00
....((((...))))........  \PYGZhy{}4.80
(((.((((...))))..)))...  \PYGZhy{}4.20
...((.((.((...)).)).)).  \PYGZhy{}4.10
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The text output shows an energy sorted list (option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}s}}) of all secondary
structures within 1\textasciitilde{}kcal/mol of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} structure. Our sequence actually
has a ground state structure (\sphinxhyphen{}5.70) and three structures within 1\textasciitilde{}kcal/mol
range.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} folding alone gives no indication that there are actually a number
of plausible structures. Remember that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} cannot automatically
plot structures, therefore you can use the tool \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAplot}}. Note that you
\sphinxstylestrong{can’t} simply pipe the  output of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAplot}} using:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAsubopt \PYGZlt{} test.seq | RNAplot
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You need to manually create a file for each structure you want to plot.
Here, for example we created a new file named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{suboptstructure.txt}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}} \PYG{n}{suboptstructure}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{4.20}
\PYG{n}{CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA}
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fasta header is optional, but useful (without it the outputfile will
be named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rna.ps}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The next two lines contain the sequence and the suboptimal structure you
want to plot; in this case we plotted the structure with the folding
energy of \sphinxhyphen{}4.20.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Then plot it with

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAplot \PYGZlt{} suboptstructure.txt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the number of suboptimal structures grows exponentially with
sequence length and therefore this approach is only tractable for
sequences with less than 100 nt. To keep the number of suboptimal
structures manageable the option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}noLP}} can be used, forcing
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} to produce only structures without isolated base
pairs. While \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} produces \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} structures within an
energy range, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mfold}} produces only a few, hopefully representative,
structures. Try folding the sequence on the mfold
server at \sphinxurl{http://mfold.rna.albany.edu/?q=mfold}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sometimes you want to get information about unusual properties of the
Boltzmann ensemble (the sum of all RNA structures possible) for which no
specialized program exists. For example you want to know all fractions
of a bacterial mRNA in the Boltzmann ensemble where the Shine\sphinxhyphen{}Dalgarno (SD)
sequence is unpaired. If the SD sequence is concealed by secondary
structure the translation efficiency is reduced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In such cases you can resort to drawing a representative sample of
structures from the Boltzmann ensemble by using the option
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}p}}. Now you can simply count how many structures in the sample
possess the feature you are looking for. This number divided by the
size of your sample gives you the desired fraction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following example calculates the fraction of structures in the
ensemble that have bases 6 to 8 unpaired.


\subsubsection{Sampling the Boltzmann Ensemble}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAsubopt:sampling-the-boltzmann-ensemble}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} also implements a statisctical sampling algorithm to
draw secondary structures from the ensemble according to their equilibrium
probability {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id56}{Ding and Lawrence, 2003}{]}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Draw a sample of size 10,000 from the Boltzmann ensemble

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the desired property, e.g. by using a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{perl}} script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAsubopt \PYGZhy{}p 10000 \PYGZlt{} test.seq \PYGZgt{} tt
\PYGZdl{} perl \PYGZhy{}nle \PYGZsq{}\PYGZdl{}h++ if substr(\PYGZdl{}\PYGZus{},5,3) eq \PYGZdq{}...\PYGZdq{};
  END \PYGZob{}print \PYGZdl{}h/\PYGZdl{}.\PYGZcb{}\PYGZsq{} tt
  0.391960803919608
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A far better way to calculate this property is to use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold \sphinxhyphen{}p}}
to get the ensemble free energy, which is related to the partition
function via \(F = -RT\ln(Q)\), for the unconstrained (\(F_u\))
and the constrained case (\(F_c\)), where the three bases are not
allowed to form base pairs (use option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C}}), and evaluate
\(p_c = \exp((F_u - F_c)/RT)\) to get the desired probability.

\sphinxAtStartPar
So let’s do the calculation using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}p
Input string (upper or lower case); @ to quit
....,....1....,....2....,....3....,....4....,....5....,....6....,....7....,....8
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA
length = 23
CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA
...........((((...)))).
 minimum free energy =  \PYGZhy{}5.00 kcal/mol
....\PYGZob{},\PYGZob{}\PYGZob{}...||||...)\PYGZcb{}\PYGZcb{}\PYGZcb{}.
 free energy of ensemble =  \PYGZhy{}5.72 kcal/mol
....................... \PYGZob{}  0.00 d=4.66\PYGZcb{}
 frequency of mfe structure in ensemble 0.311796; ensemble diversity 6.36
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now we have calculated the free ensemble energy of the ensemble over all structures
\(F_u\), in the next step we have to calculate it for the structures using a
constraint (\(F_c\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following notation has to be used for defining the constraint:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{|}} : paired with another base

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}} : no constraint at all

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{x}} : base must not pair

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}}} : base i is paired with a base j\textless{}i

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textgreater{}}} : base i is paired with a base j\textgreater{}i

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
matching brackets \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{( )}}: base i pairs base j

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
So our constraint should look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{xxx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Next call the application with following command and provide the sequence
and constraint we just created:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZhy{}C
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output should look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{length} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{23}
\PYG{n}{CUACGGCGCGGCGCCCUUGGCGA}
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}
 \PYG{n}{minimum} \PYG{n}{free} \PYG{n}{energy} \PYG{o}{=}  \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{5.00} \PYG{n}{kcal}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{mol}
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}
 \PYG{n}{free} \PYG{n}{energy} \PYG{n}{of} \PYG{n}{ensemble} \PYG{o}{=}  \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{5.14} \PYG{n}{kcal}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{mol}
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{5.00} \PYG{n}{d}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.42}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
 \PYG{n}{frequency} \PYG{n}{of} \PYG{n}{mfe} \PYG{n}{structure} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{ensemble} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.792925}\PYG{p}{;} \PYG{n}{ensemble} \PYG{n}{diversity} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.79}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Afterwards evaluate the desired probability according to the formula given before
e.g. with a simple \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{perl}} script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} perl \PYGZhy{}e \PYGZsq{}print exp(\PYGZhy{}(5.72\PYGZhy{}5.14)/(0.00198*310.15)).\PYGZdq{}\PYGZbs{}n\PYGZdq{}\PYGZsq{}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can see that there is a slight difference between the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} run with 10,000
samples and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} run including all structures.


\section{Consensus Structure Prediction}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:consensus-structure-prediction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consensus structures can be predicted by a modified version of the
secondary structure prediction algorithm that takes as input a set of
aligned sequences instead of a single sequence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sequence co\sphinxhyphen{}variations are a direct consequence of RNA base pairing
rules and can be deduced to alignments. RNA helices normally contain
only 6 out of the 16 possible combinations: the Watson\sphinxhyphen{}Crick pairs
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CG}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{AU}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UA}}, and the somewhat weaker wobble pairs
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GU}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UG}}. Mutations in helical regions therefore have to be
correlated. In particular we often find \sphinxstyleemphasis{compensatory mutations}
where a mutation on one side of the helix is compensated by a second
mutation on the other side, e.g. a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CG}} pair changes into a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UA}} pair. Mutations where only one pairing partner changes (such
as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CG}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UG}} are termed \sphinxstyleemphasis{consistent mutations}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy function consists of the mean energy averaged over the
sequences, plus a covariance term that favors pairs with consistent
and compensatory mutations and penalizes pairs that cannot be formed
by all structures. For details see Hofacker \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id20}{2002}{]} and
Bernhart \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id22}{2008}{]}.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAalifold:the-program-rnaalifold}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAalifold::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAalifold:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} generalizes the folding algorithm for multiple sequence
alignments (MSA), treating the entire alignment as a single \sphinxstyleemphasis{generalized
sequence}.  To assign an energy to a structure on such a generalized
sequence, the energy is simply averaged over all sequences in the
alignment. This average energy is augmented by a covariance term, that
assigns a bonus or penalty to every possible base pair \((i,j)\)
based on the sequence variation in columns \(i\) and \(j\) of
the alignment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compensatory mutations are a strong indication of structural
conservation, while consistent mutations provide a weaker signal. The
covariance term used by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} therefore assigns a bonus
of 1 kcal/mol to each consistent and 2 kcal/mol for each compensatory
mutation. Sequences that cannot form a standard base pair incur a
penalty of \(-1\) kcal/mol. Thus, for every possible consensus pair
between two columns \(i\) and \(j\) of the alignment a covariance score
\(C_{ij}\) is computed by counting the fraction of sequence pairs
exhibiting consistent and compensatory mutations, as well as the
fraction of sequences that are inconsistent with the pair. The weight
of the covariance term relative to the normal energy function, as well
as the penalty for inconsistent mutations can be changed via command
line parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Apart from the covariance term, the folding algorithm in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} is essentially the same as for single sequence
folding. In particular, folding an alignment containing just one
sequence will give the same result as single sequence folding using
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}. For \(N\) sequences of length \(n\) the required CPU
time scales as \(\mathcal{O}(N\cdot n^2 + n^3)\) while memory
requirements grow as the square of the sequence length. Thus
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} is in general faster than folding each sequence
individually. The main advantage, however, is that the accuracy of
consensus structure predictions is generally much higher than for
single sequence folding, where typically only between 40\% and 70\% of
the base pairs are predicted correctly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Apart from prediction of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}} structures \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}}
also implements an algorithm to compute the partition function over
all possible (consensus) structures and the thermodynamic equilibrium
probability for each possible pair. These base pairing probabilities
are useful to see structural alternatives, and to distinguish well
defined regions, where the predicted structure is most likely correct,
from ambiguous regions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a first example we’ll produce a consensus structure prediction for
the following four tRNA sequences.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} cat \PYGZgt{} four.seq
\PYGZgt{}M10740 Yeast\PYGZhy{}PHE
GCGGAUUUAGCUCAGUUGGGAGAGCGCCAGACUGAAGAUUUGGAGGUCCUGUGUUCGAUCCACAGAAUUCGCA
\PYGZgt{}K00349 Drosophila\PYGZhy{}PHE
GCCGAAAUAGCUCAGUUGGGAGAGCGUUAGACUGAAGAUCUAAAGGUCCCCGGUUCAAUCCCGGGUUUCGGCA
\PYGZgt{}K00283 Halobacterium volcanii Lys\PYGZhy{}tRNA\PYGZhy{}1
GGGCCGGUAGCUCAUUUAGGCAGAGCGUCUGACUCUUAAUCAGACGGUCGCGUGUUCGAAUCGCGUCCGGCCCA
\PYGZgt{}AF346993
CAGAGUGUAGCUUAACACAAAGCACCCAACUUACACUUAGGAGAUUUCAACUUAACUUGACCGCUCUGA
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} uses aligned sequences as input. Thus, our first step will be
to align the sequences. We use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clustalw2}} in this example, since it’s one
of the most widely used alignment programs and has been shown to work well on
structural RNAs. Other alignment programs can be used (including programs that
attempt to do structural alignment of RNAs), but for this example the resulting
multiple sequence alignment should be in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Clustal}} format. Get \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clustalw2}}
and install it as you have done it with the other packages:
\sphinxurl{http://www.clustal.org/clustal2}.


\subsubsection{Consensus Structure from related Sequences}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAalifold:consensus-structure-from-related-sequences}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prepare a sequence file (use file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{four.seq}} and copy it to your working directory)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Align the sequences

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the consensus structure from the alignment

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inspect the output files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alifold.out}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alirna.ps}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alidot.ps}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For comparison fold the sequences individually using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} clustalw2 four.seq \PYGZgt{} four.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Clustalw2}} creates two more output files, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{four.aln}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{four.dnd}}.
For \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} you need the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.aln}} file.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAalifold \PYGZhy{}p four.aln
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZlt{} four.seq
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

The output contains a consensus sequence and the consensus structure in
dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation. The consensus structure has an energy of
\(-15.12\) kcal/mol, which in turn consists of the average free energy of
the structure \(-13.70\) kcal/mol and the covariance term \(-1.43\)
kcal/mol. The strongly negative covariance term shows that there must be a
fair number of consistent and compensatory mutations, but in contrast to the
average free energy it’s not meaningful in the biophysical sense.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare the predicted consensus structure with the structures predicted for
the individual sequences using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}}. How often is the correct
{\color{red}\bfseries{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}clover\sphinxhyphen{}leaf’’ shape predicted?

\sphinxAtStartPar

structure drawing can be generated by using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}aln}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}color}}
options of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last output file produced by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold \sphinxhyphen{}p}}, named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alifold.out}},
is a plain text file with detailed information on all plausible base pairs
sorted by the likelihood of the pair.  In the example above we see that the
pair \((6,72)\) has no inconsistent sequences, is predicted almost with
probability 1, and occurs as a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GC}} pair in two sequences, a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GU}} pair
in one, and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{AU}} pair in another.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} automatically produces a drawing of the consensus structure
in Postscript format and writes it to the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alirna.ps}}. In the
structure graph consistent and compensatory mutations are marked by a
circle around the variable base(s), i.e. pairs where one pairing partner
is encircled exhibit consistent mutations, whereas pairs supported by
compensatory mutations have both bases marked. Pairs that cannot be formed
by some of the sequences are shown gray instead of black.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The structure layout and dotplot files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alirna.ps}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alidot.ps}}
should look as follows:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.450\linewidth]{{alirna}.png} \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.450\linewidth]{{alidot}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the example given, many pairs show such inconsistencies. This is because
one of the sequences (AF346993) is not aligned well by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clustalw}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subsequent calls to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} will overwrite any existing output
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alirna.ps}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alidot.ps}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alifold.out}}) files in the current
directory. Be sure to rename any files you want to keep.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Structure predictions for the individual sequences}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAalifold:structure-predictions-for-the-individual-sequences}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The consensus structure computed by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}} will contain only
pairs that can be formed by most of the sequences. The structures of the
individual sequences will typically have additional base pairs that are not
part of the consensus structure. Moreover, ncRNA may exhibit a highly
conserved core structure while other regions are more variable. It may
therefore be desirable to produce structure predictions for one particular
sequence, while still using covariance information from other sequences.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be accomplished by first computing the consensus structure for all
sequences using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAalifold}}, then folding individual sequences using
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold \sphinxhyphen{}C}} with the consensus structure as a constraint. In
constraint folding mode \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold \sphinxhyphen{}C}} allows only base pairs to form
which are compatible with the constraint structure. This resulting
structure typically contains most of the constraint (the consensus
structure)  plus some additional pairs that are specific for this sequence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{refold.pl}} script removes gaps and maps the consensus structure to
each individual sequence.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAalifold  RNaseP.aln \PYGZgt{} RNaseP.alifold
\PYGZdl{} gv alirna.ps
\PYGZdl{} refold.pl RNaseP.aln RNaseP.alifold | head \PYGZhy{}3 \PYGZgt{} RNaseP.cfold
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold \PYGZhy{}C \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}noLP \PYGZlt{} RNaseP.cfold \PYGZgt{} RNaseP.refold
\PYGZdl{} gv E\PYGZhy{}coli\PYGZus{}ss.ps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you compare the refolded structure (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E\sphinxhyphen{}coli\_ss.ps}}) with the
structure you get by simply folding the E.coli sequence in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNaseP.seq}} file (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}noLP}}) you find a clear rearrangement.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In cases where constrained folding results in a structure that is very
different from the consensus, or if the energy from constrained
folding is much worse than from unconstrained folding, this may
indicate that the sequence in question does not really share a common
structure with the rest of the alignment or is misaligned. One should
then either remove or re\sphinxhyphen{}align that sequence and recompute the
consensus structure.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that since RNase P forms sizable pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots, a perfect
prediction is impossible in this case.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA interaction}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:rna-rna-interaction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A common problem is the prediction of binding sites between two RNAs, as in
the case of miRNA\sphinxhyphen{}mRNA interactions. Following tools of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}}
can be used to calculate base pairing probabilities.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAcofold:the-program-rnacofold}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAcofold::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAcofold:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}} works much like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} but uses two RNA sequences as input
which are then allowed to form a dimer structure. In the input the two RNA
sequences should be concatenated using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\&}} character as separator. As
in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAfold}} the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}p}} option can be used to compute partition function
and base pairing probabilities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since dimer formation is concentration dependent, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}} can be used
to compute equilibrium concentrations for all five monomer and
(homo/hetero)\sphinxhyphen{}dimer species, given input concentrations for the monomers
(see the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{man}} page for details).


\subsubsection{Two Sequences one Structure}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAcofold:two-sequences-one-structure}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prepare a sequence file (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t.seq}}) for input that looks like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{t}
\PYG{n}{GCGCUUCGCCGCGCGCC}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{GCGCUUCGCCGCGCGCA}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAcofold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZlt{} t.seq
\PYGZgt{}t
GCGCUUCGCCGCGCGCC\PYGZam{}GCGCUUCGCCGCGCGCA
((((..((..((((...\PYGZam{}))))..))..))))... (\PYGZhy{}17.70)

\subsubsection{Concentration Dependency}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAcofold:concentration-dependency}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Cofolding is an intermolecular process, therefore whether duplex formation will
actually occur is concentration dependent. Trivially, if one of the molecules is
not present, no dimers are going to be formed. The partition functions of the
molecules give us the equilibrium constants:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}K_{AB} = \frac{[AB]}{[A][B]} = \frac{Z_{AB}}{Z_AZ_B}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with these and mass conservation, the equilibrium concentration of homodimers,
heterodimers and monomers can be computed in dependence of the start concentrations
of the two molecules.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is most easily done by creating a file with the initial concentrations of
molecules \(A\) and \(B\) in two columns:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{a\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{l}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{b\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{l}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{a\PYGZus{}2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{l}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{b\PYGZus{}2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{l}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{]}

\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{a\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{l}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{b\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{l}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prepare a concentration file for input with this little \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{perl}} script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} perl \PYGZhy{}e \PYGZsq{}\PYGZdl{}c=1e\PYGZhy{}07; do \PYGZob{}print \PYGZdq{}\PYGZdl{}c\PYGZbs{}t\PYGZdl{}c\PYGZbs{}n\PYGZdq{}; \PYGZdl{}c*=1.71;\PYGZcb{} while \PYGZdl{}c\PYGZlt{}0.2\PYGZsq{} \PYGZgt{} concfile
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This script creates a file displaying values from 1e\sphinxhyphen{}07 to just below 0.2,
with 1.71\sphinxhyphen{}fold steps in between. For convenience, concentration of molecule A
is the same as concentration of molecule B in each row. This will facilitate
visualization of the results.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MFE}}, the ensemble properties and the concentration dependency
of hybridization:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAcofold \PYGZhy{}f concfile \PYGZlt{} t.seq \PYGZgt{} cofold.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Look at the generated output with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} less cofold.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which should be similar to:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{n}{Free} \PYG{n}{Energies}\PYG{p}{:}
\PYG{n}{AB}              \PYG{n}{AA}              \PYG{n}{BB}              \PYG{n}{A}               \PYG{n}{B}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{18.261023}      \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{17.562553}      \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{18.274376}      \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{7.017902}       \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{7.290237}
\PYG{n}{Initial} \PYG{n}{concentrations}          \PYG{n}{relative} \PYG{n}{Equilibrium} \PYG{n}{concentrations}
\PYG{n}{A}                \PYG{n}{B}               \PYG{n}{AB}              \PYG{n}{AA}              \PYG{n}{BB}              \PYG{n}{A}               \PYG{n}{B}
\PYG{l+m+mf}{1e\PYGZhy{}07}           \PYG{l+m+mf}{1e\PYGZhy{}07}           \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.00003}         \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.00002}         \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.00002}         \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.49994}         \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.49993}
\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The five different free energies were printed out first, followed by a list
of all the equilibrium concentrations, where the first two columns denote the
initial (absolute) concentrations of molecules \(A\) and \(B\),
respectively. The next five columns denote the equilibrium concentrations
of dimers and monomers, relative to the total particle number.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The concentrations don’t add up to one, except in the case where no dimers
are built \textendash{} if you want to know the fraction of particles in a dimer, you
have to take the relative dimer concentrations times 2.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since relative concentrations of species depend on two independent values \sphinxhyphen{}
initial concentration of A as well as initial concentration of B \sphinxhyphen{} it is not
trivial to visualize the results. For this reason we used the same concentration
for A and for B. Another possibility would be to keep the initial concentration of
one molecule constant.
As an example we show the following plot of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t.seq}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now we use some commandline tools to render our plot. We use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tail \sphinxhyphen{}n +11}} to
show all lines starting with line 11 (1\sphinxhyphen{}10 are cut) and pipe it into an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{awk}}
command, which prints every column but the first from our input.
This is then piped to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xmgrace}}.
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}log x \sphinxhyphen{}nxy \sphinxhyphen{}}} we tell it to plot the x axis in logarithmic scale and to
read data file in X Y1 Y2 … format.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} tail \PYGZhy{}n +11 cofold.out | awk \PYGZsq{}\PYGZob{}print \PYGZdl{}2, \PYGZdl{}3, \PYGZdl{}4, \PYGZdl{}5, \PYGZdl{}6, \PYGZdl{}7\PYGZcb{}\PYGZsq{} | xmgrace \PYGZhy{}log x \PYGZhy{}nxy \PYGZhy{}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Concentration Dependency Plot}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAcofold:concentration-dependency-plot}}
\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.660\linewidth]{{tconcdep}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since the two sequences are almost identical, the monomer and homo\sphinxhyphen{}dimer
concentrations behave very similarly. In this example, at a concentration of
about 1 mmol 50\% of the molecule is still in monomer form.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAduplex:the-program-rnaduplex}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAduplex::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAduplex:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the sequences are very long (many kb) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}} is too slow
to be useful. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} program is a fast alternative, that works by
predicting \sphinxstyleemphasis{only} intermolecular base pairs. It’s almost as fast as simple
sequence alignment, but much more accurate than a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLAST}} search.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The example below searches the 3’ UTR of an mRNA for a miRNA binding site.


\subsubsection{Binding site prediction with \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAduplex:binding-site-prediction-with-rnaduplex}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{duplex.seq}} contains the 3’UTR of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NM\_024615}} and the
microRNA mir\sphinxhyphen{}145.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAduplex \PYGZlt{} duplex.seq
\PYGZgt{}NM\PYGZus{}024615
\PYGZgt{}hsa\PYGZhy{}miR\PYGZhy{}145
.(((((.(((...((((((((((.\PYGZam{})))))))))))))))))).  34,57  :   1,19  (\PYGZhy{}21.90)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most favorable binding has an interaction energy of \sphinxhyphen{}21.90 kcal/mol and pairs
up on positions 34\sphinxhyphen{}57 of the UTR with positions 1\sphinxhyphen{}22 of the miRNA.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} can also produce alternative binding sites, e.g. running
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex \sphinxhyphen{}e 10}} would list all binding sites within 10 kcal/mol of
the best one.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} forms only intermolecular pairs, it neglects the
competition between intramolecular folding and hybridization. Thus, it is
recommended to use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} as a pre\sphinxhyphen{}filter and analyse good
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} hits additionally with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAup}}. Using the example above, running \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAup}} will yield:


\subsubsection{Binding site prediction with \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAup}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAduplex:binding-site-prediction-with-rnaup}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAup \PYGZhy{}b \PYGZlt{} duplex.seq
\PYGZgt{}NM\PYGZus{}024615
\PYGZgt{}hsa\PYGZhy{}miR\PYGZhy{}145
(((((((\PYGZam{})))))))  50,56  :   1,7   (\PYGZhy{}8.41 = \PYGZhy{}9.50 + 0.69 + 0.40)
GCUGGAU\PYGZam{}GUCCAGU
RNAup output in file: hsa\PYGZhy{}miR\PYGZhy{}145\PYGZus{}NM\PYGZus{}024615\PYGZus{}w25\PYGZus{}u1.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The free energy of the duplex is \sphinxhyphen{}9.50 kcal/mol and shows a discrepancy to the
structure and energy value computed by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} (differences may arise from
the fact that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAup}} computes partition functions rather than optimal
structures).

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, the total free energy of binding is less favorable (\sphinxhyphen{}8.41 kcal/mol),
since it includes the energetic penalty for opening the binding site on the
mRNA (0.69 kcal/mol) and miRNA (0.40 kcal/mol). The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}b}} option includes the
probability of unpaired regions in both RNAs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}} on the example to see the complete structure
after hybridization (neither \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} nor \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAup}} produce structure
drawings). Note however, that the input format for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}} is different.
An input file suitable for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAcofold}} has to be created from the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{duplex.seq}} file first (use any text editor).

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a more difficult example, let’s look at the interaction of the bacterial
smallRNA RybB and its target mRNA ompN. First we’ll try predicting the binding
site using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAduplex \PYGZlt{} RybB.seq
\PYGZgt{}RybB
\PYGZgt{}ompN
.((((..((((((.(((....((((((((..(((((.((..((.((....((((..(((((((((((..((((((\PYGZam{}
.))))))..))))))).)))).....))))....)).)).)).))).))..))))........))))..))).)))))).)))).
 5,79  :  80,164 (\PYGZhy{}34.60)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note, that the predicted structure spans almost the full length of the RybB small RNA.
Compare the predicted interaction to the structures predicted for RybB and ompN alone,
and ask yourself whether the predicted interaction is indeed plausible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below the structure of ompN on the left and RybB on the right side. The respective
binding regions predicted by RNAduplex are marked in red:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.450\linewidth]{{ompN_ss}.png} \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.250\linewidth]{{RybB_ss}.png}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{GCCAC}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{TGCTTTTCTTTGATGTCCCCATTTT}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{GTGGA}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{GC}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{CCATCAACCCCGCCATTTCGGTT}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{CAAG}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{GTTGGTGGGTTTTTT}
 \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}      \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}  \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}    \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}        \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}  \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}    \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}     \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}  \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}  \PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{40.30}
\PYG{n}{AGGTCAAACAACGGC}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{AGAAACAATATT}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{TAAAGTCGCCGCACACGACGCGGTCGTCGGT}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{CGTCTCGGCCCTACTGTTCACGGTTATGAAAAGAAACC}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

Compare the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAduplex}} prediction with the interaction predicted by

\section{Plotting Structures}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:plotting-structures}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAplot}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAplot:the-program-rnaplot}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAplot::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAplot:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can manually add additional annotation to structure drawings using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAplot}}
program (for information see its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{man}} page). Here’s a somewhat complicated example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAfold 5S.seq \PYGZgt{} 5S.fold
\PYGZdl{} RNAplot \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}pre \PYGZdq{}76 107 82 102 GREEN BFmark 44 49 0.8 0.8 0.8 Fomark \PYGZbs{}
  1 15 8 RED omark 80 cmark 80 \PYGZhy{}0.23 \PYGZhy{}1.2 (pos80) Label 90 95 BLUE Fomark\PYGZdq{} \PYGZlt{} 5S.fold
\PYGZdl{} gv 5S\PYGZus{}ss.ps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.500\linewidth]{{5S_ss}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}


\subsubsection{PostScript macros}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAplot:postscript-macros}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAplot}} is a very useful tool to color structure layout plots. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}pre}} tag adds
PostScript code required to color distinct regions of your molecule. There are some predefined
statements with different options for annotations listed below:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxstyletheadfamily 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Command
&\sphinxstyletheadfamily 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Description
\\
\sphinxmidrule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{i cmark}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
draws circle around base i
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{i j c gmark}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
draw basepair i,j with c counter examples in grey
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{i j lw rgb omark}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
stroke segment i…j with linewidth lw and color (rgb)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{i j rgb Fomark}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
fill segment i…j with color (rgb)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{i j k l rgb BFmark}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
fill block between pairs i,j and k,l with color (rgb)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{i dx dy (text) Label}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
adds a textlabel with an offset dx and dy relative to base i
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Predefined color options are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLACK, RED, GREEN, BLUE, WHITE}} but you can also
replace the value to some standard RGB code (e.g. 0 5 8 for lightblue).

\sphinxAtStartPar
To simply add the annotation macros to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PostScript}} file without
any actual annotation you can use the following program call

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{}\PYG{+w}{ }RNAplot\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}pre\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZlt{}\PYG{+w}{ }5S.fold
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you now open the structure layout file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{5S\_ss.ps}} with a text editor you’ll see
the additional macros for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmark}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omark}}, etc. along with some show synopsis
on how to use them. Actual annotations can then be added between the lines:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}} \PYG{n}{Start} \PYG{n}{Annotations}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}} \PYG{n}{End} \PYG{n}{Annotations}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, you simply need to add the same string of commands you would provide through the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}pre}} option of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAplot}}.


\section{RNA Design}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:rna-design}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNAinverse}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAinverse:the-program-rnainverse}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAinverse::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAinverse:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAinverse}} searches for sequences folding into a predefined structure,
thereby inverting the folding algorithm. Input consists of the target
structures (in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation) and a starting sequence, which is
optional.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lower case characters in the start sequence indicate fixed positions,
i.e. they can be used to add sequence constraints. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{N}}’s in the
starting sequence will be replaced by a random nucleotide.
For each search the best sequence found and its Hamming distance to the
start sequence are printed to \sphinxstyleemphasis{stdout}. If the the search was
unsuccessful a structure distance to the target is appended.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default the program stops as soon as it finds a sequence that has the
target as MFE structure. The option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}Fp}} switches \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAinverse}} to
the partition function mode where the probability of the target structure
\(\exp(-E(S)/RT) / Z\) is maximized. This tends to produce sequences
with a more well\sphinxhyphen{}defined structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This probability is written in dot\sphinxhyphen{}brackets after the found sequence
and Hamming distance. With the option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}R}} you can specify how often
the search should be repeated.


\subsubsection{Sequence Design}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAinverse:sequence-design}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prepare an input file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{inv.in}} containing the target structure and
sequence constraints:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{NNNgNNNNNNNNNNaNNN}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Design sequences using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAinverse}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAinverse \PYGZlt{} inv.in
  GGUgUUGGAUCCGAaACC    5
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or design even more sequences with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNAinverse \PYGZhy{}R5 \PYGZhy{}Fp \PYGZlt{} inv.in
  GGUgUGAACCCUCGaACC    5
  GGCgCCCUUUUGGGaGCC   12  (0.967418)
  CUCgAUCUCACGAUaGGG    6
  GGCgCCCGAAAGGGaGCC   13  (0.967548)
  GUUgAGCCCAUGCUaAGC    6
  GGCgCCCUUAUGGGaGCC   10  (0.967418)
  CGGgUGUUGUGACAaCCG    5
  GCGgGUCGAAAGGCaCGC   12  (0.925482)
  GCCgUAUCCGGGUGaGGC    6
  GGCgCCCUUUUGGGaGCC   13  (0.967418)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output consists of the calculated sequence and the number of mutations
needed to get the MFE\sphinxhyphen{}structure from the start sequence (start sequence not
shown). Additionaly, with the partition function folding (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}Fp}}) set, the
second output is another refinement so that the ensemble preferes the MFE
and folds into your given structure with a distinct probability, shown in
brackets.


\subsubsection{Other RNA design tools}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNAinverse:other-rna-design-tools}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Another useful program for inverse folding is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA designer}}, see
\sphinxurl{http://www.rnasoft.ca}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA Designer}} takes a secondary structure description
as input and returns an RNA strand that is likely to fold in the given
secondary structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sequence design application}} of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Design Webservices}},
see \sphinxurl{http://nibiru.tbi.univie.ac.at/rnadesign/index.html}, uses a different approach,
allowing for more than one secondary structure as input. For more detail read
the online Documentation and the next section of this tutorial.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{switch.pl}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/switch:the-program-switch-pl}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/switch::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/switch:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.pl}} script can be used to design bi\sphinxhyphen{}stable structures, i.e.
structures with two almost equally good foldings. For two given structures
there are always a lot of sequences compatible with both structures. If both
structures are reasonably stable you can find sequences where both target
structures have almost equal energy and all other structures have much higher
energies.
Combined with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barriers}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}}, this is a very
useful tool for designing RNA switches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The input requires two structures in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation and additionally
you can add a sequence. It is also possible to calculate the switching
function at two different temperatures with option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}T}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}T2}}.


\subsubsection{Designing a Switch}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/switch:designing-a-switch}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now we try to create an RNA switch using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.pl}} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id31}{Flamm \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.}, 2001}{]}.
First we create our inputfile, then invoke the program using ten optimization
runs  (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}n 10}}) and do not allow \sphinxstyleemphasis{lonely pairs}. Write it out to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.out}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} cat \PYGZgt{} switch.in
((((((((......))))))))....((((((((.......))))))))
((((((((((((((((((........)))))))))))))))))).....

\PYGZdl{} switch.pl \PYGZhy{}n 10 \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}noLP \PYGZlt{} switch.in \PYGZgt{} switch.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.out}} should look similar like this, the first block represents our
bi\sphinxhyphen{}stable structures in random order, the second block shows the resulting
sequences ordered by their score.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} cat switch.out
GGGUGGACGUUUCGGUCCAUCCUUACGGACUGGGGCGUUUACCUAGUCC   0.9656
CAUUUGGCUUGUGUGUCGAAUGGCCCCGGUACGUAGGCUAAAUGUACCG   1.2319
GGGGGGUGCGUUCACACCCCUCAUUUGGUGUGGAUGUGCUUUCUACACU   1.1554
[...]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
the resulting sequences are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{CAUUUGGCUUGUGUGUCGAAUGGCCCCGGUACGUAGGCUAAAUGUACCG}   \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.2319}
\PYG{n}{GGGGGGUGCGUUCACACCCCUCAUUUGGUGUGGAUGUGCUUUCUACACU}   \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.1554}
\PYG{n}{CGGGUUGUAACUGGAUAGCCUGGAAACUGUUUGGUUGUAAUCCGAACAG}   \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0956}
\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given all 10 suggestions in our \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.out}}, we select the one with the
best score with some command line tools to use it as an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} input
file and build up the barriers tree.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} tail \PYGZhy{}10 switch.out | awk \PYGZsq{}\PYGZob{}print(\PYGZdl{}1)\PYGZcb{}\PYGZsq{}  | head \PYGZhy{}n 1 \PYGZgt{} subopt.in
\PYGZdl{} RNAsubopt \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}noLP \PYGZhy{}s \PYGZhy{}e 25 \PYGZlt{} subopt.in \PYGZgt{} subopt.out
\PYGZdl{} barriers \PYGZhy{}G RNA\PYGZhy{}noLP \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}bsize \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rates \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}minh 2 \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}max 30 \PYGZlt{} subopt.out \PYGZgt{} barriers.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tail \sphinxhyphen{}10}} cuts the last 10 lines from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.out}} file and pipes
them into an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{awk}} script. The function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{print(\$1)}} echoes only the first
column and this is piped into the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{head}} program where the first line, which
equals the best scored sequence, is taken and written into \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{subopt.in}}.
Then \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}} is called to process our sequence and write the output to
another file which is the input for the barriers calculation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below you find an example of the barrier tree calculation above done with the
right settings (connected root) on the left side and the wrong \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubobt \sphinxhyphen{}e}}
value on the right. Keep in mind that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.pl}} performs a stochastic search
and the output sequences are different every time because there are a lot of
sequences which fit the structure and switch calculates a new one everytime.
Simply try to make sure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.480\linewidth]{{switch_barriertree}.png} \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.480\linewidth]{{switch_barriertree_e13}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
left: Barriers tree as it should look like, all branches connected to the main root
right: disconnected tree due to a too low energy range (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}e}}) parameter set in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAsubopt}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Be careful to set the range \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}e}} high enough, otherwise we get a problem when
calculation the kinetics using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}}. Every branch should be somehow connected
to the main root of the tree. Try \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}e 20}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}e 30}} to see the difference in
the trees and choose the optimal value. By using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}max 30}} we shorten our tree
to focus only on the lowest minima.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We then select a branch preferably outside of the two main branches, here branch
30 (may differ from your own calculation). Look at the barrier tree to find the
best branch to start and replace \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{30}} by the branch you would choose. Now use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}} to plot concentration kinetics and think about the graph you just
created.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} treekin \PYGZhy{}m I \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}p0 30=1  \PYGZlt{} barriers.out \PYGZgt{} treekin.out
\PYGZdl{} xmgrace \PYGZhy{}log x \PYGZhy{}nxy treekin.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The graph could look like the one below, remember everytime you use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{switch.pl}}
it can give you different sequences so the output varies too. Here the one from
the example.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.660\linewidth]{{switch_treekin}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}


\section{RNA folding kinetics}
\label{\detokenize{getting_started:rna-folding-kinetics}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
RNA folding kinetics describes the dynamical process of how a RNA molecule
approaches to its unique folded biological active conformation (often
referred to as the native state) starting from an initial ensemble of
disordered conformations e.g. the unfolded open chain. The key for
resolving the dynamical behavior of a folding RNA chain lies in the
understanding of the ways in which the molecule explores its astronomically
large free energy landscape, a rugged and complex hyper\sphinxhyphen{}surface established
by all the feasible base pairing patterns a RNA sequence can form. The
challenge is to understand how the interplay of formation and break up of
base pairing interactions along the RNA chain can lead to an efficient
search in the energy landscape which reaches the native state of the
molecule on a biologically meaningful time scale.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{The Program \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNA2Dfold}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNA2Dfold:the-program-rna2dfold}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/RNA2Dfold::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA2Dfold}} is a tool for computing the MFE structure, partition function and
representative sample structures of \(\kappa, \lambda\) neighborhoods
and projects an high dimensional energy landscape of RNA into two dimensions {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id30}{Lorenz \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.}, 2009}{]}.
Therefore a sequence and two user\sphinxhyphen{}defined reference structures are expected by
the program. For each of the resulting distance class, the MFE representative,
the Boltzmann probabilities and the Gibbs free energy is computed. Additionally,
representative suboptimal secondary structures from each partition can be
calculated.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} RNA2Dfold \PYGZhy{}p \PYGZlt{} 2dfold.inp \PYGZgt{} 2dfold.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

For visualizing the output the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}} includes two scripts
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2Dlandscape\_pf.gri}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2Dlandscape\_mfe.gri}} located in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/share/ViennaRNA/}}.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gri}} (a language for scientific graphics programing) is needed to create a colored
postscript plot. We use the partition function script to show the free energies of
the distance classes (graph below, left):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} gri ../Progs/VRP/share/ViennaRNA/2Dlandscape\PYGZus{}pf.gri 2dfold.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare the output file with the colored plot and determine the MFE minima with
corresponding distance classes. For easier comparision the outputfile of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA2Dfold}}
can be sorted by a simple sort command. For further information regarding sort use
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}help}} option.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} sort \PYGZhy{}k6 \PYGZhy{}n 2dfold.out \PYGZgt{} sort.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now we choose the structure with the lowest energy besides our startstructure,
replace the open chain structure from our old input with that structure and repeat
the steps above with our new values:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA2Dfold}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
plot it using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2Dlandscape\_pf.gri}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The new projection (right graph) shows the two major local minima which are
separated by 39 bp (red dots in figure below) and both are likely to be populated
with high probability. The landscape gives an estimate of the energy barrier
separating the two minima (about \sphinxhyphen{}20 kcal/mol).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The red dots mark the distance from open chain to the MFE structure respectively
the distance from the 2nd best structure to the MFE. Note that the red dots were
manually added to the image afterwards so don’t panic if you don’t see them in your
gri output.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{The Programs \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{barriers}} and \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{treekin}}}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/barriers_treekin:the-programs-barriers-and-treekin}}\label{\detokenize{tutorial/barriers_treekin::doc}}

\subsubsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/barriers_treekin:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following assumes you already have the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barriers}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}}
programs installed. They are \sphinxstylestrong{not} part of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}}
but their latest releases can be found at
\sphinxurl{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/Barriers/} and
\sphinxurl{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/Treekin/}, respectively.
Installation proceeds as shown for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA Package}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One problem that often occurs during \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}} installation is the
dependency on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blas}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lapack}} packages. For further information
according to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barriers}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}} program also see the website.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{A short recall on howto install/compile a program}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/barriers_treekin:a-short-recall-on-howto-install-compile-a-program}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Get the barriers source from \sphinxurl{https://www.tbi.univie.ac.at/RNA/Barriers/}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
extract the archive and go to the directory:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} tar \PYGZhy{}xzf Barriers\PYGZhy{}1.5.2.tar.gz
\PYGZdl{} cd Barriers\PYGZhy{}1.5.2
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}prefix}} option to install in your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Progs/}} directory:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} ./configure \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}prefix=\PYGZdl{}HOME/Tutorial/Progs/barriers\PYGZhy{}1.5.2
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
make install:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} make
\PYGZdl{} make install
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barriers}} is ready to use. Apply the same steps to install \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Copy the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barriers}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}} binaries to your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bin}} folder
or add the path to your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}} environment variable.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Calculate the Barrier Tree}
\label{\detokenize{tutorial/barriers_treekin:calculate-the-barrier-tree}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{} echo UCCACGGCUGUUAGUGGAUAACGGC | RNAsubopt \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}noLP \PYGZhy{}s \PYGZhy{}e 10 \PYGZgt{} barseq.sub
\PYGZdl{} barriers \PYGZhy{}G RNA\PYGZhy{}noLP \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}bsize \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rates \PYGZlt{} barseq.sub \PYGZgt{} barseq.bar
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can restrict the number of local minima using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barriers}}
command\sphinxhyphen{}line option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}max}} followed by a number. The option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}G RNA\sphinxhyphen{}noLP}}
instructs barriers that the input consists of RNA secondary structures without
isolated basepairs. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}bsize}} adds size of the gradient basins and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}rates}}
tells \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barriers}} to compute rates between macro states/basins for use with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{treekin}}. Another useful options is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}minh}} to print only minima with
a barrier \(> dE\). Look at the output file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{barseq.bar}}, its content
should be like:
