\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAsubopt:cmdoption-shapeMethod}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod}}\DUrole{p}{=}method}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select SHAPE reactivity data incorporation strategy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(default=”D”)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following methods can be used to convert SHAPE reactivities into pseudo
energy contributions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{D}}: Convert by using the linear equation according to Deigan et al 2009.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Derived pseudo energy terms will be applied for every nucleotide involved in
a stacked pair. This method is recognized by a capital \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{D}} in the provided
parameter, i.e.: {\hyperref[\detokenize{man/RNALalifold:cmdoption-shapeMethod}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod=}}}}}”D” is the default setting. The slope \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}}
and the intercept \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{b}} can be set to a non\sphinxhyphen{}default value if necessary,
otherwise m=1.8 and b=\sphinxhyphen{}0.6. To alter these parameters, e.g. m=1.9 and b=\sphinxhyphen{}0.7,
use a parameter string like this: {\hyperref[\detokenize{man/RNALalifold:cmdoption-shapeMethod}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod=}}}}}”Dm1.9b\sphinxhyphen{}0.7”. You may also
provide only one of the two parameters like: {\hyperref[\detokenize{man/RNALalifold:cmdoption-shapeMethod}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod=}}}}}”Dm1.9” or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{man/RNALalifold:cmdoption-shapeMethod}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod=}}}}}”Db\sphinxhyphen{}0.7”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Z}}: Convert SHAPE reactivities to pseudo energies according to Zarringhalam

\sphinxAtStartPar
et al 2012. SHAPE reactivities will be converted to pairing probabilities by
using linear mapping. Aberration from the observed pairing probabilities will
be penalized during the folding recursion. The magnitude of the penalties can
affected by adjusting the factor beta (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{man/RNALalifold:cmdoption-shapeMethod}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeMethod=}}}}}”Zb0.8”).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{W}}: Apply a given vector of perturbation energies to unpaired nucleotides

\sphinxAtStartPar
according to Washietl et al 2012. Perturbation vectors can be calculated by
using RNApvmin.

\end{fulllineitems}

\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeConversion@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeConversion}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeConversion@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeConversion}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAsubopt:cmdoption-shapeConversion}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}shapeConversion}}\DUrole{p}{=}method}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select method for SHAPE reactivity conversion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(default=”O”)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This parameter is useful when dealing with the SHAPE incorporation according
to Zarringhalam et al. The following methods can be used to convert SHAPE
reactivities into the probability for a certain nucleotide to be unpaired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{M}}: Use linear mapping according to Zarringhalam et al.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}}: Use a cutoff\sphinxhyphen{}approach to divide into paired and unpaired nucleotides
(e.g. “C0.25”)
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S}}: Skip the normalizing step since the input data already represents
probabilities for being unpaired rather than raw reactivity values
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{L}}: Use a linear model to convert the reactivity into a probability for
being unpaired (e.g. “Ls0.68i0.2” to use a slope of 0.68 and an intercept
of 0.2)
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{O}}: Use a linear model to convert the log of the reactivity into a
probability for being unpaired (e.g. “Os1.6i\sphinxhyphen{}2.29” to use a slope of 1.6
and an intercept of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}2}}.29)

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Commands include hard and soft constraints, but also structure motifs in

commands can be set for unstructured and structured domains.

\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}m@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}m}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}m@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}m}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}modifications@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}modifications}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}modifications@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}modifications}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAsubopt:cmdoption-m}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAsubopt:cmdoption-modifications}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}m}}\DUrole{p}{,}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}modifications}}\DUrole{p}{{[}}=STRING\DUrole{p}{{]}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Allow for modified bases within the RNA sequence string.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(default=”7I6P9D”)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Treat modified bases within the RNA sequence differently, i.e. use
corresponding energy corrections and/or pairing partner rules if available.
For that, the modified bases in the input sequence must be marked by their
corresponding one\sphinxhyphen{}letter code. If no additional arguments are supplied, all
available corrections are performed. Otherwise, the user may limit the
modifications to a particular subset of modifications, resp. one\sphinxhyphen{}letter
codes, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}mP6}} will only correct for pseudouridine and m6A bases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently supported one\sphinxhyphen{}letter codes and energy corrections are:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{7}}: 7\sphinxhyphen{}deaza\sphinxhyphen{}adenonsine (7DA)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{I}}: Inosine

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{6}}: N6\sphinxhyphen{}methyladenosine (m6A)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{P}}: Pseudouridine

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{9}}: Purine (a.k.a. nebularine)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{D}}: Dihydrouridine

\end{fulllineitems}

\subsubsection{Model Details:}
\label{\detokenize{man/RNAsubopt:model-details}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tweak the energy model and pairing rules additionally using the following
parameters
\end{quote}
\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}d@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}d}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}d@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}d}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dangles@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dangles}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dangles@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dangles}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAsubopt:cmdoption-d}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAsubopt:cmdoption-dangles}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d}}\DUrole{p}{,}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dangles}}\DUrole{p}{=}INT}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
How to treat “dangling end” energies for bases adjacent to helices in free ends and multi\sphinxhyphen{}loops.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(default=”2”)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d1}} only unpaired bases can participate in at most one dangling end.
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d2}} this check is ignored, dangling energies will be added for the bases
adjacent to a helix on both sides in any case; this is the default for mfe
and partition function folding ({\hyperref[\detokenize{man/RNA2Dfold:cmdoption-p}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}p}}}}}).
The option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d0}} ignores dangling ends altogether (mostly for debugging).
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d3}} mfe folding will allow coaxial stacking of adjacent helices in
multi\sphinxhyphen{}loops. At the moment the implementation will not allow coaxial stacking
of the two interior pairs in a loop of degree 3 and works only for mfe
folding.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d1}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d3}} only the MFE computations will be using this
setting while partition function uses \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d2}} setting, i.e. dangling ends will be
treated differently.

\end{fulllineitems}

\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}noLP@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}noLP}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}noLP@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}noLP}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}

\subsection{DESCRIPTION}
\label{\detokenize{man/RNAup:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
RNAup 2.6.4

\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the thermodynamics of RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA interactions

\sphinxAtStartPar
RNAup calculates the thermodynamics of RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA interactions, by decomposing the
binding into two stages. (1) First the probability that a potential binding
sites remains unpaired (equivalent to the free energy needed to open the site)
is computed. (2) Then this accessibility is combined with the interaction
energy to obtain the total binding energy. All calculations are done by
computing partition functions over all possible conformations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
RNAup provides two different modes: By default RNAup computes accessibilities,
in terms of the free energies needed to open a region (default length 4). It
prints the region of highest accessibility and its opening energy to stdout,
opening energies for all other regions are written to a file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
.br
In interaction mode the interaction between two RNAs is calculated. It is
invoked if the input consists of two sequences concatenated with an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\&}},
or if the options \sphinxhyphen{}X{[}pf{]} or \sphinxhyphen{}b are given. Unless the \sphinxhyphen{}b option is specified
RNAup assumes that the longer RNA is a structured target sequence
while the shorter one is an unstructured small RNA.
.br
Additionally, for every position along the target sequence we write the best
free energy of binding for an interaction that includes this position to the
the output file.
Output to stdout consists of the location and free energy, dG,
for the optimal region of interaction. The binding energy dG is also split into
its components the interaction energy dGint and the opening energy dGu\_l (and
possibly dGu\_s for the shorter sequence).
.br
In addition we print the optimal interaction structure as computed by RNAduplex
for this region. Note that it can happen that the RNAduplex computed optimal
interaction does not coincide with the optimal RNAup region. If the two
predictions don’t match the structure string is replaced by a run of “.”
and a message is written to stderr.
.br

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each sequence should be in 5\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{} to 3\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{} direction. If the sequence is preceded
by a line of the form
.. code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}} \PYG{n}{name}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
the output file “name\_ux\_up.out” is produced, where the “x” in “ux” is the
value set by the \sphinxhyphen{}u option. Otherwise the file name defaults to
RNA\_ux\_up.out. The output is concatenated if a file with the same name exists.
.br

\sphinxAtStartPar
RNA sequences are read from stdin as strings of characters. White space and
newline within a sequence cause an error! Newline is used to separate
sequences. The program will continue to read new sequences until a line
consisting of the single character @ or an end of file condition is
encountered.

\subsubsection{Structure Constraints:}
\label{\detokenize{man/RNAup:structure-constraints}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Command line options to interact with the structure constraints feature of

\end{quote}
\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}C@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}C}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}C@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}C}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}\index{command line option@\spxentry{command line option}!\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}constraint@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}constraint}}\index{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}constraint@\spxentry{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}constraint}!command line option@\spxentry{command line option}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAup:cmdoption-C}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{man/RNAup:cmdoption-constraint}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C}}\DUrole{p}{,}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}constraint}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Apply structural constraint(s) during prediction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(default=off)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The program first reads the sequence(s), then a dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket like string
containing constraints on the structure. The following symbols are
recognized:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}} … no constraint for this base

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{x}} … the base is unpaired

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}}} … the base pairs downstream, i.e. i is paired with j \textgreater{} i

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textgreater{}}} … the base pairs upstream, i.e. i is paired with j \textless{} i

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{()}} … base i pairs with base j

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{|}} … the corresponding base has to be paired intermolecularily (only for

\sphinxAtStartPar
interaction mode)

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify “dangling end” model for bases adjacent to helices in free ends and multi\sphinxhyphen{}loops.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}d0}} ignores dangling ends altogether (mostly for debugging).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Allow other pairs in addition to the usual AU,GC,and GU pairs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Its argument is a comma separated list of additionally allowed pairs. If the
first character is a “\sphinxhyphen{}” then AB will imply that AB and BA are allowed
pairs, e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{man/RNALalifold:cmdoption-nsp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}nsp=}}}}}”\sphinxhyphen{}GA”  will allow GA and AG pairs. Nonstandard pairs are
given 0 stacking energy.

\end{fulllineitems}

\subsection{EXAMPLES}
\label{\detokenize{man/RNAup:examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
.B Output to stdout:

\sphinxAtStartPar
In Interaction mode RNAup prints the most favorable interaction energy
between the two sequences to stdout. The most favorable interaction energy
(dG) depends on the position in the longer sequence (region {[}i,j{]}) and the
position in the shorter sequence (region{[}k,l{]}): dG{[}i,j;k,l{]}.  dG{[}i,j;k,l{]} is the
largest contribution to dG{[}i,j{]} = sum\_kl dG{[}i,j;k,l{]} which is given in the
output file: therefore dG{[}i,j;k,l{]} \textless{}= dG{[}i,j{]}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
``....,....1....,....2....,....3....,....4....,....5....,....6....,....7....,....8``
\PYGZgt{} franz
GGAGUAGGUUAUCCUCUGUU
\PYGZgt{} sissi
AGGACAACCU
dG = dGint + dGu\PYGZus{}l
(((((.((((\PYGZam{})))).)))))   6,15  :   1,10  (\PYGZhy{}6.66 = \PYGZhy{}9.89 + 3.23)
AGGUUAUCCU\PYGZam{}AGGACAACCU
RNAup output in file: franz\PYGZus{}sissi\PYGZus{}w25\PYGZus{}u3\PYGZus{}4\PYGZus{}up.out
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where the result line contains following information

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{RNAduplex} \PYG{n}{results}       \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]}     \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{k}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{l}\PYG{p}{]}    \PYG{n}{dG} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{dGint} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{n}{dGu\PYGZus{}l}
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}   \PYG{l+m+mi}{6}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mi}{15}   \PYG{p}{:}  \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}     \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{6.66}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{9.89}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{l+m+mf}{3.23}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
.RD
.B Output to file:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Output to file contains a header including date, the command line of the
call to RNAup, length and names of the input sequence(s) followed
by the sequence(s). The first sequence is the target sequence.
Printing of the header can be turned off using the \sphinxhyphen{}nh option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The line directly after the header gives the column names for the output:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{position}     \PYG{n}{dGu\PYGZus{}l} \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{u} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}      \PYG{n}{dGu\PYGZus{}l} \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{u} \PYG{l+m+mi}{4}       \PYG{n}{dG}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}     pos      u3S       u3H       u4S       u4H        dG}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where all information refers to the target sequence. The dGu\_l column contains
information about the \sphinxhyphen{}u value (u=3 or u=4) and the contribution to the free
energy to open all structures “S” or only hairpin loops “H”, see option \sphinxhyphen{}c.
NA means that no results is possible (e.g. column u3S row 2: no region of
length 3 ending at position 2 exists).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  Thu Apr 10 09:15:11 2008}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  RNAup \PYGZhy{}u 3,4 \PYGZhy{}c SH \PYGZhy{}b}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  20 franz}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  GGAGUAGGUUAUCCUCUGUU}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  10 sissi}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  AGGACAACCU}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}     pos      u3S       u3H       u4S       u4H        dG}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}    \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.540}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}    \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.540}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.371}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}        \PYG{n}{NA}    \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.217}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{4}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.754}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{5.777}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.761}        \PYG{n}{NA}    \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.393}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.664}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{3.140}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.811}     \PYG{l+m+mf}{5.800}    \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.393}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxhyphen{}b option is selected position and dGu\_s values for the shorter sequence
are written after the information for the target sequence.

\chapter{Using RNAlib}
\label{\detokenize{using_rnalib:using-rnalib}}\label{\detokenize{using_rnalib::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Linking against RNAlib}
\label{\detokenize{linking:linking-against-rnalib}}\label{\detokenize{linking::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to use our implemented algorithms you simply need to link your program
to our \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} C\sphinxhyphen{}library that usually comes along with the ViennaRNA Package
installation. If you’ve installed the ViennaRNA Package as a pre\sphinxhyphen{}build binary package,
you probably need the corresponding development package, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{viennarna\sphinxhyphen{}devel}}, or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{viennarna\sphinxhyphen{}dev}}. The only thing that is left is to include the ViennaRNA header
files into your source code, e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}ViennaRNA/mfe.h\PYGZgt{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and start using our fast and efficient algorithm implementations.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the {\hyperref[\detokenize{examples/c::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{C Examples}}}} section, we list a small set of example code that
usually is a good starting point for your application.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Compiler and Linker flags}
\label{\detokenize{linking:compiler-and-linker-flags}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Of course, simply adding the ViennaRNA header files into your source code is
usually not enough. You probably need to tell your compiler where to find the
header files, and sometimes add additional pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor directives. Whenever
your installation of \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} was build with default settings and the header
files were installed into their default location, a simple:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{I}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{usr}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{include}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor/compile flag should suffice. It can even be omitted in this case,
since your compiler should search this directory by default anyway. You only
need to change the path from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/include}} to the correct location whenever
the header files have been installed into a non\sphinxhyphen{}standard directory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you’ve compiled \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} with some non\sphinxhyphen{}default settings then you probably
need to define some additional pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor macros:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VRNA\_DISABLE\_C11\_FEATURES}} … Disable C11/C++11 features.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add this directive to your pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor/compile flags only if \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}
was build with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}disable\sphinxhyphen{}c11}} configure option.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:disable-c11-c-11-features}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Disable C11/C++11 features}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:c.vrna_C11_features}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_C11\_features()}}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VRNA\_WARN\_DEPRECATED}} … Enable warnings for using deprecated symbols.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding this directive enables compiler warnings whenever you use symbols
in \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} that are marked \sphinxstyleemphasis{deprecated}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:deprecated-symbols}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Deprecated symbols}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{deprecated::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Deprecated List}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{USE\_FLOAT\_PF}} … Use single precision floating point operations instead
of double precision in partition function computations.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define this macro only if \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} was build with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}enable\sphinxhyphen{}floatpf}}
configure option!
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:single-precision}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Single precision}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For instance, you might want to add the following definition(s) to your
pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor/compile flags:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{DVRNA\PYGZus{}DISABLE\PYGZus{}C11\PYGZus{}FEATURES}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, linking against \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} is achieved by adding the following linker flag:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{usr}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{lib} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{lRNA} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{flto} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{fopenmp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Again, the path to the library, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/lib}}, may be omitted if this path is
searched for libraries by default. The second flag tells the linker to include
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libRNA.a}}, and the remaining two flags activate {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:link-time-optimization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Link Time Optimization}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:openmp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{OpenMP}}}} support, respectively.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on your linker, the last two flags may differ.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on your configure time decisions, you can drop one or both of the last flags.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In case you’ve compiled \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} with LTO support (See {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:link-time-optimization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Link Time Optimization}}}}) and you are using a different compiler for your third\sphinxhyphen{}party project that
links against our library, you may add the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}fno\sphinxhyphen{}lto}} flag to disable Link Time
Optimization.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{faq:linking-fails-with-lto-error}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Linking fails with LTO error}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{The pkg\sphinxhyphen{}config tool}
\label{\detokenize{linking:the-pkg-config-tool}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Instead of hard\sphinxhyphen{}coding the required compiler and linker flags, you can also let the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pkg\sphinxhyphen{}config}} tool automatically determine the required flags. This tool is usually
packaged for any Linux distribution and should be available for MacOS X and MinGW as
well. We ship a file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNAlib2.pc}} which is installed along with the static \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libRNA.a}}
C\sphinxhyphen{}library and populated with all required compiler and linker flags that correspond to
your configure time decisions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compiler flags required for properly building your code that uses \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} can be
easily obtained via:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{pkg}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{config} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{cflags} \PYG{n}{RNAlib2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You get the corresponding linker flags using:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{pkg}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{config} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{libs} \PYG{n}{RNAlib2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With this widely accepted standard it is also very easy to integrate \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} in your
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{autotools}} project, just have a look at the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PKG\_CHECK\_MODULES}} macro.

\sphinxstepscope

\subsection{MFE Prediction (simple interface)}
\label{\detokenize{examples/c:mfe-prediction-simple-interface}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}stdlib.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}stdio.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}string.h\PYGZgt{}}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}ViennaRNA/fold.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}ViennaRNA/utils/basic.h\PYGZgt{}}

\PYG{k+kt}{int}
\PYG{n+nf}{main}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+cm}{/* The RNA sequence */}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{GAGUAGUGGAACCAGGCUAUGUUUGUGACUCGCAGACUAACA}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+cm}{/* allocate memory for MFE structure (length + 1) */}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{structure}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}alloc}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{sizeof}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{strlen}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+cm}{/* predict Minmum Free Energy and corresponding secondary structure */}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{float}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}fold}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{structure}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+cm}{/* print sequence, structure and MFE */}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s [ \PYGZpc{}6.2f ]}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{structure}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+cm}{/* cleanup memory */}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{MFE Prediction (VRNA 3.0 interface)}
\label{\detokenize{examples/c:mfe-prediction-vrna-3-0-interface}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}stdlib.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}stdio.h\PYGZgt{}}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+cm}{/* predict Minmum Free Energy and corresponding secondary structure */}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{float}\PYG{+w}{                 }\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}mfe}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{structure}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+cm}{/* print sequence, structure and MFE */}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s [ \PYGZpc{}6.2f ]}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{structure}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\subsection{Boltzmann Sampling}
\label{\detokenize{examples/python:boltzmann-sampling}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
a.k.a. Probabilistic Backtracing

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{RNA}

\PYG{n}{sequence} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{UGGGAAUAGUCUCUUCCGAGUCUCGCGGGCGACGGGCGAUCUUCGAAAGUGGAAUCCGUACUUAUACCGCCUGUGCGGACUACUAUCCUGACCACAUAGU}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{l+s+sd}{    \PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}
    \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{s}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{p}{)}


\PYG{l+s+sd}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{l+s+sd}{First we prepare a fold\PYGZus{}compound object}

\subsection{Parsing Alignments}
\label{\detokenize{examples/python:parsing-alignments}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Reading the first entry from a STOCKHOLM 1.0 formatted MSA file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{msa.stk}} may look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{num}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{names}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{aln}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{id}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ss} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{RNA}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{file\PYGZus{}msa\PYGZus{}read}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{msa.stk}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, if the file contains more than one alignment, one can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.file_msa_read_record}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.file\_msa\_read\_record()}}}}}
function to subsequently read each alignment separately:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n+nb}{open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{msa.stk}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{while} \PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{num}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{names}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{aln}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{id}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ss} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{RNA}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{file\PYGZus{}msa\PYGZus{}read\PYGZus{}record}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{num} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{k}{break}
        \PYG{k}{elif} \PYG{n}{num} \PYG{o}{==} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{empty alignment}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{k}{else}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{names}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{aln}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After successfully reading the first record, the variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{num}} contains the number of
sequences in the alignment (the actual return value of the C\sphinxhyphen{}function), while the variables
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{names}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{aln}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{id}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ss}} are lists of the sequence names and aligned sequences,
as well as strings holding the alignment ID and the structure as stated in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SS\_cons}} line,
respectively.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The last two return values may be empty strings in case the alignment does not provide
the required data.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\chapter{I/O Formats}
\label{\detokenize{io:i-o-formats}}\label{\detokenize{io::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Below, you’ll find a listing of different sections that introduce the most common notations
of sequence and structure data, specifications of bioinformatics sequence and structure file
formats, and various output file formats produced by our library.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{RNA Structures}
\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures:rna-structures}}\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, we describe the different notations and representations of RNA secondary structures
used throughout our library and prediction tools.


\subsection{Dot\sphinxhyphen{}Bracket Notation}
\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures:dot-bracket-notation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Dot\sphinxhyphen{}Bracket notation as introduced already in the early times of the ViennaRNA Package
denotes base pairs by matching pairs of parenthesis \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{()}} and unpaired nucleotides by dots
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is the standard representation of a secondary structure in our library.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Based on that notation, more elaborate representations have been developed to
include additional information, such as the loop context a nucleotide belongs
to and to annotated pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider the following secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which, drawn as a secondary structure graph, looks like:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{bracket}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is a stem\sphinxhyphen{}loop structure consisting of a an outer helix of 3 base pairs followed by
an interior loop of size 3, a second helix of length 4, and a hairpin loop of size 3.


\subsubsection{Pseudo Dot\sphinxhyphen{}Bracket Notation}
\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures:pseudo-dot-bracket-notation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Base pair probabilities are sometimes summarized in \sphinxstyleemphasis{pseudo dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation} with
the additional symbols \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{,}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{|}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\}}}. Here, the usual \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{)}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}},
represent bases with a strong preference (more than 2/3) to pair upstream (with a partner
further 3’), pair down\sphinxhyphen{}stream, or do not pair, respectively. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\}}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{,}} are
just the weaker version of the above and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{|}} represents a base that is mostly paired
but has pairing partners both upstream and downstream. In this case opening and closing
brackets do not need to match.


\subsubsection{Extended Dot\sphinxhyphen{}Bracket Notation}
\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures:extended-dot-bracket-notation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A more generalized version of the original Dot\sphinxhyphen{}Bracket notation may use additional pairs
of brackets, such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}\textgreater{}}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{\}}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{{[}{]}}}, and matching pairs of
uppercase/lowercase letters. This allows for anotating pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots, since different
pairs of brackets are not required to be nested.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The follwing annotations of a simple structure with two crossing helices of size 4 are equivalent:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{AAAA}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{aaaa}
\PYG{n}{AAAA}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{aaaa}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_pack}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_pack()}}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_unpack}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_unpack()}}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_flatten}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_flatten()}}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_flatten_to}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_flatten\_to()}}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_from_ptable}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_from\_ptable()}}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_from_plist}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_from\_plist()}}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_to_element_string}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_to\_element\_string()}}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/dotbracket:c.vrna_db_pk_remove}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_pk\_remove()}}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{WUSS notation}
\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures:wuss-notation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Washington University Secondary Structure (WUSS) notation is frequently used for
consensus secondary structures, e.g. in {\hyperref[\detokenize{io/msa:stockholm-1-0-format}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Stockholm 1.0 format}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This notation allows for a fine\sphinxhyphen{}grained annotation of base pairs and unpaired nucleotides,
including pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
WUSS notation in the infernal user guide at \sphinxurl{http://eddylab.org/infernal/Userguide.pdf}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below, you’ll find a list of secondary structure elements and their corresponding WUSS annotation.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Base pairs}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Nested base pairs are annotated by matching pairs of the symbols \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}\textgreater{}}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{\}}},
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{{[}{]}}}. Each of the matching pairs  of parenthesis have their special meaning, however,
when used as input in our programs, e.g. structure constraint, these details are usually
ignored. Furthermore, base pairs that constitute as pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knot are denoted by letters from
the latin alphabet and are, if not denoted otherwise, ignored entirely in our programs.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Hairpin loops}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unpaired nucleotides that constitute the hairpin loop are indicated by underscores, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_}}.
Here is an example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bulges and interior loops}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Residues that constitute a bulge or interior loop are denoted by dashes, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multibranch loops}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unpaired nucleotides in multibranch loops are indicated by commas \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{,}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{External residues}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Single stranded nucleotides in the exterior loop, i.e. not enclosed by any other pair are
denoted by colons, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{:}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{p}{:}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Insertions}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In cases where an alignment represents the consensus with a known structure, insertions
relative to the known structure are denoted by periods, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}}. Regions where local
structural alignment was invoked, leaving regions of both target and query sequence
unaligned, are indicated by tildes, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textasciitilde{}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These symbols only appear in alignments of a known (query) structure annotation to a target
sequence of unknown structure.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The WUSS notation allows for annotation of pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots using pairs of upper\sphinxhyphen{}case/lower\sphinxhyphen{}case
letters. Our programs and library functions usually ignore pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots entirely treating
them as unpaired nucleotides, if not stated otherwise:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}AAA\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{aaa}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/wuss:c.vrna_db_from_WUSS}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_db\_from\_WUSS()}}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Abstract Shapes}
\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures:abstract-shapes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Abstract Shapes, introduced by Giegerich \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id42}{2004}{]}, collapse the secondary structure while
retaining the nestedness of helices and hairpin loops.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The abstract shapes representation abstracts the structure from individual base pairs
and their corresponding location in the sequence, while retaining the inherent nestedness
of helices and hairpin loops.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is a description of what is included in the abstract shapes abstraction for each
respective level together with an example structure:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{CGUCUUAAACUCAUCACCGUGUGGAGCUGCGACCCUUCCCUAGAUUCGAAGACGAG}
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{Tree Representations}
\label{\detokenize{io/rna_structures:tree-representations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Secondary structures can be readily represented as trees, where internal
nodes represent base pairs, and leaves represent unpaired nucleotides.
The dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket structure string already is a tree represented by a string
of parenthesis (base pairs) and dots for the leaf nodes (unpaired nucleotides).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively, one may find representations with two types of node labels,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{P}} for paired and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U}} for unpaired; a dot is then replaced by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(U)}}, and
each closed bracket is assigned an additional identifier \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{P}}.
We call this the expanded notation. In Fontana \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id25}{1993}{]} a condensed
representation of the secondary structure is proposed, the so\sphinxhyphen{}called
homeomorphically irreducible tree (HIT) representation. Here a stack is
represented as a single pair of matching brackets labeled \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{P}} and
weighted by the number of base pairs.  Correspondingly, a contiguous
strain of unpaired bases is shown as one pair of matching brackets
labeled \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U}} and weighted by its length.  Generally any string consisting
of matching brackets and identifiers is equivalent to a plane tree with
as many different types of nodes as there are identifiers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Shapiro {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id27}{1988}{]} proposed a coarse grained representation which
does not retain the full information of the secondary structure. He
represents the different structure elements by single matching brackets
and labels them as
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{H}}  (hairpin loop),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{I}}  (interior loop),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{B}}  (bulge),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{M}}  (multi\sphinxhyphen{}loop), and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S}}  (stack).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We extend his alphabet by an extra letter for external elements \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E}}.
Again these identifiers may be followed by a weight corresponding to the
number of unpaired bases or base pairs in the structure element.  All tree
representations (except for the dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket form) can be encapsulated into
a virtual root (labeled \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{R}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following example illustrates the different linear tree representations
used by the package:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider the secondary structure represented by the dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket string (full tree):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which is the most convenient condensed notation used by our programs and
library functions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Then, the following tree representations are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Expanded tree:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{R}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
HIT representation ({[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id25}{Fontana \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.}, 1993}{]}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U3}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P3}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{R}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Coarse Grained Tree Representation ({[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id27}{Shapiro, 1988}{]}):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Short (with root node \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{R}}, without stem nodes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{M}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{R}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Full (with root node \sphinxtitleref{R\textasciigrave{}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{M}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{R}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Extended (with root node \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{R}}, with external nodes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{M}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{E}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{R}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Weighted (with root node \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{R}}, with external nodes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H3}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S3}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{H2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{M4}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{S2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{E2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{R}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Expanded tree is rather clumsy and mostly included for the sake of
completeness. The different versions of Coarse Grained Tree Representations
are variatios of Shapiro’s linear tree notation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the output of aligned structures from string editing, different
representations are needed, where we put the label on both sides.
The above examples for tree representations would then look like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{UU}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{U}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}

\section{Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSA)}
\label{\detokenize{io/msa:multiple-sequence-alignments-msa}}\label{\detokenize{io/msa::doc}}

\subsection{ClustalW format}
\label{\detokenize{io/msa:clustalw-format}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ClustalW} format is a relatively simple text file containing a single
multiple sequence alignment of DNA, RNA, or protein sequences. It was first used
as an output format for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{clustalw} programs, but nowadays it may also be
generated by various other sequence alignment tools. The specification is straight
forward:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first line starts with the words:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{CLUSTAL} \PYG{n}{W}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{CLUSTALW}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
After the above header there is at least one empty line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, one or more blocks of sequence data are following, where each
block is separated by at least one empty line.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each line in a blocks of sequence data consists of the sequence name followed by
the sequence symbols, separated by at least one whitespace character. Usually,
the length of a sequence in one block does not exceed 60 symbols. Optionally,
an additional whitespace separated cumulative residue count may follow the sequence
symbols. Optionally, a block may be followed by a line depicting the degree of
conservation of the respective alignment columns.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sequence names and the sequences must not contain whitespace characters!
Allowed gap symbols are the hyphen (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}}}), and dot (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}}).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Please note that many programs that output this format tend to truncate
the sequence names to a limited number of characters, for instance the
first 15 characters. This can destroy the uniqueness of identifiers in
your MSA.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example alignment in ClustalW format:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{CLUSTAL} \PYG{n}{W} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.83}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{n}{multiple} \PYG{n}{sequence} \PYG{n}{alignment}


\PYG{n}{AL031296}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{85969}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{86120}      \PYG{n}{CUGCCUCACAACGUUUGUGCCUCAGUUACCCGUAGAUGUAGUGAGGGUAACAAUACUUAC}
\PYG{n}{AANU01225121}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{438}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{603}      \PYG{n}{CUGCCUCACAACAUUUGUGCCUCAGUUACUCAUAGAUGUAGUGAGGGUGACAAUACUUAC}
\PYG{n}{AAWR02037329}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{29294}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{29150}  \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{CUCGACACCACU}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{GCCUCGGUUACCCAUCGGUGCAGUGCGGGUAGUAGUACCAAU}

\PYG{n}{AL031296}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{85969}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{86120}      \PYG{n}{UCUCGUUGGUGAUAAGGAACAGCU}
\PYG{n}{AANU01225121}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{438}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{603}      \PYG{n}{UCUCGUUGGUGAUAAGGAACAGCU}
\PYG{n}{AAWR02037329}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{29294}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{29150}  \PYG{n}{GCUAAUUAGUUGUGAGGACCAACU} 
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{FASTA (Pearson) format}
\label{\detokenize{io/msa:fasta-pearson-format}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sequence names must not contain whitespace characters. Otherwise, the parts after
the first whitespace will be dropped. The only allowed gap character is the hyphen
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}}}).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example alignment in FASTA format:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{AL031296}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{85969}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{86120}
\PYG{n}{CUGCCUCACAACGUUUGUGCCUCAGUUACCCGUAGAUGUAGUGAGGGUAACAAUACUUAC}
\PYG{n}{UCUCGUUGGUGAUAAGGAACAGCU}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{AANU01225121}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{438}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{603}
\PYG{n}{CUGCCUCACAACAUUUGUGCCUCAGUUACUCAUAGAUGUAGUGAGGGUGACAAUACUUAC}
\PYG{n}{UCUCGUUGGUGAUAAGGAACAGCU}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{AAWR02037329}\PYG{l+m+mf}{.1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m+mi}{29294}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{29150}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{CUCGACACCACU}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{GCCUCGGUUACCCAUCGGUGCAGUGCGGGUAGUAGUACCAAU}
\PYG{n}{GCUAAUUAGUUGUGAGGACCAACU}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{MAF format}
\label{\detokenize{io/msa:maf-format}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The multiple alignment format (MAF) is usually used to store multiple alignments on DNA level
between entire genomes. It consists of independent blocks of aligned sequences which are
annotated by their genomic location. Consequently, an MAF formatted MSA file may contain
multiple records. MAF files start with a line:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{}maf}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which is optionally extended by whitespace delimited key=value pairs. Lines starting with
the character (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#}}) are considered comments and usually ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A MAF block starts with character (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{a}}) at the beginning of a line, optionally followed
by whitespace delimited \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{key=value}} pairs. The next lines start with character (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s}}) and
contain sequence information of the form:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{s} \PYG{n}{src} \PYG{n}{start} \PYG{n}{size} \PYG{n}{strand} \PYG{n}{srcSize} \PYG{n}{sequence}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{src} is the name of the sequence source

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{start} is the start of the aligned region within the source (0\sphinxhyphen{}based)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{size} is the length of the aligned region without gap characters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{strand} is either (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{+}}) or (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}}}), depicting the location of the aligned
region relative to the source

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{srcSize} is the size of the entire sequence source, e.g. the full chromosome

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sequence} is the aligned sequence including gaps depicted by the hyphen (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}}})

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example alignment in MAF format (bluntly taken from the
\sphinxhref{https://genome.ucsc.edu/FAQ/FAQformat.html\#format5}{UCSC Genome browser website}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{}maf version=1 scoring=tba.v8 }
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} tba.v8 (((human chimp) baboon) (mouse rat)) }
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} multiz.v7}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} maf\PYGZus{}project.v5 \PYGZus{}tba\PYGZus{}right.maf3 mouse \PYGZus{}tba\PYGZus{}C}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} single\PYGZus{}cov2.v4 single\PYGZus{}cov2 /dev/stdin}
                   
\PYG{n}{a} \PYG{n}{score}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{23262.0}

\PYG{n}{s} \PYG{n}{panTro1}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{chr6} \PYG{l+m+mi}{28869787} \PYG{l+m+mi}{13} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{l+m+mi}{161576975} \PYG{n}{gcagctgaaaaca}
\PYG{n}{s} \PYG{n}{baboon}         \PYG{l+m+mi}{249182} \PYG{l+m+mi}{13} \PYG{o}{+}   \PYG{l+m+mi}{4622798} \PYG{n}{gcagctgaaaaca}
\PYG{n}{s} \PYG{n}{mm4}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{chr6}     \PYG{l+m+mi}{53310102} \PYG{l+m+mi}{13} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{l+m+mi}{151104725} \PYG{n}{ACAGCTGAAAATA}
