\subsubsection{High Level Constraints Interfaces}
\label{\detokenize{grammar/constraints:high-level-constraints-interfaces}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
High\sphinxhyphen{}level interfaces that build upon the soft constraints framework
can be obtained by the implementations in the submodules:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{modified_bases::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Post\sphinxhyphen{}transcriptional Base Modifications}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{probing/SHAPE::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{SHAPE Reactivity Data}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ligands/constraints::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Incorporating Ligands Binding to Specific Sequence/Structure Motifs}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An implementation that generates soft constraints for unpaired nucleotides
by minimizing the discrepancy between their predicted and expected pairing
probability is available in submodule {\hyperref[\detokenize{probing/perturbation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Generate Soft Constraints from Data}}}}.


\subsection{Secondary Structure Folding Recurrences}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:secondary-structure-folding-recurrences}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To predict secondary structures composed of the four distinguished loop types
introduced before, all algorithms implemented in \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} follow a specific
recursive decomposition scheme, also known as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNA folding grammar}, or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Secondary Structure Folding Recurrences}.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{recursions}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, compared to other RNA secondary structure prediction libraries, our
implementation allows for a fine\sphinxhyphen{}grained control of the above recursions by
constraining both, the individual derivations of the grammar as well as the
evaluation of particular loop contributions. Furthermore, we provide a mechanism
to extend the above grammar with additional derivation rules, so\sphinxhyphen{}called
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Domains}.


\subsection{Additional Structural Domains}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:additional-structural-domains}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some applications of RNA secondary structure prediction require an extension
of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{regular RNA folding grammar}. For instance one would like to include
proteins and other ligands binding to unpaired loop regions while competing
with conventional base pairing. Another application could be that one may
want to include the formation of self\sphinxhyphen{}enclosed structural modules, such as
\sphinxstyleemphasis{G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplexes}. For such applications, we provide a pair of additional domains
that extend the regular RNA folding grammar, {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_struc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Structured Domains}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_up::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Unstructured Domains}}}}.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{GCrecursion}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
While unstructured domains are usually determined by a more or less precise
sequence motif, e.g. the binding site for a protein, structured domains are
considered self\sphinxhyphen{}enclosed modules with a more or less complex pairing pattern.
Our extension with these two domains introduces two production rules to fill
additional dynamic processing matrices \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U}} where we store the
pre\sphinxhyphen{}computed contributions of structured domains (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S}}), and unstructured
domains (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U}}).


\subsection{Structured Domains}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:structured-domains}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, structured domains represent self\sphinxhyphen{}enclosed structural modules that
exhibit a more or less complex base pairing pattern. This can be more or less
well\sphinxhyphen{}defined 3D motifs, such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{G\sphinxhyphen{}Quadruplexes}, or loops with additional
non\sphinxhyphen{}canonical base pair interactions, such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{kink\sphinxhyphen{}turns}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, our implementation only provides the specialized case of \sphinxstyleemphasis{G\sphinxhyphen{}Quadruplexes}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Unstructured Domains}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:unstructured-domains}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unstructured domains appear in the production rules of the RNA folding grammar
wherever new unpaired nucleotides are attached to a growing substructure
(see also Lorenz \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id34}{2016}{]}):

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{Crecursion}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The white boxes represent the stretch of RNA bound to the ligand and represented by a more or less specific
sequence motif. The motif itself is considered unable to form base pairs. The additional production rule \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U}}
is used to precompute the contribution of unpaired stretches possibly bound by one or more ligands. The
auxiliary DP matrix for this production rule is filled right before processing the other (regular) production
rules of the RNA folding grammar.


\subsection{Domain Extension API}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:domain-extension-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the sake of flexibility, each of the domains is associated with a specific
data structure serving as an abstract interface to the extension. The interface
uses callback functions to
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pre\sphinxhyphen{}compute arbitrary data, e.g. filling up additional dynamic programming matrices, and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
evaluate the contribution of a paired or unpaired structural feature of the RNA.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Implementations of these callbacks are separate for regular free energy evaluation,
e.g. MFE prediction, and partition function applications. A data structure holding
arbitrary data required for the callback functions can be associated to the domain
as well. While \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} comes with a default implementation for structured and
unstructured domains, the system is entirely user\sphinxhyphen{}customizable.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_up::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Unstructured Domains}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_struc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Structured Domains}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/gquads::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{G\sphinxhyphen{}Quadruplexes}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ligands/unstructured_domains::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Ligands Binding to Unstructured Domains}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Constraints on the Folding Grammar}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:constraints-on-the-folding-grammar}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Secondary Structure constraints can be subdivided into two groups:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hard Constraints

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Soft Constraints

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
While Hard\sphinxhyphen{}Constraints directly influence the production rules used in the folding
recursions by allowing, disallowing, or enforcing certain decomposition steps,
Soft\sphinxhyphen{}constraints on the other hand are used to change position specific contributions
in the recursions by adding bonuses/penalties in form of pseudo free energies
to certain loop configurations.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Secondary structure constraints are always applied at decomposition level, i.e.
in each step of the recursive structure decomposition, for instance during MFE
prediction.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Hard Constraints API}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:hard-constraints-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hard constraints as implemented in our library can be specified for individual loop
types, i.e. the atomic derivations of the RNA folding grammar rules. Hence, the pairing
behavior of both, single nucleotides and pairs of bases, can be constrained in every
loop context separately. Additionally, an abstract implementation using a callback
mechanism allows for full control of more complex hard constraints.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/constraints/hard::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Hard Constraints}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Soft Constraints API}
\label{\detokenize{grammar:soft-constraints-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the sake of memory efficiency, we do not implement a loop context aware version of
soft constraints. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{static} soft constraints as implemented only distinguish unpaired
from paired nucleotides. This is usually sufficient for most use\sphinxhyphen{}case scenarios.
However, similar to hard constraints, an abstract soft constraints implementation using
a callback mechanism exists, that allows for any soft constraint that is compatible with
the RNA folding grammar. Thus, loop contexts and even individual derivation rules can
be addressed separately for maximum flexibility in soft\sphinxhyphen{}constraints application.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/constraints/soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Soft Constraints}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{ligands/constraints::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Incorporating Ligands Binding to Specific Sequence/Structure Motifs}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{probing/SHAPE::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{SHAPE Reactivity Data}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\section{The RNA Secondary Structure Landscape}
\label{\detokenize{landscape:the-rna-secondary-structure-landscape}}\label{\detokenize{landscape::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Neighborhood Relation and Move Sets for Secondary Structures}
\label{\detokenize{landscape/neighbors:neighborhood-relation-and-move-sets-for-secondary-structures}}\label{\detokenize{landscape/neighbors::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Different functions to generate structural neighbors of a secondary
structure according to a particular Move Set.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This module contains methods to compute the neighbors of an RNA
secondary structure. Neighbors of a given structure are all structures
that differ in exactly one base pair. That means one can insert an
delete base pairs in the given structure. These insertions and
deletions of base pairs are usually called moves. A third move which
is considered in these methods is a shift move. A shifted base pair
has one stable position and one position that changes. These moves
are encoded as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
insertion: \((i, j)\) where \(i,j > 0\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
deletion: \((i, j)\) where \(i,j\) \textless{} 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
shift: \((i, j)\) where either \(i > 0, j < 0\) or \(i < 0, j > 0\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The negative position of a shift indicates the position that has changed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{We} \PYG{n}{are} \PYG{n}{given} \PYG{n}{a} \PYG{n}{sequence} \PYG{o+ow}{and} \PYG{n}{a} \PYG{n}{structure}\PYG{o}{.}
\PYG{n}{Sequence}  \PYG{n}{AAGGAAACC}
 \PYG{n}{Structure} \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
 \PYG{n}{Indices}   \PYG{l+m+mi}{123456789}

 \PYG{n}{The} \PYG{n}{given} \PYG{n}{base} \PYG{n}{pair} \PYG{o+ow}{is} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mi}{9}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o+ow}{and} \PYG{n}{the} \PYG{n}{neighbors} \PYG{n}{are} \PYG{n}{the} \PYG{n}{insertion} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{4}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
 \PYG{n}{the} \PYG{n}{deletion} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{9}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{the} \PYG{n}{shift} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o+ow}{and} \PYG{n}{the} \PYG{n}{shift} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{4}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{9}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}
 \PYG{n}{This} \PYG{n}{leads} \PYG{n}{to} \PYG{n}{the} \PYG{n}{neighbored} \PYG{n}{structures}\PYG{p}{:}
 \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
 \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
 \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}
 \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A simple method to construct all insertions is to iterate over the positions of a sequence twice. The first
iteration has the index i in {[}1, sequence length{]}, the second iteration has the index j in {[}i+1, sequence length{]}.
All pairs (i,j) with compatible letters and which are non\sphinxhyphen{}crossing with present base pairs are valid neighbored
insertion moves.
Valid deletion moves are all present base pairs with negative sign.
Valid shift moves are constructed by taking all paired positions as fix position of a shift move and iterating over
all positions of the sequence. If the letters of a position are compatible and if it the move is non\sphinxhyphen{}crossing with
existing base pairs, we have a valid shift move.
The method of generating shift moves can be accelerated by skipping neighbored base pairs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If we need to construct all neighbors several times for subsequent moves, we can speed up the task by using
the move set of the previous structure. The previous move set has to be filtered, such that all moves that would
cross the next selected move are non\sphinxhyphen{}crossing. Next, the selected move has to be removed. Then one has to only
to generate all moves that were not possible before.
One move is the inverted selected move (if it was an insertion, simply make the indices negative).
The generation of all other new moves is different and depends on the selected move. It is easy for an insertion move,
because we have only to include all non\sphinxhyphen{}crossing shift moves, that are possible with the new base pair. For that we can
either iterate over the sequence or we can select all crossing shift moves in the filter procedure and convert them into
shifts.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The generation of new moves given a deletion is a little bit more complex, because we can create more moves. At first
we can insert the deleted pair as insertion move. Then we generate all insertions that would have crossed the deleted
base pair. Finally we construct all crossing shift moves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the given move is a shift, we can save much time by specifying the intervals for the generation of new moves.
The interval which was enclosed by the positive position of the shift move and the previous paired position is the
freed interval after applying the move. This freed interval includes all positions and base pairs that we need to
construct new insertions and shifts. All these new moves have one position in the freed interval and the other position
in the environment of the freed interval. The environment are all position which are outside the freed interval, but within
the same enclosing loop of the shift move. The environment for valid base pairs can be divided into one or more intervals,
depending on the shift move. The following examples describe a few scenarios to specify the intervals of the environment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example 1:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{increase} \PYG{n}{the} \PYG{n}{freed} \PYG{n}{interval} \PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n}{a} \PYG{n}{shift} \PYG{n}{move}
\PYG{n}{AAAAGACAAGAAACAAAAGAGAAACAACAAACAAGAAACAAACAAAA}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{shift_move_intervals}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given the intervals of the environment and the freed interval, the new shift moves can be constructed quickly.
One has to take all positions of pairs from the environment in order to create valid pairs with positions in the freed interval.
The same procedure can be applied for the other direction. This is taking all paired positions within the freed interval
in order to look for pairs with valid positions in the intervals of the environment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare two moves. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The function compares two moves \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{b}} and returns whether move \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} is lexicographically smaller (\sphinxhyphen{}1), larger (1) or equal to move \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{b}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If any of the moves \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{b}} is a shift move, this comparison only makes sense in a structure context. Thus, the third argument with the current structure must be provided.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function returns 0 (equality) upon any error, e.g. missing input
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, shift moves are not supported!
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{m}} \textendash{} The first move of the comparison 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{b}} \textendash{} The second move of the comparison 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{pt}} \textendash{} The pair table of the current structure that is compatible with both moves (maybe NULL if moves are guaranteed to be no shifts) 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhyphen{}1 if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} \textless{} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{b}}, 1 if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} \textgreater{} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{b}}, 0 otherwise 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

This function allows one to generate all structural neighbors (according to a particular move set) of an RNA secondary structure. The neighborhood is then returned as a list of transitions / moves required to transform the current structure into the actual neighbor.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Generate neighbors of a secondary structure (the fast way) 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function implements a fast way to generate all neighbors of a secondary structure that results from successive applications of individual moves. The speed\sphinxhyphen{}up results from updating an already known list of valid neighbors before the individual move towards the current structure took place. In essence, this function removes neighbors that are not accessible anymore and inserts neighbors emerging after a move took place.

\sphinxAtStartPar

Apply a move to a secondary structure and indicate which neighbors have changed consequentially. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function applies a move to a secondary structure and explores the local neighborhood of the affected loop. Any changes to previously compatible neighbors that have been affected by this loop will be reported through a callback function. In particular, any of the three cases might appear:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A previously available neighbor move has changed, usually the free energy change of the move ({\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/neighbors:group__neighbors_1gae72b0e349b6108c00737df51cce44622}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_NEIGHBOR\_CHANGE}}}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A previously available neighbor move became invalid ({\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/neighbors:group__neighbors_1gaf7e3417828057ae0ed4d0de03178116a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_NEIGHBOR\_INVALID}}}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A new neighbor move becomes available ({\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/neighbors:group__neighbors_1ga9343dd62daad15b6b8c55c1260c09228}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_NEIGHBOR\_NEW}}}})

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/landscape/move.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An atomic representation of the transition / move from one structure to its neighbor. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
An atomic transition / move may be one of the following:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a \sphinxstylestrong{base pair insertion},

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a \sphinxstylestrong{base pair removal}, or

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a \sphinxstylestrong{base pair shift} where an existing base pair changes one of its pairing partner.

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar
These moves are encoded by two integer values that represent the affected 5’ and 3’ nucleotide positions. Furthermore, we use the following convention on the signedness of these encodings:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
both values are positive for \sphinxstyleemphasis{insertion moves}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
both values are negative for \sphinxstyleemphasis{base pair removals}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
both values have different signedness for \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift moves}, where the positive value indicates the nucleotide that stays constant, and the others absolute value is the new pairing partner

\end{itemize}


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A value of 0 in either field is used as list\sphinxhyphen{}end indicator and doesn’t represent any valid move. 
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\subsection{(Re\sphinxhyphen{})folding Paths, Saddle Points, Energy Barriers, and Local Minima}
\label{\detokenize{landscape/paths:re-folding-paths-saddle-points-energy-barriers-and-local-minima}}\label{\detokenize{landscape/paths::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
API for various RNA folding path algorithms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This part of our API allows for generating RNA secondary structure (re\sphinxhyphen{})folding
paths between two secondary structures or simply starting from a single
structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is most important if an estimate of the refolding energy barrier between
two structures is required, or a structure’s corresponding local minimum needs
to be determined, e.g. through a gradient\sphinxhyphen{}descent walk.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This part of the interface is further split into the following sections:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths_direct::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Direct Refolding Paths between two Secondary Structures}}}}, and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths_walk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Folding Paths that start at a single Secondary Structure}}}}

\end{itemize}

An element of a refolding path list. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, one has to deal with an array of {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s}}}}, e.g. returned from one of the refolding\sphinxhyphen{}path algorithms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since in most cases the length of the list is not known in advance, such lists have an \sphinxstyleemphasis{end\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}list} marker, which is either:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} for {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a141b70a59cb81d10bc65bbb7a0f6db77}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::s}}}} if {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a5fc9e0a7dc0e0f8ad67f24c18f2dc852}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::type}}}} = {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:group__paths_1ga3e964156b52440b65fae5e2a48750d8e}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PATH\_TYPE\_DOT\_BRACKET}}}}, or

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a13da6bb5167362199947765b06a84005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::move}}}} with zero in both fields {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/neighbors:structvrna__move__s_1a8af908c74786675a456d0f20cc8fcb9b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_move\_t::pos\_5}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/neighbors:structvrna__move__s_1a3849db905a45c4e399991df38705a36b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_move\_t::pos\_3}}}} if {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a5fc9e0a7dc0e0f8ad67f24c18f2dc852}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::type}}}} = {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:group__paths_1gaa73703da105dc6c98957fb8247c93f1f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PATH\_TYPE\_MOVES}}}}.

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar

The type of the path element. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
A value of {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:group__paths_1ga3e964156b52440b65fae5e2a48750d8e}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PATH\_TYPE\_DOT\_BRACKET}}}} indicates that {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a141b70a59cb81d10bc65bbb7a0f6db77}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::s}}}} consists of the secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1ac25160bf31d28097358278f367e41227}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::en}}}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the corresponding free energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar

{\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:group__paths_1gaa73703da105dc6c98957fb8247c93f1f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PATH\_TYPE\_MOVES}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a141b70a59cb81d10bc65bbb7a0f6db77}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::s}}}} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a13da6bb5167362199947765b06a84005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::move}}}} is set to the transition move that transforms a previous structure into it’s neighbor along the path. In this case, the attribute {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1ac25160bf31d28097358278f367e41227}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::en}}}} states the change in free energy with respect to the structure before application of {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths:structvrna__path__s_1a13da6bb5167362199947765b06a84005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_path\_s::move}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar

Determine an optimal direct (re\sphinxhyphen{})folding path between two secondary structures. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is the generic wrapper function to retrieve (an optimal) (re\sphinxhyphen{})folding path between two secondary structures \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s1}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s2}}. The actual algorithm that is used to generate the (re\sphinxhyphen{})folding path is determined by the settings specified in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} data structure. This data structure also determines the return type, which might be either:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a list of dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket structures with corresponding free energy, or

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a list of transition moves with corresponding free energy change

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter is passed a \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} pointer, this function defaults to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{findpath heuristic} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id31}{Flamm \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.}, 2001}{]}  with a breadth\sphinxhyphen{}first search width of \( 10 \), and the returned path consists of dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket structures with corresponding free energies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute a path, store the final structure, and return a list of transition moves from the start to the final structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function computes, given a start structure in pair table format, a transition path, updates the pair table to the final structure of the path. Finally, if not requested otherwise by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths_walk:group__paths__walk_1ga1ee63e54ecf136491e12ff03ede2622d}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PATH\_NO\_TRANSITION\_OUTPUT}}}} flag in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} field, this function returns a list of individual transitions that lead from the start to the final structure if requested.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The currently available transition paths are\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Steepest Descent / Gradient walk (flag: {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths_walk:group__paths__walk_1ga705cea2b3243a38a2d6e3b1e141ed061}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PATH\_STEEPEST\_DESCENT}}}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Random walk (flag: {\hyperref[\detokenize{landscape/paths_walk:group__paths__walk_1ga0b84bd36bfd783130297797c51dd85ae}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PATH\_RANDOM}}}})

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar
The type of transitions must be set through the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter

\section{Minimum Free Energy (MFE) Algorithms}
\label{\detokenize{mfe:minimum-free-energy-mfe-algorithms}}\label{\detokenize{mfe::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Computing the Minimum Free Energy (MFE), i.e. the most stable conformation
in thermodynamic equilibrium.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Global MFE Prediction}
\label{\detokenize{mfe/global:global-mfe-prediction}}\label{\detokenize{mfe/global::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Variations of the global Minimum Free Energy (MFE) prediction algorithm.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We provide implementations of the global MFE prediction algorithm for
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Single sequences,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiple sequence alignments (MSA), and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA hybrids

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute minimum free energy and an appropriate secondary structure of an RNA sequence, or RNA sequence alignment. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on the type of the provided {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}, this function predicts the MFE for a single sequence (or connected component of multiple sequences), or an averaged MFE for a sequence alignment. If backtracking is activated, it also constructs the corresponding secondary structure, or consensus structure. Therefore, the second parameter, \sphinxstyleemphasis{structure}, has to point to an allocated block of memory with a size of at least \(\mathrm{strlen}(\mathrm{sequence})+1\) to store the backtracked MFE structure. (For consensus structures, this is the length of the alignment + 1. If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} is passed, no backtracking will be performed.

Compute Minimum Free Energy (MFE), and a corresponding secondary structure for a circular RNA sequence. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This simplified interface to {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:group__mfe__global_1ga5577af664e5b9056b44fa5df29e9befb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe()}}}} computes the MFE and, if required, a secondary structure for a circular RNA sequence using default options. Memory required for dynamic programming (DP) matrices will be allocated and free’d on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly. Hence, after return of this function, the recursively filled matrices are not available any more for any post\sphinxhyphen{}processing, e.g. suboptimal backtracking, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Folding of circular RNA sequences is handled as a post\sphinxhyphen{}processing step of the forward recursions. See   Hofacker and Stadler {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id21}{2006}{]}  for further details.

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/mfe.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute Minimum Free Energy (MFE), and a corresponding consensus secondary structure for a sequence alignment of circular RNAs using a comparative method. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This simplified interface to {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:group__mfe__global_1ga5577af664e5b9056b44fa5df29e9befb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe()}}}} computes the MFE and, if required, a consensus secondary structure for an RNA sequence alignment using default options. Memory required for dynamic programming (DP) matrices will be allocated and free’d on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly. Hence, after return of this function, the recursively filled matrices are not available any more for any post\sphinxhyphen{}processing, e.g. suboptimal backtracking, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Folding of circular RNA sequences is handled as a post\sphinxhyphen{}processing step of the forward recursions. See   Hofacker and Stadler {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id21}{2006}{]}  for further details.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/fold.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute minimum free energy and an appropriate secondary structure of an RNA sequence. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first parameter given, the RNA sequence, must be \sphinxstyleemphasis{uppercase} and should only contain an alphabet \(\Sigma\)
\sphinxAtStartPar
that is understood by the RNAlib

\sphinxAtStartPar
(e.g.
\( \Sigma = \{A,U,C,G\} \)
\sphinxAtStartPar
)

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second parameter,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{structure}, must always point to an allocated block of memory with a size of at least \(\mathrm{strlen}(\mathrm{sequence})+1\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the third parameter is NULL, global model detail settings are assumed for the folding recursions. Otherwise, the provided parameters are used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fourth parameter indicates whether a secondary structure constraint in enhanced dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation is passed through the structure parameter or not. If so, the characters “ | x \textless{} \textgreater{} “ are recognized to mark bases that are paired, unpaired, paired upstream, or downstream, respectively. Matching brackets “ ( ) “ denote base pairs, dots “.” are used for unconstrained bases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To indicate that the RNA sequence is circular and thus has to be post\sphinxhyphen{}processed, set the last parameter to non\sphinxhyphen{}zero

\sphinxAtStartPar
After a successful call of {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global_deprecated:group__mfe__global__deprecated_1ga2bc41df5d71fee6fd8da9904ee65d8fb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{fold\_par()}}}}, a backtracked secondary structure (in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation) that exhibits the minimum of free energy will be written to the memory \sphinxstyleemphasis{structure} is pointing to. The function returns the minimum of free energy for any fold of the sequence given.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{deprecated:deprecated_1_deprecated000065}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Deprecated:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
use {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:group__mfe__global_1ga5577af664e5b9056b44fa5df29e9befb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe()}}}} instead!

\end{fulllineitems}



\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:group__mfe__global_1ga5577af664e5b9056b44fa5df29e9befb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global_deprecated:group__mfe__global__deprecated_1gaadafcb0f140795ae62e5ca027e335a9b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{fold()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global_deprecated:group__mfe__global__deprecated_1ga4ac63ab3e8d9a80ced28b8052d94e423}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{circfold()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/model_details:group__model__details_1ga1f8a10e12a0a1915f2a4eff0b28ea17c}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_md\_t}}}}, set\_energy\_model(), {\hyperref[\detokenize{eval/energy_parameters:group__energy__parameters_1gacdbcef8d5022d9e2eaac347374f5b3a9}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{get\_scaled\_parameters()}}}}


\end{sphinxseealso}



\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
OpenMP: Passing NULL to the ‘parameters’ argument involves access to several global model detail variables and thus is not to be considered threadsafe
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sequence}} \textendash{} RNA sequence 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{structure}} \textendash{} A pointer to the character array where the secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation will be written to 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{parameters}} \textendash{} A data structure containing the pre\sphinxhyphen{}scaled energy contributions and the model details. (NULL may be passed, see OpenMP notes above) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{is\_constrained}} \textendash{} Switch to indicate that a structure constraint is passed via the structure argument (0==off) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{is\_circular}} \textendash{} Switch to (de\sphinxhyphen{})activate post\sphinxhyphen{}processing steps in case RNA sequence is circular (0==off)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the minimum free energy (MFE) in kcal/mol 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\subsection{Local (sliding window) MFE Prediction}
\label{\detokenize{mfe/window:local-sliding-window-mfe-prediction}}\label{\detokenize{mfe/window::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Variations of the local (sliding window) Minimum Free Energy (MFE) prediction algorithm.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We provide implementations for the local (sliding window) MFE prediction algorithm for
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Single sequences,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiple sequence alignments (MSA), and

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note, that our implementation scans an RNA sequence (or MSA) from the 3’ to the 5’
end, and reports back locally optimal (consensus) structures, the corresponding free
energy, and the position of the sliding window in global coordinates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For any particular RNA sequence (or MSA) multiple locally optimal (consensus)
secondary structures may be predicted. Thus, we tried to implement an interface that
allows for an effortless conversion of the corresponding hits into any target data
structure. As a consequence, we provide two distinct ways to retrieve the corresponding
predictions, either
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
through directly writing to an open \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FILE}} stream on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly, or

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
through a callback function mechanism.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The latter allows one to store the results in any possible target data structure. Our
implementations then pass the results through the user\sphinxhyphen{}implemented callback as soon as
the prediction for a particular window is finished.

\pysigstartsignatures

\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{mfe/window:group__mfe__window_1gacdbc049dcfc7a0e2eb37a327efab91e2}}\DUrole{kt}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_mfe\_window}}}}{{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{fc}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{n}{FILE}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{file}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/mfe\_window.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Local MFE prediction using a sliding window approach. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Computes minimum free energy structures using a sliding window approach, where base pairs may not span outside the window. In contrast to {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:group__mfe__global_1ga5577af664e5b9056b44fa5df29e9befb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe()}}}}, where a maximum base pair span may be set using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/model_details:structvrna__md__s_1a659e5fcc6e8c9f1a68e7de6548eef3b0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_md\_t.max\_bp\_span}}}} attribute and one globally optimal structure is predicted, this function uses a sliding window to retrieve all locally optimal structures within each window. The size of the sliding window is set in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/model_details:structvrna__md__s_1abea42f9229f8d8d6bcbedef316315bfc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_md\_t.window\_size}}}} attribute, prior to the retrieval of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}} using {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gab89fe9844031711d42c70d1b9277c0d5}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound()}}}} with option {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga2b2a8009ccdccc3eb1571556261aee8e}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_WINDOW}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The predicted structures are written on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly, either to stdout, if a NULL pointer is passed as file parameter, or to the corresponding filehandle.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
This simplified interface to {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/window:group__mfe__window_1gacdbc049dcfc7a0e2eb37a327efab91e2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe\_window()}}}} computes the MFE and locally optimal secondary structure using default options. Structures are predicted using a sliding window approach, where base pairs may not span outside the window. Memory required for dynamic programming (DP) matrices will be allocated and free’d on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly. \sphinxAtStartPar
Backtrack an MFE (sub)structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function allows one to backtrack the MFE structure for a (sub)sequence

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000112}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is attached as overloaded method \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{backtrack()}} to objects of type \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fold\_compound}}. The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{length}} defaults to the total length of the RNA sequence and may be omitted. The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{structure}} is returned along with the MFE und must not be provided. See e.g.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.fold_compound.backtrack}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.fold\_compound.backtrack()}}}}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}. 

\end{fulllineitems}



\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:group__mfe__global_1ga5577af664e5b9056b44fa5df29e9befb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga72ebbe45bcbce147a12f27f62b38db78}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5()}}}}


\end{sphinxseealso}



\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
On error, the function returns INF / 100. and stores the empty string in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{structure}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{fc}} \textendash{} fold compound 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{length}} \textendash{} The length of the subsequence, starting from the 5’ end 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{structure}} \textendash{} A pointer to the character array where the secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation will be written to. (Must have size of at least \$p length + 1)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Pre}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Requires pre\sphinxhyphen{}filled MFE dynamic programming matrices, i.e. one has to call {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:group__mfe__global_1ga5577af664e5b9056b44fa5df29e9befb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe()}}}} prior to calling this function

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimum free energy (MFE) for the specified \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{length}} in kcal/mol and a corresponding secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation (stored in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{structure}})

\end{description}\end{quote}

\subsection{Zuker’s Algorithm}
\label{\detokenize{mfe:zuker-s-algorithm}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Our library provides fast dynamic programming Minimum Free Energy (MFE)
folding algorithms derived from the decomposition scheme as described by
Zuker and Stiegler {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id2}{1981}{]}.


\subsection{MFE for circular RNAs}
\label{\detokenize{mfe:mfe-for-circular-rnas}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Folding of \sphinxstyleemphasis{circular} RNA sequences is handled as a post\sphinxhyphen{}processing step
of the forward recursions. See Hofacker and Stadler {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id21}{2006}{]} for further details.


\subsection{MFE Algorithm API}
\label{\detokenize{mfe:mfe-algorithm-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Predicting the Minimum Free Energy (MFE) and a corresponding (consensus)
secondary structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a nutshell we provide two different flavors for MFE prediction:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Global MFE Prediction}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} to compute the MFE for the entire sequence

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/window::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Local (sliding window) MFE Prediction}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} to compute MFEs for each window using a sliding window approach

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each of these flavors, again, provides two implementations to either compute the MFE based on
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
single RNA (DNA) sequence(s), or

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
multiple sequences interacting with each other, or

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a comparative approach using multiple sequence alignments (MSA).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the latter, a consensus secondary structure is predicted and our implementations compute
an average of free energies for each sequence in the MSA plus an additional covariance
pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}energy term.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The implementations for {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/backtracking::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Backtracking MFE structures}}}} are generally agnostic with respect to whether
local or global structure prediction is in place.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Partition Function and Equilibrium Properties}
\label{\detokenize{pf_fold:partition-function-and-equilibrium-properties}}\label{\detokenize{pf_fold::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In contrast to methods that compute the property of a single structure in the ensemble,
e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Minimum Free Energy (MFE) Algorithms}}}}, the partition function algorithms always consider the \sphinxstyleemphasis{entire}
equilibrium ensemble. For that purpose, the algorithm(s) made available by
McCaskill {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id3}{1990}{]} and its variants can be used to efficiently compute
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the partition function, and from that

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
various equilibrium probabilities, for instance base pair probabilities,
probabilities of individual structure motifs, and many more.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The principal idea behind this approach is that in equilibrium, statistical mechanics
and polymer theory tells us that the frequency or probability \(p(s)\) of a particular
state \(s\) depends on its energy \(E(s)\) and follows a Boltzmann distribution, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(s) \propto e^{-\beta E(s)} \text{ with } \beta = \frac{1}{kT}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(k \approx 1.987 \cdot 10^{-3} \frac{kcal}{mol~K}\) is the Boltzmann constant,
and \(T\) the thermodynamic temperature. From that relation, the actual probability
of state \(s\) can then be obtained using a proper scaling factor, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{canonical
partition function}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Z = \sum_{s \in \Omega} e^{-\beta E(s)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\Omega\) is the finite set of all states. Finally, the equilibrium probability
of state \(s\) can be computed as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(s) = \frac{e^{-\beta E(s)}}{Z}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Instead of enumerating all states exhaustively to compute \(Z\) one can apply the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar:secondary-structure-folding-recurrences}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Secondary Structure Folding Recurrences}}}} again for an efficient computation
in cubic time. An \sphinxstyleemphasis{outside} variant of the same recursions is then used to compute
probabilities for base pairs, stretches of consecutive unpaired nucleotides, or structural
motifs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Further details of the Partition function and Base Pair Probability algorithm
can be obtained from McCaskill {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id3}{1990}{]}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope

This function applies a sliding window scan for the sequence provided with the argument \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fc}} and reports back equilibrium probabilities through the callback function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cb}}. The data reported to the callback depends on the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} flag.

\begin{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/window:group__part__func__window_1ga296217b76e76e5f7e6927e7210aa9b1f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PROBS\_WINDOW\_BPP}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Trigger base pairing probabilities.  

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/window:group__part__func__window_1ga18325811c7dfc7b7d9d4ac37f4353615}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PROBS\_WINDOW\_UP}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Trigger unpaired probabilities.  

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/window:group__part__func__window_1ga9068f4ec008bf1c042a9357f5c2c5e13}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PROBS\_WINDOW\_UP\_SPLIT}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Trigger detailed unpaired probabilities split up into different loop type contexts.  

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute probability of contiguous unpaired segments. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a simplified wrapper to {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/window:group__part__func__window_1ga86ebf4399ab22f7d3126c81b5c75b9f4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_probs\_window()}}}} that given a nucleic acid sequence, a maximum length of unpaired segments (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ulength}}), a window size, and a maximum base pair span computes the equilibrium probability of any segment not exceeding \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ulength}}. The probabilities to be unpaired are returned as a 1\sphinxhyphen{}based, 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional matrix with dimensions \( N \times M \), where \(N\) is the length of the sequence and \(M\) is the maximum segment length. As an example, the probability of a segment of size 5 starting at position 100 is stored in the matrix entry \(X[100][5]\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is the users responsibility to free the memory occupied by this matrix.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function uses default model settings! For custom model settings, we refer to the function {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/window:group__part__func__window_1ga86ebf4399ab22f7d3126c81b5c75b9f4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_probs\_window()}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ulength}} \textendash{} The maximal length of an unpaired segment 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{window\_size}} \textendash{} The size of the sliding window 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{max\_bp\_span}} \textendash{} The maximum distance along the backbone between two nucleotides that form a base pairs 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\subsection{Predicting various Thermodynamic Properties}
\label{\detokenize{partfunc/thermodynamics:predicting-various-thermodynamic-properties}}\label{\detokenize{partfunc/thermodynamics::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute various thermodynamic properties using the partition function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many thermodynamic properties can be derived from the partition function
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Z = \sum_{s \in \omega} e^{\frac{-E(s)}{kT}}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In particular, for nucleic acids in equilibrium the probabilty \(p(F)\)
of a particular structural feature \(F\) follows Boltzmanns law, i.e.:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(F) \propto \sum_{s \mid F \in s} e^{\frac{-E(s)}{kT}}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The actual probabilities can then be obtained from the ratio of those
structures containing \(F\) and \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} structures, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(F) = \frac{1}{Z} \sum_{s \mid F \in s} e^{\frac{-E(s)}{kT}}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consequently, a particular secondary structure \(s\) has equilibrium
probability
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(s) = \frac{1}{Z} e^{\frac{-E(s)}{kT}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
which can be easily computed once \(Z\) and \(E(s)\) are known.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Efficient dynamic programming algorithms exist to compute the equilibrium
probabilities
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_{ij} = \frac{1}{Z} \sum_{s \mid (i,j) \in s} e^{\frac{-E(s)}{kT}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
of base pairs \((i,j)\) without the need for exhaustive enumeration
of \(s\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This interface provides the functions for all thermodynamic property
computations implemented in \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}.

Get the mean base pair distance in the thermodynamic ensemble from a probability matrix. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
<d> = \sum_{a,b} p_a p_b d(S_a,S_b)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
this can be computed from the pair probs \( p_{ij} \) as

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
<d> = \sum_{ij} p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the Ensemble Defect for a given target structure provided as a \sphinxstylestrong{vrna\_ptable}. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given a target structure \(s\), compute the average dissimilarity of a randomly drawn structure from the ensemble, i.e.:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  ED(s) = 1 - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{ij, (i,j) \in s} p_{ij} - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i}(1 - s_i)q_i
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with sequence length \(n\), the probability \(p_{ij}\) of a base pair \((i,j)\), the probability \(q_i = 1 - \sum_j p_{ij}\) of nucleotide \(i\) being unpaired, and the indicator variable \(s_i = 1\) if \(\exists (i,j) \in s\), and \(s_i = 0\) otherwise.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute a vector of positional entropies. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function computes the positional entropies from base pair probabilities as

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
S(i) = - \sum_j p_{ij} \log(p_{ij}) - q_i \log(q_i)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with unpaired probabilities \( q_i = 1 - \sum_j p_{ij} \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Low entropy regions have little structural flexibility and the reliability of the predicted structure is high. High entropy implies many structural alternatives. While these alternatives may be functionally important, they make structure prediction more difficult and thus less reliable.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{partfunc/thermodynamics:group__thermodynamics_1ga882c35d9dd775c1275593b3b6a966bec}}\DUrole{kt}{double}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_pr\_structure}}}}{{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{fc}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{k}{const}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{structure}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/equilibrium\_probs.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the equilibrium probability of a particular secondary structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The probability \(p(s)\) of a particular secondary structure \(s\) can be computed as

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  p(s) = \frac{exp(-\beta E(s)}{Z}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
from the structures free energy \(E(s)\) and the partition function

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  Z = \sum_s exp(-\beta E(s)),\quad\mathrm{with}\quad\beta = \frac{1}{RT}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(R\) is the gas constant and \(T\) the thermodynamic temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/heat\_capacity.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the specific heat for an RNA. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function computes an RNAs specific heat in a given temperature range from the partition function by numeric differentiation. The result is returned as a list of pairs of temperature in C and specific heat in Kcal/(Mol*K).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Users can specify the temperature range for the computation from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_min}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_max}}, as well as the increment step size \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_increment}}. The latter also determines how many times the partition function is computed. Finally, the parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpoints}} determines how smooth the curve should be. The algorithm itself fits a parabola to \( 2 \cdot mpoints + 1 \) data points to calculate 2nd derivatives. Increasing this parameter produces a smoother curve.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

If the optional function arguments \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_min}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_max}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_increment}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpoints}} are omitted, they default to 0.0, 100.0, 1.0 and 2, respectively. \pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{partfunc/thermodynamics:group__thermodynamics_1ga0c2664e15dded704d805a9d2a625ff21}}{\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/thermodynamics:c.vrna_heat_capacity_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_heat\_capacity\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_heat\_capacity\_simple}}}}{\DUrole{k}{const}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{sequence}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{T\_min}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{T\_max}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{T\_increment}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{unsigned}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{mpoints}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/heat\_capacity.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the specific heat for an RNA (simplified variant) 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/thermodynamics:group__thermodynamics_1gafd95c2350d67d8f4374369c19cf111f1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_heat\_capacity()}}}}, this function computes an RNAs specific heat in a given temperature range from the partition function by numeric differentiation. This simplified version, however, only requires the RNA sequence as input instead of a vrna\_fold\_compound\_t data structure. The result is returned as a list of pairs of temperature in C and specific heat in Kcal/(Mol*K).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Users can specify the temperature range for the computation from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_min}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_max}}, as well as the increment step size \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_increment}}. The latter also determines how many times the partition function is computed. Finally, the parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpoints}} determines how smooth the curve should be. The algorithm itself fits a parabola to \( 2 \cdot mpoints + 1 \) data points to calculate 2nd derivatives. Increasing this parameter produces a smoother curve.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000109}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is available as overloaded function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{heat\_capacity()}}. If the optional function arguments \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_min}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_max}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T\_increment}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpoints}} are omitted, they default to 0.0, 100.0, 1.0 and 2, respectively. See, e.g.  \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.head\_capacity()}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}. 

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{T\_min}} \textendash{} Lowest temperature in C 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{description}\end{quote}

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/part\_func.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the partition function \(Q\) for a given RNA sequence. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{structure} is not a NULL pointer on input, it contains on return a string consisting of the letters “ . , | \{ \} ( ) “ denoting bases that are essentially unpaired, weakly paired, strongly paired without preference, weakly upstream (downstream) paired, or strongly up\sphinxhyphen{} (down\sphinxhyphen{})stream paired bases, respectively. If fold\_constrained is not 0, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{structure} string is interpreted on input as a list of constraints for the folding. The character “x” marks bases that must be unpaired, matching brackets “ ( ) “ denote base pairs, all other characters are ignored. Any pairs conflicting with the constraint will be forbidden. This is usually sufficient to ensure the constraints are honored. If the parameter calculate\_bppm is set to 0 base pairing probabilities will not be computed (saving CPU time), otherwise after calculations took place pr will contain the probability that bases \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} pair.

\sphinxAtStartPar

Successive calls will first free previously allocated memory before starting the computation.

Consider using {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global_deprecated:group__part__func__global__deprecated_1gac4f95bee734b2563a3d6e9932117ebdf}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_fold\_par()}}}} for a really threadsafe implementation.

\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Pre}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function takes its model details from the global variables provided in \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}

\sphinxlineitem{Post}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After successful run the hidden folding matrices are filled with the appropriate Boltzmann factors. Depending on whether the global variable {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/model_details:group__model__details_1gad512b5dd4dbec60faccfe137bb474489}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{do\_backtrack}}}} was set the base pair probabilities are already computed and may be accessed for further usage via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global_deprecated:group__part__func__global__deprecated_1gad2bba2bdfef5a24f69fe10bbb9fc6de9}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{export\_bppm()}}}} function. A call of {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global_deprecated:group__part__func__global__deprecated_1gae73db3f49a94f0f72e067ecd12681dbd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{free\_pf\_arrays()}}}} will free all memory allocated by this function. Successive calls will first free previously allocated memory before starting the computation.

\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sequence}} \textendash{} \sphinxstylestrong{{[}in{]}} The RNA sequence input 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{structure}} \textendash{} \sphinxstylestrong{{[}inout{]}} A pointer to a char array where a base pair probability information can be stored in a pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation (may be NULL, too) 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ensemble free energy \(G = -RT \cdot \log(Q) \) in kcal/mol 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Recalculate energy parameters. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function recalculates all energy parameters given the current model settings. It’s second argument can either be NULL or a data structure containing the precomputed Boltzmann factors. In the first scenario, the necessary data structure will be created automatically according to the current global model settings, i.e. this mode might not be threadsafe. However, if the provided data structure is not NULL, threadsafety for the model parameters {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/model_details:group__model__details_1ga72b511ed1201f7e23ec437e468790d74}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{dangles}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/model_details:group__model__details_1gad3b22044065acc6dee0af68931b52cfd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_scale}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/model_details:group__model__details_1gab4b11c8d9c758430960896bc3fe82ead}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{temperature}}}} is regained, since their values are taken from this data structure during subsequent calculations.

\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/LPfold.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute partition functions for locally stable secondary structures. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
pfl\_fold computes partition functions for every window of size ‘winSize’ possible in a RNA molecule, allowing only pairs with a span smaller than ‘pairSize’. It returns the mean pair probabilities averaged over all windows containing the pair in ‘pl’. ‘winSize’ should always be \textgreater{}= ‘pairSize’. Note that in contrast to {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/window_deprecated:group__mfe__window__deprecated_1gafdd1e11b5c7ad443b9f86b818e67bab4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Lfold()}}}}, bases outside of the window do not influence the structure at all. Only probabilities higher than ‘cutoffb’ are kept.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If ‘pU’ is supplied (i.e is not the NULL pointer), {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/window_deprecated:group__part__func__window__deprecated_1gaf6d77f10775c1d58c8199d5ec95d4228}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pfl\_fold()}}}} will also compute the mean probability that regions of length ‘u’ and smaller are unpaired. The parameter ‘u’ is supplied in ‘pup{[}0{]}{[}0{]}’. On return the ‘pup’ array will contain these probabilities, with the entry on ‘pup{[}x{]}{[}y{]}’ containing the mean probability that x and the y\sphinxhyphen{}1 preceding bases are unpaired. The ‘pU’ array needs to be large enough to hold n+1 float* entries, where n is the sequence length.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If an array dpp2 is supplied, the probability of base pair (i,j) given that there already exists a base pair (i+1,j\sphinxhyphen{}1) is also computed and saved in this array. If pUfp is given (i.e. not NULL), pU is not saved but put out imediately. If spup is given (i.e. is not NULL), the pair probabilities in pl are not saved but put out imediately.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sequence}} \textendash{} RNA sequence 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{winSize}} \textendash{} size of the window 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{pairSize}} \textendash{} maximum size of base pair 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{cutoffb}} \textendash{} cutoffb for base pairs 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{pU}} \textendash{} array holding all unpaired probabilities 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{dpp2}} \textendash{} array of dependent pair probabilities 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{pUfp}} \textendash{} file pointer for pU 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{spup}} \textendash{} file pointer for pair probabilities 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
list of pair probabilities 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\subsection{Partition Function API}
\label{\detokenize{pf_fold:partition-function-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to our {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Minimum Free Energy (MFE) Algorithms}}}}, we provide two different flavors for partition
function computations:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Global Partition Function and Equilibrium Probabilities}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} to compute the partition function for a full length sequence

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/window::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Local (sliding window) Partition Function and Equilibrium Probabilities}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} to compute the partition function of each window using a sliding window approach

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
While the global partition function approach supports predictions using single sequences as
well as consensus partition functions for multiple sequence alignments (MSA), we currently
do not support MSA input for the local variant.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparative prediction computes an average of the free energy contributions plus an additional
covariance pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}energy term, exactly as we do for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Minimum Free Energy (MFE) Algorithms}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Boltzmann weights for the free energy contributions of individual loops can be
found in {\hyperref[\detokenize{eval/eval_loops::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Energy Evaluation for Individual Loops}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Our implementations also provide a stochastic backtracking procedure to draw
@ref subopt\_stochbt according to their equilibrium probabilty.

a particular base pair has been published by Zuker {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id32}{1989}{]}
and is based on ideas for predicting structures for circular RNAs,

\sphinxAtStartPar
Generate suboptimal structures within an energy band arround the MFE. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is the most generic implementation of the suboptimal structure generator according to   Wuchty \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id33}{1999}{]} . Identical to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/wuchty:group__subopt__wuchty_1gad0cce16455fda0737873d8e1c5846480}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_subopt()}}}}, it computes all secondary structures within an energy band \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delta}} arround the MFE. However, this function does not print the resulting structures and their corresponding free energies to a file pointer, or returns them as a list. Instead, it calls a user\sphinxhyphen{}provided callback function which it passes the structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket format, the corresponding free energy in kcal/mol, and a user\sphinxhyphen{}provided data structure each time a structure was backtracked successfully. This function indicates the final output, i.e. the end of the backtracking procedure by passing NULL instead of an actual dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket string to the callback.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/boltzmann\_sampling.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sample a secondary structure of a subsequence from the Boltzmann ensemble according its probability. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a probabilistic (stochastic) backtracing in the partition function DP arrays to obtain a secondary structure. The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{length}} specifies the length of the substructure starting from the 5’ end.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The structure \( s \) with free energy \( E(s) \) is picked from the Boltzmann distributed ensemble according to its probability

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
p(s) = \frac{exp(-E(s) / kT)}{Z}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with partition function \( Z = \sum_s exp(-E(s) / kT) \), Boltzmann constant \( k \) and thermodynamic temperature \( T \).

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/boltzmann\_sampling.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Obtain a set of secondary structure samples for a subsequence from the Boltzmann ensemble according their probability. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a probabilistic (stochastic) backtracing in the partition function DP arrays to obtain a set of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{num\_samples}} secondary structures. The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{length}} specifies the length of the substructure starting from the 5’ end.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any structure \( s \) with free energy \( E(s) \) is picked from the Boltzmann distributed ensemble according to its probability

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
p(s) = \frac{exp(-E(s) / kT)}{Z}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with partition function \( Z = \sum_s exp(-E(s) / kT) \), Boltzmann constant \( k \) and thermodynamic temperature \( T \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} flag one can switch between regular ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga760aa2fb2d5e3d7521a11454a21e9b9f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_DEFAULT}}}}) backtracing mode, and non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant sampling ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga9d580ce645aa0c38b69afdf56c332200}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_NON\_REDUNDANT}}}}) along the lines of   Michálik \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id40}{2017}{]} .

\sphinxAtStartPar

Using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} flag one can switch between regular ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga760aa2fb2d5e3d7521a11454a21e9b9f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_DEFAULT}}}}) backtracing mode, and non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant sampling ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga9d580ce645aa0c38b69afdf56c332200}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_NON\_REDUNDANT}}}}) along the lines of   Michálik \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id40}{2017}{]} .

\sphinxAtStartPar
In contrast to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga0849bf555110d546ac81bc2aefdfe507}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5\_cb()}}}} this function allows for resuming a previous sampling round in specialized Boltzmann sampling, such as non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant backtracking. For that purpose, the user passes the address of a Boltzmann sampling data structure ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1gaa59c30efbed96bf9aaf8005584c72e63}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack\_mem\_t}}}}) which will be re\sphinxhyphen{}used in each round of sampling, i.e. each successive call to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga1c4cd7156224ef96147b22c5f7c4ddc3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5\_resume\_cb()}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga7917f94e9dfef04a7a2ca666ff4987fb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5\_resume()}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Obtain a set of secondary structure samples for a subsequence from the Boltzmann ensemble according their probability. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a probabilistic (stochastic) backtracing in the partition function DP arrays to obtain a set of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{num\_samples}} secondary structures. The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{length}} specifies the length of the substructure starting from the 5’ end.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any structure \( s \) with free energy \( E(s) \) is picked from the Boltzmann distributed ensemble according to its probability

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 p(s) = \frac{exp(-E(s) / kT)}{Z}
 \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with partition function \( Z = \sum_s exp(-E(s) / kT) \), Boltzmann constant \( k \) and thermodynamic temperature \( T \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} flag one can switch between regular ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga760aa2fb2d5e3d7521a11454a21e9b9f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_DEFAULT}}}}) backtracing mode, and non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant sampling ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga9d580ce645aa0c38b69afdf56c332200}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_NON\_REDUNDANT}}}}) along the lines of   Michálik \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id40}{2017}{]} .

\sphinxAtStartPar
In contrast to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga7917f94e9dfef04a7a2ca666ff4987fb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5\_resume()}}}} this function yields the structure samples through a callback mechanism.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A successive sample call to this function may look like:
