\PYG{c+c1}{// sample the first 100 structures}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack5\PYGZus{}resume\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{length}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{callback\PYGZus{}function}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{callback\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// sample another 500 structures}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack5\PYGZus{}resume\PYGZus{}cb}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{l+m+mi}{500}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{length}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{callback\PYGZus{}function}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{callback\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{,}

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/boltzmann\_sampling.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sample a secondary structure from the Boltzmann ensemble according its probability. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a probabilistic (stochastic) backtracing in the partition function DP arrays to obtain a secondary structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The structure \( s \) with free energy \( E(s) \) is picked from the Boltzmann distributed ensemble according to its probability

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
p(s) = \frac{exp(-E(s) / kT)}{Z}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with partition function \( Z = \sum_s exp(-E(s) / kT) \), Boltzmann constant \( k \) and thermodynamic temperature \( T \).

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Obtain a set of secondary structure samples from the Boltzmann ensemble according their probability. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a probabilistic (stochastic) backtracing in the partition function DP arrays to obtain a set of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{num\_samples}} secondary structures.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any structure \( s \) with free energy \( E(s) \) is picked from the Boltzmann distributed ensemble according to its probability

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 p(s) = \frac{exp(-E(s) / kT)}{Z}
 \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with partition function \( Z = \sum_s exp(-E(s) / kT) \), Boltzmann constant \( k \) and thermodynamic temperature \( T \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} flag one can switch between regular ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga760aa2fb2d5e3d7521a11454a21e9b9f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_DEFAULT}}}}) backtracing mode, and non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant sampling ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga9d580ce645aa0c38b69afdf56c332200}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_NON\_REDUNDANT}}}}) along the lines of   Michálik \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id40}{2017}{]} .

\sphinxAtStartPar
In contrast to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1gad6d1de3371ebe6fd1db3c318e50e6488}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack\_cb()}}}} this function allows for resuming a previous sampling round in specialized Boltzmann sampling, such as non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant backtracking. For that purpose, the user passes the address of a Boltzmann sampling data structure ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1gaa59c30efbed96bf9aaf8005584c72e63}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack\_mem\_t}}}}) which will be re\sphinxhyphen{}used in each round of sampling, i.e. each successive call to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1gabaaec8b80274f8e7b86d2b2226469d9f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack\_resume\_cb()}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1gae175129ece546fe7c092f27072e039d1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack\_resume()}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A successive sample call to this function may look like: 
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack\PYGZus{}mem\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// sample the first 100 structures}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack\PYGZus{}resume}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                       }\PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                       }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                       }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// sample another 500 structures}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack\PYGZus{}resume}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                       }\PYG{l+m+mi}{500}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                       }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                       }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// release memory occupied by the non\PYGZhy{}redundant memory data structure}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack\PYGZus{}mem\PYGZus{}free}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/boltzmann\_sampling.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sample a secondary structure of a subsequence from the Boltzmann ensemble according its probability. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a probabilistic (stochastic) backtracing in the partition function DP arrays to obtain a secondary structure. The parameters \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{end}} specify the interval \( [start:end] \) of the subsequence with \( 1 \leq start < end \leq n\) for sequence length \( n \), the structure \( s_{start,end} \) should be drawn from.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The resulting substructure \( s_{start,end} \) with free energy \( E(s_{start, end}) \) is picked from the Boltzmann distributed sub ensemble of all structures within the interval \( [start:end] \) according to its probability

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
p(s_{start,end}) = \frac{exp(-E(s_{start,end}) / kT)}{Z_{start,end}}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with partition function \( Z_{start,end} = \sum_{s_{start,end}} exp(-E(s_{start,end}) / kT) \), Boltzmann constant \( k \) and thermodynamic temperature \( T \).

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Obtain a set of secondary structure samples for a subsequence from the Boltzmann ensemble according their probability. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a probabilistic (stochastic) backtracing in the partition function DP arrays to obtain a set of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{num\_samples}} secondary structures. The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{length}} specifies the length of the substructure starting from the 5’ end.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any structure \( s \) with free energy \( E(s) \) is picked from the Boltzmann distributed ensemble according to its probability

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 p(s) = \frac{exp(-E(s) / kT)}{Z}
 \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with partition function \( Z = \sum_s exp(-E(s) / kT) \), Boltzmann constant \( k \) and thermodynamic temperature \( T \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} flag one can switch between regular ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga760aa2fb2d5e3d7521a11454a21e9b9f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_DEFAULT}}}}) backtracing mode, and non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant sampling ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga9d580ce645aa0c38b69afdf56c332200}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PBACKTRACK\_NON\_REDUNDANT}}}}) along the lines of   Michálik \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id40}{2017}{]} .

\sphinxAtStartPar
In contrast to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga0849bf555110d546ac81bc2aefdfe507}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5\_cb()}}}} this function allows for resuming a previous sampling round in specialized Boltzmann sampling, such as non\sphinxhyphen{}redundant backtracking. For that purpose, the user passes the address of a Boltzmann sampling data structure ({\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1gaa59c30efbed96bf9aaf8005584c72e63}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack\_mem\_t}}}}) which will be re\sphinxhyphen{}used in each round of sampling, i.e. each successive call to {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga1c4cd7156224ef96147b22c5f7c4ddc3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5\_resume\_cb()}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{subopt/stochbt:group__subopt__stochbt_1ga7917f94e9dfef04a7a2ca666ff4987fb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pbacktrack5\_resume()}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A successive sample call to this function may look like: 
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack\PYGZus{}mem\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// sample the first 100 structures}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack5\PYGZus{}resume}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{length}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// sample another 500 structures}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack5\PYGZus{}resume}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{l+m+mi}{500}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{length}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// release memory occupied by the non\PYGZhy{}redundant memory data structure}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}pbacktrack\PYGZus{}mem\PYGZus{}free}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nonredundant\PYGZus{}memory}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{Compute the Structure with Maximum Expected Accuracy (MEA)}
\label{\detokenize{subopt/mea:compute-the-structure-with-maximum-expected-accuracy-mea}}\label{\detokenize{subopt/mea::doc}}

\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{subopt/mea:group__mea__fold}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{breathe-sectiondef}\subsubsection*{Functions}
\index{vrna\_MEA (C function)@\spxentry{vrna\_MEA}\spxextra{C function}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{subopt/mea:c.vrna_MEA}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigstartmultiline
\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{subopt/mea:group__mea__fold_1ga9b87b664ef014c1266aa50d5bc39f2ac}}\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_MEA}}}}{{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{fc}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{double}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{gamma}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{mea}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/MEA.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute a MEA (maximum expected accuracy) structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The algorithm maximizes the expected accuracy

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  A(S) = \sum_{(i,j) \in S} 2 \gamma p_{ij} + \sum_{i \notin S} p^u_i
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Higher values of \(\gamma\) result in more base pairs of lower probability and thus higher sensitivity. Low values of \(\gamma\) result in structures containing only highly likely pairs (high specificity). The code of the MEA function also demonstrates the use of sparse dynamic programming scheme to reduce the time and memory complexity of folding.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000154}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is attached as overloaded method \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MEA}}(gamma = 1.) to objects of type \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fold\_compound}}. Note, that it returns the MEA structure and MEA value as a tuple (MEA\_structure, MEA). See, e.g.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.fold_compound.MEA}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.fold\_compound.MEA()}}}}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}. 

\end{fulllineitems}


\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{fc}} \textendash{} The fold compound data structure with pre\sphinxhyphen{}filled base pair probability matrix 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{gamma}} \textendash{} The weighting factor for base pairs vs. unpaired nucleotides

\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/MEA.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute a MEA (maximum expected accuracy) structure from a list of probabilities. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The algorithm maximizes the expected accuracy

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  A(S) = \sum_{(i,j) \in S} 2 \gamma p_{ij} + \sum_{i \notin S} p^u_i
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Higher values of \(\gamma\) result in more base pairs of lower probability and thus higher sensitivity. Low values of \(\gamma\) result in structures containing only highly likely pairs (high specificity). The code of the MEA function also demonstrates the use of sparse dynamic programming scheme to reduce the time and memory complexity of folding.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstartsignatures

\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is available as overloaded function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MEA\_from\_plist}}(gamma = 1., md = NULL). Note, that it returns the MEA structure and MEA value as a tuple (MEA\_structure, MEA). See, e.g.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.MEA_from_plist}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.MEA\_from\_plist()}}}}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}. 

\end{fulllineitems}



\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The unpaired probabilities \(p^u_i = 1 - \sum_{j \neq i} p_{ij}\) are usually computed from the supplied pairing probabilities \(p_{ij}\) as stored in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plist}} entries of type {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/plist:group__struct__utils__plist_1ga7c7484a8a1e6704b1aefaf589f3b27c1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PLIST\_TYPE\_BASEPAIR}}}}. To overwrite individual \(p^u_o\) values simply add entries with type {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/plist:group__struct__utils__plist_1ga7961043acc4f183a7bc7cf2505a8c8b9}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PLIST\_TYPE\_UNPAIRED}}}}

\section{RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA Interaction}
\label{\detokenize{cofold:rna-rna-interaction}}\label{\detokenize{cofold::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The function of an RNA molecule often depends on its interaction with
other RNAs. The following routines therefore allows one to predict structures
formed by two RNA molecules upon hybridization.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Partition Function for Two Hybridized Sequences}
\label{\detokenize{rip/pf:partition-function-for-two-hybridized-sequences}}\label{\detokenize{rip/pf::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To simplify the implementation the partition function computation is done
internally in a null model that does not include the duplex initiation
energy, i.e. the entropic penalty for producing a dimer from two
monomers). The resulting free energies and pair probabilities are initially
relative to that null model. In a second step the free energies can be
corrected to include the dimerization penalty, and the pair probabilities
can be divided into the conditional pair probabilities given that a re
dimer is formed or not formed. See Bernhart \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id23}{2006}{]} for further details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As for folding one RNA molecule, this computes the partition function
of all possible structures and the base pair probabilities. Uses the
same global \#pf\_scale variable to avoid overflows.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After computing the partition functions of all possible dimeres one
can compute the probabilities of base pairs, the concentrations out of
start concentrations and sofar and soaway.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dimer formation is inherently concentration dependent. Given the free
energies of the monomers A and B and dimers AB, AA, and BB one can compute
the equilibrium concentrations, given input concentrations of A and B, see
e.g. Dimitrov \& Zuker (2004)

\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate partition function and base pair probabilities of nucleic acid/nucleic acid dimers. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This simplified interface to {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global:group__part__func__global_1gae796019c176a158f0e9d7741a85c1743}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pf\_dimer()}}}} computes the partition function and, if required, base pair probabilities for an RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA interaction using default options. Memory required for dynamic programming (DP) matrices will be allocated and free’d on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly. Hence, after return of this function, the recursively filled matrices are not available any more for any post\sphinxhyphen{}processing.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{sphinxseealso}



\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In case you want to use the filled DP matrices for any subsequent post\sphinxhyphen{}processing step, or you require other conditions than specified by the default model details, use {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global:group__part__func__global_1gae796019c176a158f0e9d7741a85c1743}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pf\_dimer()}}}}, and the data structure {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}} instead.

\subsection{RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA interaction as a stepwise process}
\label{\detokenize{rip/up:rna-rna-interaction-as-a-stepwise-process}}\label{\detokenize{rip/up::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In this approach to cofolding the interaction between two RNA molecules is
seen as a stepwise process. In a first step, the target molecule has to
adopt a structure in which a binding site is accessible. In a second step,
the ligand molecule will hybridize with a region accessible to an
interaction. Consequently the algorithm is designed as a two step process:
The first step is the calculation of the probability
that a region within the target is unpaired, or equivalently, the
calculation of the free energy needed to expose a region. In the second step
we compute the free energy of an interaction for every possible binding site.

\pysigstartsignatures

\sphinxAtStartPar
You have to call function {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global_deprecated:group__part__func__global__deprecated_1gadc3db3d98742427e7001a7fd36ef28c2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_fold()}}}} providing the same sequence before calling {\hyperref[\detokenize{rip/up:group__up__cofold_1ga2a7fb78dfbfb00eccf8d79f38e3384c3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_unstru()}}}}. If you want to calculate unpaired regions for a constrained structure, set variable ‘structure’ in function ‘{\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global_deprecated:group__part__func__global__deprecated_1gadc3db3d98742427e7001a7fd36ef28c2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_fold()}}}}’ to the constrain string. It returns a {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structpu__contrib}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pu\_contrib}}}} struct containing four arrays of dimension {[}i = 1 to length(sequence){]}{[}j = 0 to u\sphinxhyphen{}1{]} containing all possible contributions to the probabilities of unpaired regions of maximum length u. Each array in {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structpu__contrib}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pu\_contrib}}}} contains one of the contributions to the total probability of being unpaired: The probability of being unpaired within an exterior loop is in array {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structpu__contrib}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pu\_contrib}}}}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}E, the probability of being unpaired within a hairpin loop is in array {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structpu__contrib}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pu\_contrib}}}}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}H, the probability of being unpaired within an interior loop is in array {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structpu__contrib}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pu\_contrib}}}}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}I and probability of being unpaired within a multi\sphinxhyphen{}loop is in array {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structpu__contrib}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pu\_contrib}}}}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}M. The total probability of being unpaired is the sum of the four arrays of {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structpu__contrib}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pu\_contrib}}}}.

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/part\_func\_up.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculates the probability of a local interaction between two sequences. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The function considers the probability that the region of interaction is unpaired within ‘s1’ and ‘s2’. The longer sequence has to be given as ‘s1’. The shorter sequence has to be given as ‘s2’. Function {\hyperref[\detokenize{rip/up:group__up__cofold_1ga2a7fb78dfbfb00eccf8d79f38e3384c3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_unstru()}}}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
has to be called for ‘s1’ and ‘s2’, where the probabilities of being unpaired have to be given in ‘p\_c’ and ‘p\_c2’, respectively. If you do not want to include the probabilities of being unpaired for ‘s2’ set ‘p\_c2’ to NULL. If variable ‘cstruc’ is not NULL, constrained folding is done: The available constrains for intermolecular interaction are: ‘.’ (no constrain), ‘x’ (the base has no intermolecular interaction) and ‘|’ (the corresponding base has to be paired intermolecularily).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter ‘w’ determines the maximal length of the interaction. The parameters ‘incr5’ and ‘incr3’ allows inclusion of unpaired residues left (‘incr5’) and right (‘incr3’) of the region of interaction in ‘s1’. If the ‘incr’ options are used, function
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rip/up:group__up__cofold_1ga2a7fb78dfbfb00eccf8d79f38e3384c3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_unstru()}}}} has to be called with w=w+incr5+incr3 for the longer sequence ‘s1’.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It returns a structure of type {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structinteract}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{interact}}}} which contains the probability of the best local interaction including residue i in Pi and the minimum free energy in Gi, where i is the position in sequence ‘s1’. The member Gikjl of structure {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/data_structures:structinteract}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{interact}}}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
is the best interaction between region {[}k,i{]} k\textless{}i in longer sequence ‘s1’ and region {[}j,l{]} j\textless{}l in ‘s2’. Gikjl\_wo is Gikjl without the probability of beeing unpaired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rip/up:group__up__cofold_1gadde308fd5f696dc271b1532aa96fd12f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{free\_interact()}}}} to free the returned structure, all other stuff is freed inside {\hyperref[\detokenize{rip/up:group__up__cofold_1ga5adcc9222fe42d943e407e79a3f4558d}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{pf\_interact()}}}}.

\subsection{Concatenating RNA sequences}
\label{\detokenize{cofold:concatenating-rna-sequences}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One approach to co\sphinxhyphen{}folding two RNAs consists of concatenating the two
sequences and keeping track of the concatenation point in all energy
evaluations. Correspondingly, many of the cofold() and
co\_pf\_fold() routines take one sequence string as argument
and use the the global variable \#cut\_point to mark the concatenation
point. Note that while the \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAcofold} program uses the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\&}} character
to mark the chain break in its input.


\subsection{RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA interaction as a Stepwise Process}
\label{\detokenize{cofold:rna-rna-interaction-as-a-stepwise-process}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In a second approach to co\sphinxhyphen{}folding two RNAs, cofolding is seen as a
stepwise process. In the first step the probability of an unpaired region
is calculated and in a second step this probability of an unpaired region
is  multiplied with the probability of an interaction between the two RNAs.
This approach is implemented for the interaction between a long
target sequence and a short ligand RNA. Function pf\_unstru() calculates
the partition function over all unpaired regions in the input
sequence. Function pf\_interact(), which calculates the
partition function over all possible interactions between two
sequences, needs both sequence as separate strings as input.

\section{Classified Dynamic Programming Variants}
\label{\detokenize{class_fold:classified-dynamic-programming-variants}}\label{\detokenize{class_fold::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, thermodynamic properties using the basic recursions for {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Minimum Free Energy (MFE) Algorithms}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pf_fold::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Partition Function and Equilibrium Properties}}}}, and so forth, are computed over the entire structure space. However,
sometimes it is desired to partition the structure space \sphinxstyleemphasis{a priori} and compute
the above properties for each of the resulting partitions. This approach directly leads
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Classified Dynamic Programming}.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Distance Based Partitioning of the Secondary Structure Space}
\label{\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood:distance-based-partitioning-of-the-secondary-structure-space}}\label{\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The secondary structure space is divided into partitions according to the base
pair distance to two given reference structures and all relevant properties are
calculated for each of the resulting partitions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute MFE’s and representative for distance partitioning. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function computes the minimum free energies and a representative secondary structure for each distance class according to the two references specified in the datastructure ‘vars’. The maximum basepair distance to each of both references may be set by the arguments ‘distance1’ and ‘distance2’, respectively. If both distance arguments are set to ‘\sphinxhyphen{}1’, no restriction is assumed and the calculation is performed for each distance class possible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The returned list contains an entry for each distance class. If a maximum basepair distance to either of the references was passed, an entry with k=l=\sphinxhyphen{}1 will be appended in the list, denoting the class where all structures exceeding the maximum will be thrown into. The end of the list is denoted by an attribute value of INF in the k\sphinxhyphen{}attribute of the list entry.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Backtrack a minimum free energy structure from a 5’ section of specified length. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function allows one to backtrack a secondary structure beginning at the 5’ end, a specified length and residing in a specific distance class. If the argument ‘k’ gets a value of \sphinxhyphen{}1, the structure that is backtracked is assumed to reside in the distance class where all structures exceeding the maximum basepair distance specified in TwoDfold() belong to.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{deprecated:deprecated_1_deprecated000005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Deprecated:}}}}}

\subsubsection{Partition Function Variants}
\label{\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood:partition-function-variants}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the partition function and stochastically sample secondary structures for
a partitioning of the secondary structure space according to the base pair distance
to two fixed reference structures.


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood:group__kl__neighborhood__pf}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{breathe-sectiondef}\subsubsection*{Functions}
\index{vrna\_pf\_TwoD (C function)@\spxentry{vrna\_pf\_TwoD}\spxextra{C function}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood:c.vrna_pf_TwoD}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigstartmultiline
\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood:group__kl__neighborhood__pf_1gac3bf71cefa4414f695e51f5da7269ebb}}{\hyperref[\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood:c.vrna_sol_TwoD_pf_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_sol\_TwoD\_pf\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_pf\_TwoD}}}}{{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{fc}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{maxDistance1}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{maxDistance2}}{}

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/2Dpfold.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the partition function for all distance classes. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function computes the partition functions for all distance classes according the two reference structures specified in the datastructure ‘vars’. Similar to {\hyperref[\detokenize{classified/kl_neighborhood:group__kl__neighborhood__mfe_1ga264ac71e75add31dfb1fc72a0b2de709}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mfe\_TwoD()}}}} the arguments maxDistance1 and maxDistance2 specify the maximum distance to both reference structures. A value of ‘\sphinxhyphen{}1’ in either of them makes the appropriate distance restrictionless, i.e. all basepair distancies to the reference are taken into account during computation. In case there is a restriction, the returned solution contains an entry where the attribute k=l=\sphinxhyphen{}1 contains the partition function for all structures exceeding the restriction. A value of INF in the attribute ‘k’ of the returned list denotes the end of the list

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/inverse.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find sequences with predefined structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function searches for a sequence with minimum free energy structure provided in the parameter ‘target’, starting with sequence ‘start’. It returns 0 if the search was successful, otherwise a structure distance in terms of the energy difference between the search result and the actual target ‘target’ is returned. The found sequence is returned in ‘start’. If {\hyperref[\detokenize{inverse:group__inverse__fold_1ga7ec4ba51f86e1717a1e174264e4a75ce}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{give\_up}}}} is set to 1, the function will return as soon as it is clear that the search will be unsuccessful, this speeds up the algorithm if you are only interested in exact solutions.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{start}} \textendash{} The start sequence 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{target}} \textendash{} The target secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The distance to the target in case a search was unsuccessful, 0 otherwise 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

Find sequence that maximizes probability of a predefined structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function searches for a sequence with maximum probability to fold into the provided structure ‘target’ using the partition function algorithm. It returns \(-kT \cdot \log(p)\) where \(p\) is the frequency of ‘target’ in the ensemble of possible structures. This is usually much slower than {\hyperref[\detokenize{inverse:group__inverse__fold_1ga7af026de55d4babad879f2c92559cbbc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{inverse\_fold()}}}}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The distance to the target in case a search was unsuccessful, 0 otherwise 

\end{description}\end{quote}

recursions by means of soft constraints.

secondary structure prediction can be found in Lorenz \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id35}{2016}{]}.

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/constraints/SHAPE.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add SHAPE reactivity data as soft constraints (Deigan et al. method) 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This approach of SHAPE directed RNA folding uses the simple linear ansatz

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \Delta G_{\text{SHAPE}}(i) = m \ln(\text{SHAPE reactivity}(i)+1)+ b \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
to convert SHAPE reactivity values to pseudo energies whenever a nucleotide \( i \) contributes to a stacked pair. A positive slope \( m \) penalizes high reactivities in paired regions, while a negative intercept \( b \) results in a confirmatory \textasciigrave{}bonus’ free energy for correctly predicted base pairs. Since the energy evaluation of a base pair stack involves two pairs, the pseudo energies are added for all four contributing nucleotides. Consequently, the energy term is applied twice for pairs inside a helix and only once for pairs adjacent to other structures. For all other loop types the energy model remains unchanged even when the experimental data highly disagrees with a certain motif.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Add SHAPE reactivity data as soft constraints (Zarringhalam et al. method) 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method first converts the observed SHAPE reactivity of nucleotide \( i \) into a probability \( q_i \) that position \( i \) is unpaired by means of a non\sphinxhyphen{}linear map. Then pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}energies of the form

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \Delta G_{\text{SHAPE}}(x,i) = \beta\ |x_i - q_i| \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
are computed, where \( x_i=0 \) if position \( i \) is unpaired and \( x_i=1 \) if \( i \) is paired in a given secondary structure. The parameter \( \beta \) serves as scaling factor. The magnitude of discrepancy between prediction and experimental observation is represented by \( |x_i - q_i| \).

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Find a vector of perturbation energies that minimizes the discripancies between
predicted and observed pairing probabilities and the amount of neccessary adjustments.

Use the sum of squared aberrations as objective function. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
\( F(\vec\epsilon) = \sum_{i = 1}^n{ \frac{\epsilon_i^2}{\tau^2} } + \sum_{i = 1}^n{ \frac{(p_i(\vec\epsilon) - q_i)^2}{\sigma^2} } \to min \)

\sphinxAtStartPar
Find a vector of perturbation energies that minimizes the discripancies between predicted and observed pairing probabilities and the amount of neccessary adjustments. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use an iterative minimization algorithm to find a vector of perturbation energies whose incorporation as soft constraints shifts the predicted pairing probabilities closer to the experimentally observed probabilities. The algorithm aims to minimize an objective function that penalizes discripancies between predicted and observed pairing probabilities and energy model adjustments, i.e. an appropriate vector of perturbation energies satisfies

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
F(\vec\epsilon) = \sum_{\mu}{ \frac{\epsilon_{\mu}^2}{\tau^2} } + \sum_{i =
1}^n{ \frac{(p_i(\vec\epsilon) - q_i)^2}{\sigma^2} } \to \min.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An initialized fold compound and an array containing the observed probability for each nucleotide to be unbound are required as input data. The parameters objective\_function, sigma\_squared and tau\_squared are responsible for adjusting the aim of the objective function. Dependend on which type of objective function is selected, either squared or absolute aberrations are contributing to the objective function. The ratio of the parameters sigma\_squared and tau\_squared can be used to adjust the algorithm to find a solution either close to the thermodynamic prediction (sigma\_squared \textgreater{}\textgreater{} tau\_squared) or close to the experimental data (tau\_squared \textgreater{}\textgreater{} sigma\_squared). The minimization can be performed by makeing use of a custom gradient descent implementation or using one of the minimizing algorithms provided by the GNU Scientific Library. All algorithms require the evaluation of the gradient of the objective function, which includes the evaluation of conditional pairing probabilites. Since an exact evaluation is expensive, the probabilities can also be estimated from sampling by setting an appropriate sample size. The found vector of perturbation energies will be stored in the array epsilon. The progress of the minimization process can be tracked by implementing and passing a callback function.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For further details we refer to   Washietl \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id7}{2012}{]} .


\end{sphinxseealso}


\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{fc}} \textendash{} Pointer to a fold compound 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{q\_prob\_unpaired}} \textendash{} Pointer to an array containing the probability to be unpaired for each nucleotide 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{objective\_function}} \textendash{} The type of objective function to be used (VRNA\_OBJECTIVE\_FUNCTION\_QUADRATIC / VRNA\_OBJECTIVE\_FUNCTION\_LINEAR) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sigma\_squared}} \textendash{} A factor used for weighting the objective function. More weight on this factor will lead to a solution close to the null vector. 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{tau\_squared}} \textendash{} A factor used for weighting the objective function. More weight on this factor will lead to a solution close to the data provided in q\_prob\_unpaired. 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{algorithm}} \textendash{} The minimization algorithm (VRNA\_MINIMIZER\_*) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sample\_size}} \textendash{} The number of sampled sequences used for estimating the pairing probabilities. A value \textless{}= 0 will lead to an exact evaluation. 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{epsilon}} \textendash{} A pointer to an array used for storing the calculated vector of perturbation energies 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{callback}} \textendash{} A pointer to a callback function used for reporting the current minimization progress 

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}


\end{sphinxuseclass}

\section{Ligands Binding to RNA Structures}
\label{\detokenize{ligand_binding:ligands-binding-to-rna-structures}}\label{\detokenize{ligand_binding::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In our library, we provide two different ways to incorporate binding of small molecules
and proteins to specific RNA structures:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ligands/unstructured_domains::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Ligands Binding to Unstructured Domains}}}}, and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ligands/constraints::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Incorporating Ligands Binding to Specific Sequence/Structure Motifs}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first approach is implemented as an actual extension of the folding grammar. It adds
auxiliary derivation rules for each case when consecutive unpaired nucleotides are evaluated.
Therefore, this model is applicable to ligand binding to any loop context.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second approach, on the other hand, uses the soft\sphinxhyphen{}constraints feature to change the energy
evaluation of hairpin\sphinxhyphen{} or interior\sphinxhyphen{}loops. Hence, it can only be appleid when a ligand binds to
a hairpin\sphinxhyphen{}like, or interior\sphinxhyphen{}loop like motif.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Ligands Binding to Unstructured Domains}
\label{\detokenize{ligands/unstructured_domains:ligands-binding-to-unstructured-domains}}\label{\detokenize{ligands/unstructured_domains::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add ligand binding to loop regions using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_up::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Unstructured Domains}}}} feature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sometime, certain ligands, like single strand binding (SSB) proteins, compete with intramolecular
base pairing of the RNA. In situations, where the dissociation constant of the ligand is known and
the ligand binds to a consecutive stretch of single\sphinxhyphen{}stranded nucleotides we can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_up::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Unstructured Domains}}}}
functionality to extend the RNA folding grammar. This module provides a convenience default implementation
that covers most of the application scenarios.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The function {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_up:c.vrna_ud_add_motif}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_ud\_add\_motif()}}}}} attaches a ligands sequence motif and corresponding
binding free energy to the list of known ligand motifs within the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{domains\_up}} attribute of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}}. The first call to this function initializes the {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_up::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Unstructured Domains}}}}
feature with our default implementation. Subsequent calls of secondary structure prediction
algorithms with the modified {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}} then directly include the competition
of the ligand with regules base pairing. Since we utilize the unstructured domain extension,
The ligand binding model can be removed again using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{grammar/domains_up:c.vrna_ud_remove}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_ud\_remove()}}}}} function.

\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/pk\_plex.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pseudoknot loop scoring function prototype. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is used to evaluate a formed pseudoknot (PK) interaction in {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga1d12c3e1affefec6339a15348b1bbdca}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex()}}}}. It is supposed to take a PK\sphinxhyphen{}free secondary structure as input and coordinates of an additional interaction site. From this data, the energy (penalty) to score the PK loop is derived and returned in decakal/mol. Upon passing zero in any of the interaction site coordinates (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start\_5}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{end\_5}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start\_3}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{end\_3}}) or a \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} pointer in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pt}}, the function must return a PK loop score. This minimum PK loop score is used in the first phase of the heuristic implemented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga1d12c3e1affefec6339a15348b1bbdca}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex()}}}} to assess whether a particular interaction is further taken into account in a later, more thorough evaluation step.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest scoring function would simply return a constant score for any PK loop, no matter what type of loop is formed and how large the loop is. This is the default if {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1gaa6a5f5e20804ba729134eb8ad0c8da54}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_opt\_defaults()}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga8f224a6aa666fd7444b225f676471992}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_opt()}}}} is used to generate options for {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga1d12c3e1affefec6339a15348b1bbdca}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex()}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga7209e5212f611aa1c06b1609da696d35}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_opt\_fun()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga1d12c3e1affefec6339a15348b1bbdca}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex()}}}}


\end{sphinxseealso}

\pysigstartmultiline
\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga1d12c3e1affefec6339a15348b1bbdca}}{\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:c.vrna_pk_plex_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_pk\_plex}}}}{{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{fc}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{k}{const}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{accessibility}\sphinxparamcomma {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:c.vrna_pk_plex_opt_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_opt\_t}}}}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{options}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/pk\_plex.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Predict Pseudoknot interactions in terms of a two\sphinxhyphen{}step folding process. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Computes simple pseudoknot interactions according to the PKplex algorithm. This simple heuristic first compiles a list of potential interaction sites that may form a pseudoknot. The resulting candidate interactions are then fixed and an PK\sphinxhyphen{}free MFE structure for the remainder of the sequence is computed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{accessibility}} argument is a list of opening energies for potential interaction sites. It is used in the first step of the algorithm to identify potential interactions. Upon passing \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL}, the opening energies are determined automatically based on the current model settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}}, the function can return the MFE (incl. PK loops) or suboptimal structures within an energy band around the MFE. The PK loop is internally scored by a scoring function that in the simplest cases assigns a constant value for each PK loop. More complicated scoring functions can be passed as well, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1gaa3c616a490113feba261bed7a92981eb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_score\_f}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1ga7209e5212f611aa1c06b1609da696d35}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_opt\_fun()}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The function returns \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} on any error. Otherwise, a list of structures and interaction coordinates with corresponding energy contributions is returned. If no PK\sphinxhyphen{}interaction that satisfies the options is found, the list only consists of the PK\sphinxhyphen{}free MFE structure.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{fc}} \textendash{} fold compound with the input sequence and model settings 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{accessibility}} \textendash{} An array of opening energies for the implemented heuristic (maybe \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL}) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{options}} \textendash{} An {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:group__pseudoknots_1gab5afc6c459727dbdc37257711f062090}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_opt\_t}}}} options data structure that determines the algorithm parameters 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A list of potentially pseudoknotted structures (Last element in the list indicated by \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} value in {\hyperref[\detokenize{modules/pseudoknots:structvrna__pk__plex__result__s_1a31fe3dea3cb3799621cd111ab3e31629}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_pk\_plex\_result\_s.structure}}}}) 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/gquad.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Get a triangular matrix prefilled with minimum free energy contributions of G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplexes. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
At each position ij in the matrix, the minimum free energy of any G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex delimited by i and j is stored. If no G\sphinxhyphen{}quadruplex formation is possible, the matrix element is set to INF. Access the elements in the matrix via matrix{[}indx{[}j{]}+i{]}. To get the integer array indx see get\_jindx().

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
get\_jindx(), encode\_sequence()


\end{sphinxseealso}

\sphinxAtStartPar
given a dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket structure (possibly) containing gquads encoded by ‘+’ signs, find first gquad, return end position or 0 if none found Upon return L and l{[}{]} contain the number of stacked layers, as well as the lengths of the linker regions. To parse a string with many gquads, call parse\_gquad repeatedly e.g. end1 = parse\_gquad(struc, \&L, l); … ; end2 = parse\_gquad(struc+end1, \&L, l); end2+=end1; … ; end3 = parse\_gquad(struc+end2, \&L, l); end3+=end2; … ; 

\end{fulllineitems}

\begin{quote}\begin{description}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Post\sphinxhyphen{}transcriptional Base Modifications}
\label{\detokenize{modified_bases:post-transcriptional-base-modifications}}\label{\detokenize{modified_bases::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy parameter corrections for modified bases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many RNAs are known to be (heavily) modified post\sphinxhyphen{}trasnciptionaly. The best
known examples are tRNAs and rRNAs. To\sphinxhyphen{}date, more than 150 different modifications
are listed in the MODOMICS database (\sphinxurl{http://genesilico.pl/modomics/}) {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id50}{Boccaletto \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.}, 2022}{]}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many of the modified bases change the pairing behavior compared to their
unmodified version, affecting not only the pairing partner preference, but
also the resulting stability of the loops the base pairs may form.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, we provide a simple soft constraints callback implementation to
correct for some well known modified bases where energy parameters are
available for. This mechanism also supports arbitrary new modified base
energy parameters supplied in JSON format
(see {\hyperref[\detokenize{io/parameters:modified-bases}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Modified Bases}}}} for details).


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{modified_bases:group__modified__bases}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Support of modified bases in secondary structure prediction.

Safely append a formatted string to another string. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is a safe implementation for appending a formatted character array, similar to a cobination of \sphinxstyleemphasis{strcat} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{sprintf}. The function automatically allocates enough memory to store both, the previous content stored at \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dest}} and the appended format string. If the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dest}} pointer is NULL, the function allocate memory only for the format string. The function returns the number of characters in the resulting string or \sphinxhyphen{}1 in case of an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Trim a string by removing (multiple) occurences of a particular character. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function removes (multiple) consecutive occurences of a set of characters (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delimiters}}) within an input string. It may be used to remove leading and/or trailing whitespaces or to restrict the maximum number of consecutive occurences of the delimiting characters \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delimiters}}. Setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{keep=0}} removes all occurences, while other values reduce multiple consecutive occurences to at most \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{keep}} delimiters. This might be useful if one would like to reduce multiple whitespaces to a single one, or to remove empty fields within a comma\sphinxhyphen{}separated value string.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delimiters}} may be a pointer to a 0\sphinxhyphen{}terminated char string containing a set of any ASCII character. If \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} is passed as delimiter set or an empty char string, all whitespace characters are trimmed. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter is a bit vector that specifies which part of the string should undergo trimming. The implementation distinguishes the leading ({\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/strings:group__string__utils_1ga658ff8ea3e4ae6838d77ece7024a583f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_TRIM\_LEADING}}}}), trailing ({\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/strings:group__string__utils_1ga4b551fba1b2bbecafd335471b2c002dd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_TRIM\_TRAILING}}}}), and in\sphinxhyphen{}between ({\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/strings:group__string__utils_1gac500a0f17fff9c60ac98ed178f0a8fa3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_TRIM\_IN\_BETWEEN}}}}) part with respect to the delimiter set. Combinations of these parts can be specified by using logical\sphinxhyphen{}or operator.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following example code removes all leading and trailing whitespace characters from the input string: 
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{n}{string}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{20}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{  }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}t}\PYG{l+s}{ blablabla   }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{unsigned}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{r}\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}strtrim}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{string}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                                         }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                                         }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                                         }\PYG{n}{VRNA\PYGZus{}TRIM\PYGZus{}DEFAULT}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since many scripting languages treat strings as immutable objects, this function does not modify the input string directly. Instead, it returns the modified string as second return value, together with the number of removed delimiters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scripting language interface provides an overloaded version of this function, with default parameters \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delimiters=NULL}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{keep=0}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options={\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/strings:group__string__utils_1gab6272ec12f482870fa81d3d84d9b7370}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_TRIM\_DEFAULT}}}}}}. In case of alternative delimiters and non\sphinxhyphen{}null \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{keep}} parameter, the first \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{keep}} delimiters are preserved within the string. Use {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/strings:group__string__utils_1ga974e5e82e496e20290ec0f54c0e1d1da}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_TRIM\_SUBST\_BY\_FIRST}}}} to substitute all remaining delimiting characters with the first from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delimiters}} list.

Split a string into tokens using a delimiting character. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function splits a string into an array of strings using a single character that delimits the elements within the string. The default delimiter is the ampersand \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textquotesingle{}\&\textquotesingle{}}} and will be used when \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} is passed as a second argument. The returned list is NULL terminated, i.e. the last element is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}}. If the delimiter is not found, the returned list contains exactly one element: the input string.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For instance, the following code:

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{tok}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}strsplit}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{GGGG\PYGZam{}CCCC\PYGZam{}AAAAA}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tok}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{free}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{n}{free}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{tok}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
 produces this output:

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{GGGG}
\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{CCCC}
\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{AAAAA}
\PYG{o}{*}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
 and properly free’s the memory occupied by the returned element array.

Retrieve a DNA sequence which resembles the complement of the input sequence. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function returns a mew DNA string which is the complement of the input, i.e. the nucleotide letters \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{A}},\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}},\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{G}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T}} are substituted by their complements \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T}},\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{G}},\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{A}}, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any characters not belonging to the alphabet of the 4 canonical bases of DNA are not altered.

\sphinxAtStartPar

Remove pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots from an input structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function removes pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knots from an input structure by determining the minimum number of base pairs that need to be removed to make the structure pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}knot free.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To accomplish that, we use a dynamic programming algorithm similar to the Nussinov maxmimum matching approach.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The input structure must be in a dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket string like form where crossing base pairs are denoted by the use of additional types of matching brackets, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}\textgreater{}}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{\}}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{}}{[}{]}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{\}}}. Furthermore, crossing pairs may be annotated by matching uppercase/lowercase letters from the alphabet \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{A\sphinxhyphen{}Z}}. For the latter, the uppercase letter must be the 5’ and the lowercase letter the 3’ nucleotide of the base pair. The actual type of brackets to be recognized by this function must be specifed through the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Convert a Dot\sphinxhyphen{}Bracket structure string into tree string representation. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function allows one to convert a secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation into one of the various tree representations for secondary structures. The resulting tree is then represented as a string of parenthesis and node symbols, similar to to the Newick format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently we support conversion into the following formats, denoted by the value of parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{type:}} \begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/trees:group__struct__utils__tree_1ga3ad5609bc93ef20034c3ab989365c1f0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_STRUCTURE\_TREE\_HIT}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Homeomorphically Irreducible Tree (HIT) representation of a secondary structure.   (See also   Fontana \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id25}{1993}{]} )

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/trees:group__struct__utils__tree_1ga549e259a963d77e2d5b7e14083fc016e}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_STRUCTURE\_TREE\_SHAPIRO\_SHORT}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  (short) Coarse Grained representation of a secondary structure   (same as   Shapiro {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id27}{1988}{]} , but with root node \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{R}} and without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S}} nodes for the stems)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/trees:group__struct__utils__tree_1ga4acd9991a0250ccd4cd44c4725b31927}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_STRUCTURE\_TREE\_SHAPIRO}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  (full) Coarse Grained representation of a secondary structure   (See also   Shapiro {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id27}{1988}{]} )

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/trees:group__struct__utils__tree_1ga8666a10982a4f7a26892066ff07b4b48}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_STRUCTURE\_TREE\_SHAPIRO\_EXT}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  (extended) Coarse Grained representation of a secondary structure   (same as   Shapiro {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id27}{1988}{]} , but external nodes denoted as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E}} )

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/trees:group__struct__utils__tree_1ga91f2e3a3a502d5445fd7fe5983a5fe92}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_STRUCTURE\_TREE\_SHAPIRO\_WEIGHT}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  (weighted) Coarse Grained representation of a secondary structure   (same as {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/trees:group__struct__utils__tree_1ga8666a10982a4f7a26892066ff07b4b48}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_STRUCTURE\_TREE\_SHAPIRO\_EXT}}}} but with additional weights for number of unpaired nucleotides in loop, and number of pairs in stems)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/trees:group__struct__utils__tree_1gab3b65489d1322da65d3a3e53242307ef}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_STRUCTURE\_TREE\_EXPANDED}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Expanded Tree representation of a secondary structure.  

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{sphinxseealso}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000175}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is available as an overloaded method \sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/deprecated:group__struct__utils__deprecated_1ga6ebbcd29a754f0e4f1a66d1fd84184db}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{bp\_distance()}}}}}. Note that the SWIG wrapper takes two structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation and converts them into pair tables using {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/pairtable:group__struct__utils__pair__table_1ga792503f8b2c6783248e5c8b3d56e9148}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_ptable\_from\_string()}}}}. Print a secondary structure as connect table. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Connect table file format looks like this: 
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{l+m+mi}{300}  \PYG{n}{ENERGY} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{7.0}  \PYG{n}{example}
\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1} \PYG{n}{G}       \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}    \PYG{l+m+mi}{2}   \PYG{l+m+mi}{22}    \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{l+m+mi}{2} \PYG{n}{G}       \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}    \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}   \PYG{l+m+mi}{21}    \PYG{l+m+mi}{2}
\PYG{o}{*}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
 where the headerline is followed by 6 columns with:\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\alph}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Base number: index n

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Base (A, C, G, T, U, X)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Index n\sphinxhyphen{}1 (0 if first nucleotide)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Index n+1 (0 if last nucleotide)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Number of the base to which n is paired. No pairing is indicated by 0 (zero).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Natural numbering.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{seq}} \textendash{} The RNA sequence 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{db}} \textendash{} The structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket format 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{energy}} \textendash{} The free energy of the structure 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{identifier}} \textendash{} An optional identifier for the sequence 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{file}} \textendash{} The file handle used to print to (print defaults to ‘stdout’ if(file == NULL) ) 

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigstartmultiline
\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats:group__file__formats_1ga8cfb7e271efc9e1f34640acb85475639}}\DUrole{kt}{unsigned}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_file\_fasta\_read\_record}}}}{\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{header}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{sequence}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{rest}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{n}{FILE}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{file}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{unsigned}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{options}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/io/file\_formats.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Get a (fasta) data set from a file or stdin. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function may be used to obtain complete datasets from a filehandle or stdin. A dataset is always defined to contain at least a sequence. If data starts with a fasta header, i.e. a line like 
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{some} \PYG{n}{header} \PYG{n}{info}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
 then {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats:group__file__formats_1ga8cfb7e271efc9e1f34640acb85475639}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_file\_fasta\_read\_record()}}}} will assume that the sequence that follows the header may span over several lines. To disable this behavior and to assign a single line to the argument ‘sequence’ one can pass {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga0de536599b881c787b0943a2671da476}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_NO\_SPAN}}}} in the ‘options’ argument. If no fasta header is read in the beginning of a data block, a sequence must not span over multiple lines!

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unless the options {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga0f6311f11bed1842e3a527ab27b294c6}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_NOSKIP\_COMMENTS}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1gab4db885222b3b69608310d7c7e63e286}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_NOSKIP\_BLANK\_LINES}}}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
are passed, a sequence may be interrupted by lines starting with a comment character or empty lines.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A sequence is regarded as completely read if it was either assumed to not span over multiple lines, a secondary structure or structure constraint follows the sequence on the next line, or a new header marks the beginning of a new sequence…


\sphinxAtStartPar
All lines following the sequence (this includes comments) that do not initiate a new dataset according to the above definition are available through the line\sphinxhyphen{}array ‘rest’. Here one can usually find the structure constraint or other information belonging to the current dataset. Filling of ‘rest’ may be prevented by passing {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga7a2e8c50a0c7ce82e60da1016e1367fd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_NO\_REST}}}} to the options argument.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The main purpose of this function is to be able to easily parse blocks of data in the header of a loop where all calculations for the appropriate data is done inside the loop. The loop may be then left on certain return values, e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{rest}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{rest}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{!}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}file\PYGZus{}fasta\PYGZus{}read\PYGZus{}record}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{rest}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{VRNA\PYGZus{}INPUT\PYGZus{}ERROR}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{VRNA\PYGZus{}INPUT\PYGZus{}QUIT}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

As long as data is read from stdin (we are passing NULL as the file pointer), the id is printed if it is available for the current block of data. The sequence will be printed in any case and if some more lines belong to the current block of data each line will be printed as well.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function will exit any program with an error message if no sequence could be read!
