\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gad02d5d12bda54611c915a1019323b7be}}\DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_file\_msa\_read}}}}{\DUrole{k}{const}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{filename}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{names}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{aln}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{id}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{structure}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{unsigned}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{options}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/io/file\_formats\_msa.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Read a multiple sequence alignment from file. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function reads the (first) multiple sequence alignment from an input file. The read alignment is split into the sequence id/name part and the actual sequence information and stored in memory as arrays of ids/names and sequences. If the alignment file format allows for additional information, such as an ID of the entire alignment or consensus structure information, this data is retrieved as well and made available. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter allows to specify the set of alignment file formats that should be used to retrieve the data. If 0 is passed as option, the list of alignment file formats defaults to {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga4acc255373831856a8417b68de8a94c0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_DEFAULT}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, the list of parsable multiple sequence alignment file formats consists of:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}clustal

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}stockholm

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}fasta

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}maf

\end{itemize}


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000097}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the target scripting language, only the first and last argument, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{filename}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}}, are passed to the corresponding function. The other arguments, which serve as output in the C\sphinxhyphen{}library, are available as additional return values. This function exists as an overloaded version where the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter may be omitted! In that case, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter defaults to {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga62be992445cd8ab2ad7a8fded944338b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_STOCKHOLM}}}}. See, e.g.   {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.file_msa_read}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.file\_msa\_read()}}}}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}  and   {\hyperref[\detokenize{examples/python:parsing-alignments}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Parsing Alignments}}}}  in the Python examples. 

\end{fulllineitems}



\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gad4203a438622b2df7bc2f16578d54799}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_file\_msa\_read\_record()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga79a23de2c7249f2cccd762e475c81859}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_CLUSTAL}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga62be992445cd8ab2ad7a8fded944338b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_STOCKHOLM}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gacf6274a2c825f34e4131404665b00604}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_FASTA}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gab3186d774c01570d2a47d0308eec4927}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_MAF}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga4acc255373831856a8417b68de8a94c0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_DEFAULT}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga229fb3778ecabea4782902b69fa48fd1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_NOCHECK}}}}


\end{sphinxseealso}



\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After successfully reading an alignment, this function performs a validation of the data that includes uniqueness of the sequence identifiers, and equal sequence lengths. This check can be deactivated by passing {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga229fb3778ecabea4782902b69fa48fd1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_NOCHECK}}}} in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
parameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is the users responsibility to free any memory occupied by the output arguments
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{names}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{aln}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{id}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{structure}} after calling this function. The function automatically sets the latter two arguments to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} in case no corresponding data could be retrieved from the input alignment.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{filename}} \textendash{} The name of input file that contains the alignment 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{names}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where sequence identifiers should be written to 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{aln}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where aligned sequences should be written to 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{id}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where the alignment ID should be written to (Maybe NULL) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{structure}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where consensus structure information should be written to (Maybe NULL) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{options}} \textendash{} Options to manipulate the behavior of this function 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of sequences in the alignment, or \sphinxhyphen{}1 if no alignment record could be found

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/io/file\_formats\_msa.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Read a multiple sequence alignment from file handle. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gad02d5d12bda54611c915a1019323b7be}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_file\_msa\_read()}}}}, this function reads a multiple sequence alignment from an input file handle. Since using a file handle, this function is not limited to the first alignment record, but allows for looping over all alignments within the input.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The read alignment is split into the sequence id/name part and the actual sequence information and stored in memory as arrays of ids/names and sequences. If the alignment file format allows for additional information, such as an ID of the entire alignment or consensus structure information, this data is retrieved as well and made available. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter allows to specify the alignment file format used to retrieve the data. A single format must be specified here, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gade4fa8136ebb2d0f7eb3f8b59a8658e3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_file\_msa\_detect\_format()}}}} for helping to determine the correct MSA file format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, the list of parsable multiple sequence alignment file formats consists of:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}clustal

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}stockholm

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}fasta

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msa\sphinxhyphen{}formats\sphinxhyphen{}maf

\end{itemize}


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000098}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the target scripting language, only the first and last argument, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}}, are passed to the corresponding function. The other arguments, which serve as output in the C\sphinxhyphen{}library, are available as additional return values. This function exists as an overloaded version where the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter may be omitted! In that case, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter defaults to {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga62be992445cd8ab2ad7a8fded944338b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_STOCKHOLM}}}}. See, e.g.   {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.file_msa_read_record}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.file\_msa\_read\_record()}}}}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}  and   {\hyperref[\detokenize{examples/python:parsing-alignments}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Parsing Alignments}}}}  in the Python examples. 

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gad02d5d12bda54611c915a1019323b7be}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_file\_msa\_read()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gade4fa8136ebb2d0f7eb3f8b59a8658e3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_file\_msa\_detect\_format()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga79a23de2c7249f2cccd762e475c81859}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_CLUSTAL}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga62be992445cd8ab2ad7a8fded944338b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_STOCKHOLM}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gacf6274a2c825f34e4131404665b00604}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_FASTA}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gab3186d774c01570d2a47d0308eec4927}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_MAF}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga4acc255373831856a8417b68de8a94c0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_DEFAULT}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga229fb3778ecabea4782902b69fa48fd1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_NOCHECK}}}}


\end{sphinxseealso}



\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After successfully reading an alignment, this function performs a validation of the data that includes uniqueness of the sequence identifiers, and equal sequence lengths. This check can be deactivated by passing {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga229fb3778ecabea4782902b69fa48fd1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_NOCHECK}}}} in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
parameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is the users responsibility to free any memory occupied by the output arguments
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{names}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{aln}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{id}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{structure}} after calling this function. The function automatically sets the latter two arguments to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} in case no corresponding data could be retrieved from the input alignment.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{fp}} \textendash{} The file pointer the data will be retrieved from 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{names}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where sequence identifiers should be written to 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{aln}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where aligned sequences should be written to 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{id}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where the alignment ID should be written to (Maybe NULL) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{structure}} \textendash{} An address to the pointer where consensus structure information should be written to (Maybe NULL) 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{options}} \textendash{} Options to manipulate the behavior of this function 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of sequences in the alignment, or \sphinxhyphen{}1 if no alignment record could be found

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Detect the format of a multiple sequence alignment file. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function attempts to determine the format of a file that supposedly contains a multiple sequence alignment (MSA). This is useful in cases where a MSA file contains more than a single record and therefore {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1gad02d5d12bda54611c915a1019323b7be}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_file\_msa\_read()}}}} can not be applied, since it only retrieves the first. Here, one can try to guess the correct file format using this function and then loop over the file, record by record using one of the low\sphinxhyphen{}level record retrieval functions for the corresponding MSA file format.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000096}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function exists as an overloaded version where the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter may be omitted! In that case, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter defaults to {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/io/file_formats_msa:group__file__formats__msa_1ga4acc255373831856a8417b68de8a94c0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_FILE\_FORMAT\_MSA\_DEFAULT}}}}. See, e.g.   {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.file_msa_detect_format}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.file\_msa\_detect\_format()}}}}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}} . 

\end{fulllineitems}

\index{vrna\_filename\_sanitize (C function)@\spxentry{vrna\_filename\_sanitize}\spxextra{C function}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{utils/io:c.vrna_filename_sanitize}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigstartmultiline
\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{utils/io:group__file__utils_1ga906922daed59145d1fc5dffa1a1a0785}}\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_filename\_sanitize}}}}{\DUrole{k}{const}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{name}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{k}{const}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{replacement}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/io/utils.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sanitize a file name. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Returns a new file name where all invalid characters are substituted by a replacement character. If no replacement character is supplied, invalid characters are simply removed from the filename. File names may also never exceed a length of 255 characters. Longer file names will undergo a ‘smart’ truncation process, where the filenames suffix, i.e. everything after the last dot .’, is attempted to be kept intact. Hence, only the filename part before the suffix is reduced in such a way that the total filename complies to the length restriction of 255 characters. If no suffix is present or the suffix itself already exceeds the maximum length, the filename is simply truncated from the back of the string.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For now we consider the following characters invalid:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
backslash ‘’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
slash ‘/’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
question mark ‘?’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
percent sign ‘’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
asterisk ‘*’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
colon ‘:’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pipe symbol ‘|’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
double quote ‘”’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
triangular brackets ‘\textless{}’ and ‘\textgreater{}’

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar
Furthermore, the (resulting) file name must not be a reserved file name, such as:\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
’.’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
’..’

\end{itemize}


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function allocates a new block of memory for the sanitized string. It also may return (a) NULL if the input is pointing to NULL, or (b) an empty string if the input only consists of invalid characters which are simply removed!
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{name}} \textendash{} The input file name 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{replacement}} \textendash{} The replacement character, or NULL 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sanitized file name, or NULL 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function takes a secondary structure and computes X\sphinxhyphen{}Y coordinates for each nucleotide that then can be used to create a structure plot. The parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plot\_type}} is used to select the underlying layout algorithm. Currently, the following selections are provided:\begin{itemize}

{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1gae6d17b9f0a53cf5205a9181e0f8422e9}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PLOT\_TYPE\_SIMPLE}}}}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigstartmultiline
\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1ga47ff1fd92e9658361a758fdb03122911}}\DUrole{kt}{int}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_plot\_coords\_circular}}}}{\DUrole{k}{const}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{kt}{char}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{structure}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{x}\sphinxparamcomma \DUrole{kt}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{p}{*}\DUrole{n}{y}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/plotting/layouts.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute coordinates of nucleotides mapped in equal distancies onto a unit circle. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function basically is a wrapper to {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1ga2e2adbef0283a8ff2dfe5284eb1f4a6a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plot\_coords()}}}} that passes the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plot\_type}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1ga8c9eac631348da92136c8363ecdd9fb9}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PLOT\_TYPE\_CIRCULAR}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to draw nice arcs using quadratic bezier curves that connect base pairs one may calculate a second tangential point \(P^t\) in addition to the actual R$^{\text{2}}$ coordinates. the simplest way to do so may be to compute a radius scaling factor \(rs\) in the interval \([0,1]\) that weights the proportion of base pair span to the actual length of the sequence. This scaling factor can then be used to calculate the coordinates for \(P^t\), i.e.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} P^{t}_x[i] = X[i] * rs \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} P^{t}_y[i] = Y[i] * rs \end{split}
\end{equation*}.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1ga2e2adbef0283a8ff2dfe5284eb1f4a6a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plot\_coords()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1gaeec80faa235f3ca489bc5e50adc41460}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plot\_coords\_circular\_pt()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1gaea0dada4d0113d16d4890bc0937292e6}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plot\_coords\_simple()}}}}, vrna\_plot\_coords\_naview(), {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1ga195139110e2877b92c7f82d05b6dad19}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plot\_coords\_turtle()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/layouts:group__plot__layout__utils_1gafd49896df8780c9669125429bc0da9b3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plot\_coords\_puzzler()}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Produce an encapsulate PostScript (EPS) dot\sphinxhyphen{}plot from one or two lists of base pair probabilities. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function reads two vrna\_ep\_t lists \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{upper}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lower}} (e.g. base pair probabilities and a secondary structure) and produces an EPS “dot plot” with filename \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textquotesingle{}filename\textquotesingle{}}} where data from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{upper}} is placed in the upper\sphinxhyphen{}triangular and data from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lower}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
is placed in the lower triangular part of the matrix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For default output, provide the flag
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/probabilities:group__plot__probabilities_1gaa3a3d5cf87de5120a93eab3be788b6fb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PLOT\_PROBABILITIES\_DEFAULT}}}} as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} parameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{fulllineitems}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigline{{\hyperref[\detokenize{wrappers:wrappers_1_wrappers000165}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG Wrapper Notes:}}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is available as overloaded function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plot\_dp\_EPS()}} where the last three parameters may be omitted. The default values for these parameters are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lower}} = NULL, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{auxdata}} = NULL, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} = {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/plots/probabilities:group__plot__probabilities_1gaa3a3d5cf87de5120a93eab3be788b6fb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_PLOT\_PROBABILITIES\_DEFAULT}}}}. See, e.g.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.plot_dp_EPS}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.plot\_dp\_EPS()}}}}} in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}. 

\end{fulllineitems}

\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/plotting/probabilities.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Produce a postscript dot\sphinxhyphen{}plot from two pair lists. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function reads two plist structures (e.g. base pair probabilities and a secondary structure) as produced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global:group__part__func__global_1ga2d1b1c2e37abe57911ce647123c8ae06}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plist\_from\_probs()}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/struct/plist:group__struct__utils__plist_1ga6de9e912540e36b1e231a66f6d8319df}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_plist()}}}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and produces a postscript “dot plot” that is written to ‘filename’.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using base pair probabilities in the first and mfe structure in the second plist, the resulting “dot plot” represents each base pairing probability by a square of corresponding area in a upper triangle matrix. The lower part of the matrix contains the minimum free energy structure.


\sphinxAtStartPar

Calculate nucleotide coordinates for \sphinxstyleemphasis{Circular Plot}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to draw nice arcs using quadratic bezier curves that connect base pairs one may calculate a second tangential point \(P^t\) in addition to the actual R$^{\text{2}}$ coordinates. the simplest way to do so may be to compute a radius scaling factor \(rs\) in the interval \([0,1]\) that weights the proportion of base pair span to the actual length of the sequence. This scaling factor can then be used to calculate the coordinates for \(P^t\), i.e. \( P^{t}_x[i] = X[i] * rs\) and \(P^{t}_y[i] = Y[i] * rs\).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\item {}

\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{pair\_table}} \textendash{} The pair table of the secondary structure 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{x}} \textendash{} a pointer to an array with enough allocated space to hold the x coordinates 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{y}} \textendash{} a pointer to an array with enough allocated space to hold the y coordinates 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
length of sequence on success, 0 otherwise 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Produce a postscript dot\sphinxhyphen{}plot from two pair lists. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function reads two plist structures (e.g. base pair probabilities and a secondary structure) as produced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global_deprecated:group__part__func__global__deprecated_1ga1cc05aaa9b0e7df2d3887e98321c2030}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{assign\_plist\_from\_pr()}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{partfunc/global_deprecated:group__part__func__global__deprecated_1gab61df77cf7949cd516181fce0c3d7d78}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{assign\_plist\_from\_db()}}}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and produces a postscript “dot plot” that is written to ‘filename’.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using base pair probabilities in the first and mfe structure in the second plist, the resulting “dot plot” represents each base pairing probability by a square of corresponding area in a upper triangle matrix. The lower part of the matrix contains the minimum free energy structure.


\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Enumerate all necklaces with fixed content. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function implements \sphinxstyleemphasis{A fast algorithm to generate necklaces with fixed content} as published by   Sawada {[}\hyperlink{cite.bibliography:id36}{2003}{]} .

\sphinxAtStartPar
The function receives a list of counts (the elements on the necklace) for each type of object within a necklace. The list starts at index 0 and ends with an entry that has a count of 0. The algorithm then enumerates all non\sphinxhyphen{}cyclic permutations of the content, returned as a list of necklaces. This list, again, is zero\sphinxhyphen{}terminated, i.e. the last entry of the list is a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} pointer.

\sphinxAtStartPar

Determine the order of rotational symmetry for a dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given a (permutation of multiple) RNA strand(s) and a particular secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation, compute the degree of rotational symmetry. In case there is only a single linear RNA strand, the structure always has degree 1, as there are no rotational symmetries due to the direction of the nucleic acid sequence and the fixed positions of 5’ and 3’ ends. However, for circular RNAs, rotational symmetries might arise if the sequence consists of a concatenation of \(k\) identical subsequences.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a simplified version of {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/combinatorics:group__combinatorics__utils_1ga2a4227ebe28dbc7ad55444a3a1bf7119}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_rotational\_symmetry\_db\_pos()}}}} that may be useful if one is only interested in the degree of rotational symmetry but not the actual set of rotational symmetric strings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given a (permutation of multiple) RNA strand(s) and a particular secondary structure in dot\sphinxhyphen{}bracket notation, compute the degree of rotational symmetry. In case there is only a single linear RNA strand, the structure always has degree 1, as there are no rotational symmetries due to the direction of the nucleic acid sequence and the fixed positions of 5’ and 3’ ends. However, for circular RNAs, rotational symmetries might arise if the sequence consists of a concatenation of \(k\) identical subsequences.

The first element \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{positions}}{[}0{]} always contains a shift value of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}} representing the trivial rotation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Generate a sequence of Boustrophedon distributed numbers. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function generates a sequence of positive natural numbers within the interval \( [start, end] \) in a Boustrophedon fashion. That is, the numbers \( start, \ldots, end \) in the resulting list are alternating between left and right ends of the interval while progressing to the inside, i.e. the list consists of a sequence of natural numbers of the form:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} start, end, start + 1, end - 1, start + 2, end - 2, \ldots \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The resulting list is 1\sphinxhyphen{}based and contains the length of the sequence of numbers at it’s 0\sphinxhyphen{}th position.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Upon failure, the function returns \sphinxstylestrong{NULL}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function provides an easy interface to obtain a prefilled {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}} by passing a single sequence, or two contatenated sequences as input. For the latter, sequences need to be seperated by an ‘\&’ character like this: 
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{char} \PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{sequence} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{GGGG\PYGZam{}CCCC}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{md\_p}} can be used to specify the model details for successive computations based on the content of the generated {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}. Passing NULL will instruct the function to use default model details. The third parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{options}} may be used to specify dynamic programming (DP) matrix requirements.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Options}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gacea5b7ee6181c485f36e2afa0e9089e4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_DEFAULT}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Option flag to specify default settings/requirements.  

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gae63be9127fe7dcc1f9bb14f5bb1064ee}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_MFE}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Option flag to specify requirement of Minimum Free Energy (MFE) DP matrices and corresponding set of energy parameters.  

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gabfbadcddda3e74ce7f49035ef8f058f7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_PF}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Option flag to specify requirement of Partition Function (PF) DP matrices and corresponding set of Boltzmann factors.  

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga2b2a8009ccdccc3eb1571556261aee8e}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_WINDOW}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}  Option flag to specify requirement of DP matrices for local folding approaches.  

\end{itemize}


\sphinxAtStartPar
The above options may be OR\sphinxhyphen{}ed together.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you just need the folding compound serving as a container for your data, you can simply pass {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gacea5b7ee6181c485f36e2afa0e9089e4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_DEFAULT}}}} to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{option}} parameter. This creates a {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}} without DP matrices, thus saving memory. Subsequent calls of any structure prediction function will then take care of allocating the memory required for the DP matrices. If you only intend to evaluate structures instead of actually predicting them, you may use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga61469c423131552c8483229f8b6c7e0e}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_EVAL\_ONLY}}}} macro. This will seriously speedup the creation of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/dp\_matrices.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add Dynamic Programming (DP) matrices (allocate memory) 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function adds DP matrices of a specific type to the provided {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga1b0cef17fd40466cef5968eaeeff6166}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}, such that successive DP recursion can be applied. The function caller has to specify which type of DP matrix is requested, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/dp_matrices:group__dp__matrices_1ga6042ea1d58d01931e959791be6d89343}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mx\_type\_e}}}}, and what kind of recursive algorithm will be applied later on, using the parameters type, and options, respectively. For the latter, Minimum free energy (MFE), and Partition function (PF) computations are distinguished. A third option that may be passed is {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga8f681fa12b8d4b348bf58415fd1fc82f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_HYBRID}}}}, indicating that auxiliary DP arrays are required for RNA\sphinxhyphen{}RNA interaction prediction.

\sphinxAtStartPar


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
vrna\_mx\_mfe\_add(), vrna\_mx\_pf\_add(), {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gab89fe9844031711d42c70d1b9277c0d5}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gabbaffe56b1a37f6ed1a31e9e4f5613f1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_comparative()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga576a077b418a9c3650e06f8e5d296fc2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_fold\_compound\_free()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/dp_matrices:group__dp__matrices_1gab9d4eaceb36345b71d349b12787c5e0a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mx\_pf\_free()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/dp_matrices:group__dp__matrices_1gaf429b1838e68cb677db6aef7e8f0ffc8}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mx\_mfe\_free()}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/dp_matrices:group__dp__matrices_1ga6042ea1d58d01931e959791be6d89343}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_mx\_type\_e}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gae63be9127fe7dcc1f9bb14f5bb1064ee}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_MFE}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1gabfbadcddda3e74ce7f49035ef8f058f7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_PF}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga8f681fa12b8d4b348bf58415fd1fc82f}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_HYBRID}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:group__fold__compound_1ga61469c423131552c8483229f8b6c7e0e}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_OPTION\_EVAL\_ONLY}}}}

\subsubsection{Hash Tables}
\label{\detokenize{utils/datastructures/hash_tables:hash-tables}}\label{\detokenize{utils/datastructures/hash_tables::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Various implementations of hash table functions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Hash tables are common data structures that allow for fast random
access to the data that is stored within.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, we provide an abstract implementation of a hash table interface
and a concrete implementation for pairs of secondary structure and
corresponding free energy value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Initialize a heap data structure. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function initializes a heap data structure. The implementation is based on a \sphinxstyleemphasis{min\sphinxhyphen{}heap}, i.e. the minimal element is located at the root of the heap. However, by reversing the logic of the compare function, one can easily transform this into a \sphinxstyleemphasis{max\sphinxhyphen{}heap} implementation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Beside the regular operations on a heap data structure, we implement removal and update of arbitrary elements within the heap. For that purpose, however, one requires a reverse\sphinxhyphen{}index lookup system that, (i) for a given element stores the current position in the heap, and (ii) allows for fast lookup of an elements current position within the heap. The corresponding getter\sphinxhyphen{} and setter\sphinxhyphen{} functions may be provided through the arguments \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{get\_entry\_pos}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{set\_entry\_pos}}, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sometimes, it is difficult to simply compare two data structures without any context. Therefore, the compare function is provided with a user\sphinxhyphen{}defined data pointer that can hold any context required.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{Arrays}
\label{\detokenize{utils/datastructures/arrays:arrays}}\label{\detokenize{utils/datastructures/arrays::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Interface for an abstract implementation of an array data structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Arrays of a particular \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Type}} are defined and initialized using the following code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{Type}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or equivalently:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}make}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{Type}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dynamic arrays can be used like regular pointers, i.e. elements are simply
addressed using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{{[}{]}}} operator, e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{42}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/arrays:c.vrna_array_append}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_array\_append}}}}} macro, items can be safely appended and the
array will grow accordingly if required:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{item}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, memory occupied by an array must be released using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/arrays:c.vrna_array_free}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_array\_free}}}}}
macro:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}free}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/arrays:c.vrna_array_size}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_array\_size}}}}} macro to get the number of items stored in an array,
e.g. for looping over its elements:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{// define and initialize}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}make}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// append some items}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{42}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{23}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// loop over items and print}
\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{size\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}d}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// release memory of the array}
\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}array\PYGZus{}free}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{my\PYGZus{}array}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the hood, arrays are preceded by a header that actually stores the
number of items they contain and the capacity of elements they are able
to store.  The general ideas for this implementation are taken from
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/gingerBill/gb}{Ginger Bill’s C Helper Library} (public domain).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Flush the dynamic char * output stream. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function flushes the collected char * stream, either by writing to the attached file handle, or simply by writing to \sphinxstyleemphasis{stdout} if no file handle has been attached upon construction using {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/buffers:group__buffer__utils_1gadb2818f368e10a3b60a96bb3c80228d2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vrna\_cstr()}}}}.

\index{vrna\_C11\_features (C function)@\spxentry{vrna\_C11\_features}\spxextra{C function}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{utils/data_structures:c.vrna_C11_features}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigstartmultiline
\pysiglinewithargsret{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{utils/data_structures:group__data__structures_1ga21744ae2d6a17309f9327d3547cef0cb}}\DUrole{kt}{void}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{vrna\_C11\_features}}}}{\DUrole{kt}{void}}{}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}ViennaRNA/datastructures/basic.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dummy symbol to check whether the library was build using C11/C++11 features. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, several data structures of our new v3.0 API use C11/C++11 features, such as unnamed unions, unnamed structs. However, these features can be deactivated at compile time to allow building the library and executables with compilers that do not support these features.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, the problem arises that once our static library is compiled and a third\sphinxhyphen{}party application is supposed to link against it, it needs to know, at compile time, how to correctly address particular data structures. This is usually implicitely taken care of through the API exposed in our header files. Unfortunately, we had some preprocessor directives in our header files that changed the API depending on the capabilities of the compiler the third\sphinxhyphen{}party application is build with. This in turn prohibited the use of an RNAlib compiled without C11/C++11 support in a program that compiles/links with enabled C11/C++11 support and vice\sphinxhyphen{}versa.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Therefore, we introduce this dummy symbol which can be used to check, whether the static library was build with C11/C++11 features.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{\sphinxstylestrong{Since}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
v2.2.9 

\end{description}


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the symbol is present, the library was build with enabled C11/C++11 features support and no action is required. However, if the symbol is missing in RNAlib \textgreater{}= 2.2.9, programs that link to RNAlib must define a pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor identifier \sphinxstyleemphasis{VRNA\_DISABLE\_C11\_FEATURES} before including any ViennaRNA Package header file, for instance by adding a \sphinxstyleemphasis{CPPFLAG} 
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{CPPFLAGS}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{DVRNA\PYGZus{}DISABLE\PYGZus{}C11\PYGZus{}FEATURES}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{sphinxadmonition}

\end{fulllineitems}

Retrieve a line from ‘stdin’ savely while skipping comment characters and other features This function returns the type of input it has read if recognized. An option argument allows one to switch between different reading modes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently available options are:
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1gaf2062e0eeefffd3ed639af460b3d4fab}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_COMMENT}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga0f6311f11bed1842e3a527ab27b294c6}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_NOSKIP\_COMMENTS}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga086742158293217a46ae2f71bb296937}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_NO\_TRUNCATION}}}}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\sphinxAtStartPar

Possible return values are:{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga2f0d8069e93d3ac54d9320d6bdb8e7e7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_FASTA\_HEADER}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1gad403c9ea58f1836689404c2931419c8c}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_ERROR}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga8e3241b321c9c1a78a69e59e2e019a71}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_MISC}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils:group__utils_1ga72f3c6ca5c83d2b9baed2922d19c403d}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VRNA\_INPUT\_QUIT}}}}

\section{RNAlib API v3.0}
\label{\detokenize{vrna_3.0:rnalib-api-v3-0}}\label{\detokenize{vrna_3.0::doc}}

\subsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{vrna_3.0:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With version 2.2 we introduce the new API that will take over the old one
in the future version 3.0. By then, backwards compatibility will be broken, and
third party applications using RNAlib need to be ported. This switch of API became
necessary, since many new features found their way into the RNAlib where a balance
between threadsafety and easy\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}use library functions is hard or even impossible
to establish. Furthermore, many old functions of the library are present as
slightly modified copies of themself to provide a crude way to overload functions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Therefore, we introduce the new v3.0 API very early in our development stage
such that developers have enough time to migrate to the new functions and interfaces.
We also started to provide encapsulation of the RNAlib functions, data structures,
typedefs, and macros by prefixing them with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VRNA\_}} , respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Header files should also be included using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA/}} namespace, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}ViennaRNA/fold.h\PYGZgt{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
instead of just using

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}fold.h\PYGZgt{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
as is has been required for RNAlib 1.x and 2.x.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This eases the work for programmers of third party applications that would otherwise
need to put much effort into renaming functions and data types in their own
implementations if their names appear in our library. Since we still provide backward
compatibility up to the last version of RNAlib 2.x, this advantage may be fully
exploited only starting from v3.0 which will be released in the future. However, our
plan is to provide the possibility for an early switch\sphinxhyphen{}off mechanism of the backward
compatibility in one of our next releases of ViennaRNA Package 2.x.


\subsection{Major changes}
\label{\detokenize{vrna_3.0:major-changes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…


\subsection{Porting to the new API}
\label{\detokenize{vrna_3.0:porting-to-the-new-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

section.

\section{Callback Functions}
\label{\detokenize{callbacks:callback-functions}}\label{\detokenize{callbacks::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Many functions in \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} support so\sphinxhyphen{}called \sphinxstyleemphasis{callback mechanisms} to propagate
the computation results. In essence, this means that a user defines a function
that takes computation results as input and does whatever should be done with
these results. Then, this function is provided to our algorithms in \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}
such that they can call the function and provide corresponding data as soon
as it has been computed.


\subsection{Why Callbacks?}
\label{\detokenize{callbacks:why-callbacks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using callback mechanisms, our library enables users not only to retrieve computed
data without the need for parsing complicated data structures, but also allows one
to tweak our implementation to do additional tasks without the requirement of a
re\sphinxhyphen{}implementation of basic algorithms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Our implementation of the callback mechanisms always follows the same scheme:

\sphinxAtStartPar
The user …
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
… defines a function that complies with the interface we’ve defined, and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
… passes a pointer to said function to our implementations

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to the specific arguments of our callback interfaces, virtually all callbacks
receive an additional \sphinxstyleemphasis{pass\sphinxhyphen{}through\sphinxhyphen{}pointer} as their last argument. This enables one
to …
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
… encapsulate data, and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
… provide thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe operations,

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
since this pointer is simply passed through by our library functions. It may therefore hold
the address of an arbitrary, user\sphinxhyphen{}defined data structure.


\subsection{Scripting Language Support}
\label{\detokenize{callbacks:scripting-language-support}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Our callback mechanisms also work in a cross\sphinxhyphen{}language specific manner. This
means that users can write functions (or methods) in a scripting language,
such as Python, and use them as callbacks for our C\sphinxhyphen{}library. Our scripting
language interface will take care of transforming the relevant data structures
from the target language into C and vice\sphinxhyphen{}versa. Whenever our algorithms trigger
the callback, they will then be calling the actual scripting language function
and provide the corresponding data directly to them.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keep in mind that the translation between the scripting language and C
involves many extra function calls to prepare and evaluate the corresponding
data structures. This in turn impacts the runtime of our algorithms that
can be substantial. For instance providing callbacks for the hard\sphinxhyphen{} or
soft constraints framework from a scripting language can lead to a slow\sphinxhyphen{}down
of up to a factor of 10.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\chapter{SWIG Wrappers}
\label{\detokenize{wrappers:swig-wrappers}}\label{\detokenize{wrappers::doc}}

\section{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{wrappers:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For an easy integration into scripting languages, we provide an automatically
generated interface to the RNAlib C\sphinxhyphen{}library, generated with SWIG. Currently,
we support \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Perl 5}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Python}} as target languages.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{See also…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python API}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Function Renaming}
\label{\detokenize{wrappers:function-renaming}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To provide a namespace\sphinxhyphen{}like separation of function symbols from our C library and
third\sphinxhyphen{}party code, we use the prefix \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VRNA\_}} whenever possible. This,
however, is not necessary for the scripting language interface, as it uses the
separate namespace or package \sphinxtitleref{RNA} anyway. Consequently, symbols that appear to
have the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VRNA\_}} prefix in the C\sphinxhyphen{}library have the corresponding prefix
stripped away.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For instance, the C code

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}fold}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sequence}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{structure}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
translates to

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

in the Perl 5 interface, and

for Python. Note, that in this example we also make use of the possibilty to

Functions that are dedicated to work on specific data structures only,

\subsection{Global Variables}

For the Python interface(s) SWIG places global variables of the C\sphinxhyphen{}library
into an additional namespace \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cvar}}. For instance, changing the global temperature
variable thus becomes


\section{Object Oriented Interface}
\label{\detokenize{wrappers:object-oriented-interface}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For data structures, typedefs, and enumerations the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_}} prefixes are
dropped as well, together with their suffixes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_s}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_t}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_e}}, respectively.
Furthermore, data structures are usually transformed into classes and
relevant functions of the C\sphinxhyphen{}library are attached as methods.

\chapter{Python API}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:python-api}}\label{\detokenize{api_python::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Almost all symbols of the API available in our \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} C\sphinxhyphen{}library is wrapped for
use in Python using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{swig}}. That makes our fast and efficient algorithms and
tools available for third\sphinxhyphen{}party Python programs and scripting languages.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Our Python API is automatically generated and translated from our C\sphinxhyphen{}library documentation.
If you find anything problematic or want to to help us improve the documentation, do
not hesitate to contact us or make a PR at our \sphinxhref{https://github.com/ViennaRNA/ViennaRNA}{official github repository}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Installation}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:installation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Python interface is usually part of the installation of the ViennaRNA Package,
see also {\hyperref[\detokenize{install::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Installation}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{configuration:scripting-language-interfaces}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Scripting Language Interfaces}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If for any reason your installation does not provide our Python interface or
in cases where you don’t want to install the full ViennaRNA Package but \sphinxstyleemphasis{only}
the Python bindings to \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib}, you may also install them via Pythons \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }viennarna
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Usage}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:usage}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To use our Python bindings simply \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import}} the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA}} package
like

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{RNA}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{ViennaRNA}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA}} module that provides access to our \sphinxstyleemphasis{RNAlib} C\sphinxhyphen{}library can also be imported
directly using

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{RNA} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{RNA}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{ViennaRNA} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{RNA}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In previous release of the ViennaRNA Packge, only the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA}} package/module has
been available.
Since version 2.6.2 we maintain the \sphinxhref{https://pypi.org/project/ViennaRNA/}{ViennaRNA}
project at \sphinxurl{https://pypi.org}. The former maintainer additionally introduced the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ViennaRNA}} package which we intend to keep and extend in future releases.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Global Variables}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:global-variables}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the Python interface(s) SWIG places global variables of the C\sphinxhyphen{}library
into an additional namespace \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cvar}}. For instance, changing the global temperature
variable thus becomes

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{RNA}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{cvar}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{temperature} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{25}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\section{Pythonic interface}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:pythonic-interface}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since our library is written in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}} the functions we provide in our API might
seem awkward for users more familiar with Pythons object oriented fashion. Therefore,
we spend some effort on creating a more \sphinxstyleemphasis{pythonic} interface here. In particular, we
tried to group together particular data structures and functions operating on them to
derive classes and objects with corresponding methods attached.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you browse through our {\hyperref[\detokenize{api::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{reference manual}}}}, many C\sphinxhyphen{}functions have additional
\sphinxstyleemphasis{SWIG Wrapper Notes} in their description. These descriptions should give an idea how
the function is available in the Python interface. Usually, our \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}} functions,
data structures, typedefs, and enumerations use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_}} prefixes and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_s}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_t}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_e}} suffixes. Those decorators are useful in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}} but of less use in the
context of Python packages or modules. Therefore, these prefixes and suffixes are
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dropped} from the Python interface.


\subsection{Object orientation}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:object-orientation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider the C\sphinxhyphen{}function {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_fold\_compound()}}}}}. This creates a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}} data structure that is then passed around to various
functions, e.g. to {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:c.vrna_mfe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_mfe()}}}}} to compute the {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{MFE structure}}}}.
A corresponding C\sphinxhyphen{}code may look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}stdio.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}stdlib.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}string.h\PYGZgt{}}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}ViennaRNA/utils/basic.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}ViennaRNA/fold\PYGZus{}compound.h\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZlt{}ViennaRNA/mfe.h\PYGZgt{}}

\PYG{k+kt}{int}
\PYG{n+nf}{main}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{argc}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{argv}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{ss}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{float}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}fold\PYGZus{}compound\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{AGACGACAAGGUUGAAUCGCACCCACAGUCUAUGAGUCGGUG}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{ss}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}alloc}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{sizeof}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{strlen}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}fold\PYGZus{}compound}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{VRNA\PYGZus{}OPTION\PYGZus{}DEFAULT}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vrna\PYGZus{}mfe}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ss}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}s (\PYGZpc{}6.2f)}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ss}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{EXIT\PYGZus{}SUCCESS}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In our Python interface, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound_t}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_fold\_compound\_t}}}}} data structure becomes the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.fold_compound}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.fold\_compound}}}}} class, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{utils/datastructures/fold_compound:c.vrna_fold_compound}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_fold\_compound()}}}}} becomes one of
its constructors and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:c.vrna_mfe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_mfe()}}}}} function becomes the method
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.fold_compound.mfe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.fold\_compound.mfe()}}}}}. So, the Python code would probably translate
to something like

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{RNA}

\PYG{n}{seq} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{AGACGACAAGGUUGAAUCGCACCCACAGUCUAUGAGUCGGUG}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n}{fc}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{RNA}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{fold\PYGZus{}compound}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{ss}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{fc}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{seq}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{ss}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ (}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{mfe}\PYG{l+s+si}{:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{6.2f}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{)}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The C\sphinxhyphen{}function {\hyperref[\detokenize{mfe/global:c.vrna_mfe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vrna\_mfe()}}}}} actually returns two values, the MFE in units
of \(\text{kcal} \cdot \text{mol}^{-1}\) and the corresponding MFE structure.
The latter is written to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ss}} pointer. This is necessary since \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}} functions
can at most return one single value. In Python, function and methods may return
arbitrarily many values instead, and in addition, passing parameters to a function
or method such that it changes its content is generally discouraged. Therefore,
our functions that return values through function parameters usually return them
\sphinxstyleemphasis{regularly} in the Python interface.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Lists and Tuples}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:lists-and-tuples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
C\sphinxhyphen{}functions in our API that return or receive list\sphinxhyphen{}like data usually utilize \sphinxstyleemphasis{pointers}.
Since there are no such things in Python, they would be wrapped as particular kind of
objects that would then be tedious to work with. For the Python interface, we therefore
tried to wrap the majority of these instances to \sphinxstyleemphasis{native} Python types, such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tuple}}. Therefore, one can usually pass a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list}} to a function that uses pointers
to array in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}}, and expect to receive a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tuple}} from functions that return
pointers to arrays.


\section{Energy Parameters}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:energy-parameters}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy parameters are compiled into our library, so there is usually no necessity
to load them from a file. All parameter files shipped with the ViennaRNA Package
can be loaded by simply calling any of the dedicated functions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.params_load_RNA_Turner2004}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.params\_load\_RNA\_Turner2004()}}}}} (default RNA parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.params_load_DNA_Mathews2004}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.params\_load\_DNA\_Mathews2004()}}}}} (default DNA parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.params_load_DNA_Mathews1999}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.params\_load\_DNA\_Mathews1999()}}}}} (old DNA parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.params_load_RNA_Turner1999}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.params\_load\_RNA\_Turner1999()}}}}} (old RNA parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.params_load_RNA_Andronescu2007}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.params\_load\_RNA\_Andronescu2007()}}}}} (trained RNA parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.params_load_RNA_Langdon2018}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.params\_load\_RNA\_Langdon2018()}}}}} (trained RNA parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.params_load_RNA_misc_special_hairpins}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.params\_load\_RNA\_misc\_special\_hairpins()}}}}} (special hairpin loop parameters)

\end{itemize}


\section{Examples}

\section{The \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{RNA}} Python module}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:module-RNA}}\label{\detokenize{api_python:the-rna-python-module}}\index{module@\spxentry{module}!RNA@\spxentry{RNA}}\index{RNA@\spxentry{RNA}!module@\spxentry{module}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A library for the prediction and comparison of RNA secondary structures.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Amongst other things, our implementations allow you to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
predict minimum free energy secondary structures

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
calculate the partition function for the ensemble of structures

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute various equilibrium probabilities

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
calculate suboptimal structures in a given energy range

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute local structures in long sequences

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
predict consensus secondary structures from a multiple sequence alignment

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
predict melting curves

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
search for sequences folding into a given structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compare two secondary structures

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
predict interactions between multiple RNA molecules

\end{itemize}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{api_python:RNA.E_Hairpin}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{E\_Hairpin}}}{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{size}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{type}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{si1}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{sj1}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{string}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{P}}}{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the Energy of a hairpin\sphinxhyphen{}loop.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To evaluate the free energy of a hairpin\sphinxhyphen{}loop, several parameters have to be known. A general
hairpin\sphinxhyphen{}loop has this structure:
\begin{quote}
\begin{quote}
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
a3 a4
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
a2     a5
a1     a6
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
X \sphinxhyphen{} Y
|   |
5’  3’
\end{quote}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where X\sphinxhyphen{}Y marks the closing pair {[}e.g. a \sphinxstylestrong{(G,C)} pair{]}. The length of this loop is 6 as there are
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
six unpaired nucleotides (a1\sphinxhyphen{}a6) enclosed by (X,Y). The 5’ mismatching nucleotide is a1 while the 3’
mismatch is a6. The nucleotide sequence of this loop is “a1.a2.a3.a4.a5.a6”
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{size}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The size of the loop (number of unpaired nucleotides)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{type}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The pair type of the base pair closing the hairpin

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{si1}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The 5’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatching nucleotide

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sj1}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The 3’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatching nucleotide

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{string}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{string}}) \textendash{} The sequence of the loop (May be \sphinxtitleref{NULL}, otherwise mst be at least \(size + 2\) long)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{P}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.param() *}}) \textendash{} The datastructure containing scaled energy parameters

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Free energy of the Hairpin\sphinxhyphen{}loop in dcal/mol

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Not (really) thread safe! A threadsafe implementation will replace this function in a future
release!
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy evaluation may change due to updates in global variable “tetra\_loop”
\end{quote}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scale\_parameters}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_python:RNA.param}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.param}}}}}


\end{sphinxseealso}


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter sequence should contain the sequence of the loop in capital letters of the nucleic
acid alphabet if the loop size is below 7. This is useful for unusually stable tri\sphinxhyphen{}, tetra\sphinxhyphen{} and
hexa\sphinxhyphen{}loops which are treated differently (based on experimental data) if they are tabulated.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\end{fulllineitems}

\subsection{Compute the Energy of an interior\sphinxhyphen{}loop}
\label{\detokenize{api_python:compute-the-energy-of-an-interior-loop}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function computes the free energy \(\Delta G\) of an interior\sphinxhyphen{}loop with the following
structure:
\begin{quote}
\begin{quote}
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
3’  5’
|   |
U \sphinxhyphen{} V
\end{quote}
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{a\_n       b\_1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
.        .
.        .
.        .

\sphinxlineitem{a\_1       b\_m}
\sphinxAtStartPar
X \sphinxhyphen{} Y
|   |
5’  3’

\end{description}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This general structure depicts an interior\sphinxhyphen{}loop that is closed by the base pair (X,Y). The enclosed
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
base pair is (V,U) which leaves the unpaired bases a\_1\sphinxhyphen{}a\_n and b\_1\sphinxhyphen{}b\_n that constitute the loop. In
this example, the length of the interior\sphinxhyphen{}loop is \((n+m)\) where n or m may be 0 resulting in a
bulge\sphinxhyphen{}loop or base pair stack. The mismatching nucleotides for the closing pair (X,Y) are:
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
5’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatch: a\_1
3’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatch: b\_m
and for the enclosed base pair (V,U):
5’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatch: b\_1
3’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatch: a\_n
\end{quote}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{param n1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The size of the ‘left’\sphinxhyphen{}loop (number of unpaired nucleotides)

\sphinxlineitem{type n1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param n2}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The size of the ‘right’\sphinxhyphen{}loop (number of unpaired nucleotides)

\sphinxlineitem{type n2}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair type of the base pair closing the interior loop

\sphinxlineitem{type type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param type\_2}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair type of the enclosed base pair

\sphinxlineitem{type type\_2}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param si1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The 5’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatching nucleotide of the closing pair

\sphinxlineitem{type si1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param sj1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The 3’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatching nucleotide of the closing pair

\sphinxlineitem{type sj1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param sp1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The 3’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatching nucleotide of the enclosed pair

\sphinxlineitem{type sp1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param sq1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The 5’\sphinxhyphen{}mismatching nucleotide of the enclosed pair

\sphinxlineitem{type sq1}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\sphinxlineitem{param P}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The datastructure containing scaled energy parameters

\sphinxlineitem{type P}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RNA.param() *}}

\sphinxlineitem{returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Free energy of the Interior\sphinxhyphen{}loop in dcal/mol

\sphinxlineitem{rtype}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{int}}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{sphinxseealso}


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
